We have observed a significant anisotropic cosmic ray pattern at extremely high energies, where an overall dipole moment is accompanied by quadrupole and higher-order components. Our findings show that the anisotropy's amplitude of this dipole moment increases substantially with energy, rising from approximately 12% of the total anisotropy at energies above 4 EeV to 25% at energies beyond 20 EeV. This discovery is made based on an enhanced data set of 8 years of observations from the Telescope Array. Our previous research revealed that the cosmic ray anisotropy's pattern changes from small-scale local features at lower energies to large-scale dipole patterns at higher energies. Now, with an expanded energy range, we have observed that the anisotropy's amplitude of the dipole component grows with energy, and this behavior can be explained by a specific theoretical model featuring highly anisotropic, light-particle neutrino interactions with cosmic rays at high altitudes. This model predicts that the cosmic ray anisotropy's pattern will continue to evolve as we explore higher energies. Our current measurement also constrains the density of these light particles, which could be either new neutrino species or other types of light particles, to be less than 10 times the cosmic ray density in the local universe. This research is also presented in the form of a theoretical anisotropy pattern that can be applied to any cosmic ray energy range. This study is part of the full anisotropy pattern analysis presented in another research paper. Heavy-ion collisions at the LHC allow us to study the properties of the quark-gluon plasma created in these events through observations of flow fluctuations and particle distributions. Recent findings from the ALICE experiment reveal that the plasma's fluctuations in charged particle densities influence the orientation of flow patterns, and these influences are more pronounced than expected in idealized models of hydrodynamic behavior. To better understand this phenomenon, we examine the interplay between initial conditions, hydrodynamic behavior, and particle distributions, and investigate how it affects the plasma's fluctuations in the ALICE experiment. By re-analyzing existing data and comparing it to theoretical simulations, we test the consistency of current understanding with experimental evidence. Furthermore, we explore the potential for discovering new information about the quark-gluon plasma's shear viscosity and its equation of state through more precise measurements of these phenomena. Existing data and theoretical models are found to be broadly in agreement, but there is also evidence that more viscous behavior may exist at lower transverse momenta, and new analyses are expected from ongoing and future heavy-ion collision experiments at the LHC.

We introduce a four-valued logic framework to address consistent query answering in databases with conflicts. This approach is based on a propositional logic where values represent consistency status, and we use the 4-valued Kleene algebra to facilitate reasoning. We demonstrate the utility of this framework by developing methods for resolving query answering, specifically inconsistent query answering and approximate query answering. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be viewed as a four-valued extension of existing methods for resolving approximate query answering. Additionally, we provide a data exchange perspective on our approach, highlighting how our methods for resolving conflicts are analogous to techniques used in data exchange. This includes specific cases such as data exchange with integrity constraints and peer-to-peer systems. Our approach also encompasses existing methods for approximate query answering, including an extension of our four-valued approach to a two-valued setting using truth tables. This extended version has implications for the study of existing methods and their limitations. Notably, it reveals that some methods are not as robust as others in handling conflicts. This is reflected in our characterization of a class of methods that are conflict-robust and provide guidelines for developing such methods. This includes a proposed method that is particularly efficient and straightforward. Nonlinear and time-varying components in data patterns pose significant challenges for forecasting methods relying on linear and stationary models assumptions. To address these challenges, a novel Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model has been developed, characterized by nonstationarity and nonlinear dynamics. This dynamic model leverages a Bayesian approach within an Expectation-Maximization algorithm framework to facilitate parameter estimation and forecasting. The TV-PARX model's effectiveness is demonstrated through applications to both synthetic and real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over competing methods. Although computationally intensive, the model shows promise for handling complex time series data. As part of the study, a Time-Varying Vector AutoRegressive model was also developed as a special case of TV-PARX, showcasing the model's versatility. As future work, the study suggests exploring extensions to the model, including levers of nonlinearity and structural changes, as well as a Bayesian empirical Bayes approach to reduce computational requirements. As a supplementary contribution, the study provides a Time-Varying Vector AutoRegressive model, a special case of TV-PARX, which can be employed for forecasting purposes. Learning complex manipulation tasks from a small number of demonstrations is a challenging problem that limits the applications of our approach. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel neural descriptor field framework, which represents a task as a set of probability distributions related to observed and manipulated features. By analyzing the distributions' locations, shapes, and sizes, our method learns manipulation policies that generalize to new situations. We demonstrate our approach's effectiveness by teaching a robot to arrange blocks in specific patterns and to assemble objects from a pile of parts. Our results show that our method can succeed with as few as five demonstrations, outperforming a comparison reinforcement learning approach by a significant margin. Furthermore, our method can transfer knowledge to a robot with a different sensory setup, enabling it to adapt to new environments with minimal training. Our code is available at https://github.com/stevenlho/ndf.

We derive a performance metric for the approximate message passing algorithm in the $	ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem by examining the convergence of a simplified version of the algorithm, known as the Bethe approximate message passing algorithm. This metric is linked to the average Hamming distance between the received signal and the estimated synchronized vector. Specifically, we find that the algorithm converges to either a fixed point representing successful synchronization or an unstable state if the average Hamming distance exceeds a threshold, which is directly related to $N^{-1}$ and the spectral norm of the noise matrix $W$. This result is analogous to the threshold function predicted by statistical physics theories. Moreover, we show that the algorithm's performance is determined by the largest eigenvalue of the dual covariance matrix, which is analogous to the Pareto frontier in multi-objective optimization. This finding provides a geometric explanation for the performance threshold and allows us to identify the optimal regularization matrix for improving the algorithm's success rate without compromising the quality of synchronized vectors. We've developed a method for calculating the vertical aerosol optical depth without the need for absolute calibration, and it can be applied to wide-field photometry from various satellites. This approach uses color information from certain sky conditions, as it was discovered that depth remains relatively stable across different cloud conditions and time. By taking into account the scattering properties of aerosols and comparing the observed brightness at different wavelengths, we found that the ratio of $1064nm$ to $865nm$ optical depths is nearly constant at approximately $1.37$. This value is consistent with theoretical estimates and allows us to determine the vertical aerosol optical depth at $550nm$ with an estimated error of $0.05$. We've applied this technique to 17 years of data from the GOES-8 satellite at two locations, resulting in aerosol depth maps for the southeastern United States and the Amazon region. These maps reveal distinct seasonal patterns of aerosol depth in both regions. We've also compared our findings to ground-based measurements from AERONET in the southeastern United States, finding a positive correlation between them. Furthermore, we've used the developed technique to retrieve aerosol depth maps from the GOES-8 and GOES-10 satellites over the Amazon region spanning 17 years, and these maps show a strong annual cycle of aerosol depth. This technique offers a practical solution for deriving aerosol depth from existing geostationary satellites with wide-field photometry capabilities. Given the long duration of data from these satellites, this technique can be used to study aerosol depth patterns over large regions and long periods of time. We've made the developed algorithm available online for easy use. We believe this technique can be adapted for other satellites with similar wide-field photometry capabilities. We've provided the pseudocode of the algorithm developed for easy understanding and replication. We've also included a note on the limitations of the developed technique, specifically the difficulty in distinguishing between aerosol and cloud depth, and the potential for the technique to be biased by changes in surface reflectance. We suggest that future research should focus on addressing these limitations. We introduce Object Pose Forest (OPF), a novel approach for estimating object poses in complex scenes. OPF employs a projection grouping technique that aligns projected 3D features with an image by treating the process as a subproblem of a minimum spanning tree construction, facilitated by a proposed efficient algorithm. This results in a robust pose estimation method capable of withstanding variations in viewpoint and lighting conditions. Unlike existing methods, OPF generates multiple pose hypotheses from a single depth map, eliminating the need for depth map aggregation techniques. Our proposed framework also enables the integration of multiple depth cues, including stereo and semantic segmentation, by modeling their uncertainties. Experimental evaluations using the BOP Challenge dataset reveal that OPF surpasses the performance of conventional methods and comparable baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness in estimating object poses from single-view images with accessible hardware. We introduce GLRAM, a Generalized Latent Relative Absolute Error Machine model, in an effort to enhance the performance of Graphical Lasso in multivariate regression networks. Our model integrates a non-linear, absolute error-based output function with a linear regression part, and applies Spirtz-Richardson prior distributions to encourage smoothness in the weights and biases of its components. The inclusion of latent variables within GLRAM allows for a more flexible representation of network relationships, and we develop a Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithm to solve the model's parameters and graph structure. Theoretical guarantees for the consistency of GLRAM's estimates under infinite data are also established. Experimental results demonstrate that GLRAM outperforms standard Graphical Lasso in both synthetic and real-world datasets, specifically in reconstructing the underlying graph structure of both small and large-scale networks. The code for this project can be found at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yu/GLRAM. 

Compare to the original GLM model, we find that GLRAM yields a more robust and generalizable method for inferring network structures from data. Unlike GLM, GLRAM does not require the assumption of Gaussian distribution in data, and its performance is shown to be superior in both sparse and dense network settings. Additionally, we find that the inclusion of a non-linear output function in GLRAM does not necessarily contribute to its performance improvement, implying that this component may be removed in favor of a linear output function in order to further enhance the model's interpretability. 

Our work also introduces a novel penalty term, referred to as the relative absolute error (RAE) term, which can be applied to the linear part of GLRAM in order to induce sparsity in the model's weights. We demonstrate that this term is equivalent to the Lasso penalty, and thus the model can be solved using an existing algorithm. Furthermore, we experiment with different types of prior distributions for the model's weights and biases, and find that the Spirtz-Richardson distribution yields the best results in terms of network reconstruction accuracy. 

In terms of algorithmic development, we find that the inclusion of the RAE term does not affect the block-coordinate descent algorithm for solving GLRAM, and thus existing solutions can be directly applied. We also establish the consistency of the estimated model parameters and network structure under infinite data.

The efficiency and precision of molecular dynamics simulations can be influenced by the choice of numerical integrator for the Newtonian equations of motion. In this study, we examine various numerical methods with different levels of complexity and accuracy, applied to a biomolecular system like the alanine dipeptide. We investigate six explicit integration schemes - Verlet, leapfrog, Euler, Heun, PMMP, and velocity Verlet - and two implicit methods - Newton-Krylov using MATSU and matrix-free GNUMEAU - on the alanine dipeptide at different temperatures. Our results show that higher-order schemes generally provide better energy conservation and structural fluctuations when compared to the Verlet algorithm. However, even the simpler Verlet algorithm yields acceptable results, especially when using short time steps. We also observe that the performance of the schemes is temperature-dependent and that the most efficient method varies with these conditions. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the Verlet algorithm is a straightforward and effective choice for molecular dynamics simulations. Our code is available online for further testing and development.

The surface seal phenomenon between a moving plate and a fluid-filled cavity has been studied both experimentally and computationally. A rectangular cavity with a sliding plate at one end was used in the experiments. High-speed imaging and pressure sensors were utilized to examine the pressure within the cavity and the plate's cavity interface during closure. Computational models were developed for both 2D and axisymmetric cavity geometries to compare with the experimental data. It was discovered that the pressure inside the cavity decreases more quickly as the plate's speed increases. Additionally, surface waves formed within the cavity during closure and were captured in both experimental and computational simulations. A computational study that altered the cavity's shape found that surface waves were less intense in axisymmetric geometries. A study on the surface seal's dynamics found that the pressure reduction inside the cavity accelerates as the plate's speed increases, and surface waves delay the plate's closure. As the plate's speed increases from 1 to 10 m/s, the pressure reduction inside the cavity was found to behave similarly to a pressure reduction caused by a moving wall in a computational study. Notably, surface waves were found to contribute significantly to the pressure reduction inside the cavity during closure. A study on the surface seal's dynamics found that surface waves delay the plate's closure by approximately 0.01 seconds when the plate is moving at 5 m/s. A computational study that simulated a moving wall found that the pressure reduction inside a cavity behaves similarly to the surface seal phenomenon as the plate's speed increases from 1 to 10 m/s. This suggests that surface waves generated during the closure of a moving wall can significantly delay the wall's closure by approximately 0.01 seconds when the wall is moving at 5 m/s. Cubanite, an oxidized mineral of ferric iron and potassium, has been studied using a combination of X-ray diffraction, electron energy loss spectroscopy, and density functional theory. The results reveal that cubanite exhibits charge ordering and a rigid band structure characteristic of its composition. This electronic arrangement explains the observed stability of the crystal lattice and the ferromagnetic ordering of the electrons. Furthermore, analysis of the band structure indicates that cubanite's electronic properties are intermediate between those of ilmenite and magnetite, and suggests that it may be possible to synthesize a similar material with a higher Curie temperature. Additionally, the study finds that cubanite's band structure is consistent with previous measurements of its electrical conductivity. 

Although cubanite is a naturally occurring mineral, its properties make it worth considering as a potential material for applications in spintronics and energy harvesting. This study also highlights the potential of advanced electron energy loss spectroscopy at high energy resolution and low temperatures, and provides a detailed description of the sample preparation required to study the properties of this material. 

This research was conducted at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility and the French National Center for Space Studies, with funding from the French National Research Agency and the French Ministry of Higher Education and Research. This work was also supported by the French-German beamtime program at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility. 

The samples used in this study were collected from a location in Iceland known for its geothermal activity, and were found to have undergone varying degrees of oxidation. The most fully oxidized sample was identified as cubanite, and was further characterized as having a tetragonal crystal structure with a lattice parameter of 5.93 angstroms. This is consistent with previous measurements of the same sample using X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy. 

The energy distribution of electron energy loss spectroscopies was analyzed using a combination of multiple scattering simulations and density functional theory. This allowed for the direct comparison of measured and calculated spectra, and enabled the extraction of precise information about the energy states of the electrons in cubanite. The results showed that cubanite has a rigid band structure characteristic of its composition, and that its energy states are consistent with those predicted by the density functional theory method known as the screened exchange plus U method. 

The energy loss near-edge spectroscopies were also compared to the band structure of ilmenite and magnetite, and it was found that cubanite's energy states are intermediate between these two materials.

Researchers who utilize quantum dots in semiconductor materials for quantum information processing face a significant challenge in accurately controlling the strength of coupling between the quantized acoustic cavity and quantum dots.  A novel experiment involving a quantum dot inside a coupled acoustic cavity demonstrates the impact of changing the frequency of a driving laser on the coupling properties.  By adjusting the laser frequency, the authors are able to deliberately shift the position of the quantum dot within the cavity and observe a change in the coupling strength.  This discovery allows for the precise adjustment of the cavity-dot coupling to either its minimum or maximum value by adjusting the laser frequency.  As a result, the authors are able to intentionally suppress unwanted Rabi oscillations between the quantum dot's energy levels and cavity modes, thereby significantly improving the measurement of cavity-mode absorption.  This breakthrough also enables the clear identification of the quantum state of the cavity, specifically the presence of a two-phonon state, which is a crucial milestone in developing quantum information technologies based on semiconductor materials. This discovery can be applied to various cavity-based quantum information platforms, including those utilizing quantum dots in nanowires and superconducting circuits. By applying various perturbations to the Hamiltonian, including on-site potentials, bond alternation, and asymmetry between sublattices, we observed the transition of the lattice from a trivial to a non-trivial topological state. These perturbations can be either commensurate or incommensurate, leading to different outcomes such as the emergence of multiple Weyl points, the collapse of Weyl points into a single Dirac point at the Brillouin zone center, or the formation of a trivial gap without edge states. Our findings suggest that the herringbone lattice can serve as a versatile platform for investigating different topological phases and their associated edge states. Additionally, we propose a possible realization of this lattice using ultracold atoms in an optical lattice. We have developed a comprehensive theoretical model to generate single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) via a beam splitter and a degenerate optical parametric amplifier, and have conducted simulations to compare the outcomes. Under ideal conditions, both methods are able to produce SPCCSs, however the success probabilities differ significantly. Using a beam splitter results in lower success probabilities, whereas the beam splitter's phase-dependent success probability pattern offers a potential application. The optical parametric amplifier, on the other hand, yields higher success probabilities but is more sensitive to its reflectivity and initial state of the light. The higher success probability of the optical parametric amplifier's SPCCSs makes the optical setup more appealing for creating SPCCSs, while the beam splitter setup may find use in specific scenarios. The theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations conducted using the QuTiP library. The results of these simulations align with the predictions made by the theoretical model. The generation of SPCCSs via a beam splitter has also been proposed as a possible mechanism for creating single-photon driven coherent states, which are a type of quantum state with a non-gaussian distribution of light, essential for enhancing the precision of optical metrology. The study of SPCCSs via a beam splitter or an optical parametric amplifier offers valuable insights into the creation of single-photon driven coherent states, and highlights the need for experimental verification of the predicted success probabilities and phase-dependent patterns of the generated SPCCSs. This framework provides a convenient representation of the Einstein equation in the Newman-Penrose formalism, facilitating solutions to the Einstein field equation, particularly for Kerr black hole metrics. As an example, we apply this method to derive the metric functions for Kerr black holes and compare our results with existing literature. Our approach offers a direct and efficient means of employing the Newman-Penrose formalism for solving Einstein's field equation, particularly in complex spacetime metrics. Our findings are also validated by a Mathematica code developed in conjunction with this research. Our code, along with the modified Newman-Penrose formalism, presents a valuable tool for computing solutions to Einstein's field equation in Kerr black hole metrics and related spacetimes. We've developed a new way to use approximate inference methods for representing polymers as monomers within a variational autoencoder framework. This representation allows for a polymer to be seen as a collection of smaller units, each consisting of a subsequence of the original monomer sequence. We've applied this approach to two tasks: a protein structure prediction subproblem that involves predicting local alpha-helix structures and a larger problem that requires predicting the overall 3D structure of a protein. Our method has shown improved results when compared to the standard variational autoencoder and achieves the best accuracy to date for a specific subproblem. Notably, this research has been integrated into the RoseTTAFold protein structure prediction algorithm, which ranks our method as one of the top performers in a benchmark against other state-of-the-art deep learning-based predictors. Our code is available online.

In this work, we develop a novel convolutional neural network model called Dilated Dense Attention Unet to accurately identify and outline esophageal tumors within endoscopic images. Our primary objective is to enhance image feature extraction by integrating both attention and sparse sampling techniques into the network's architecture. We achieve this through the incorporation of two distinct modules: a spatial attention mechanism to prioritize the most critical image details and a Dilated Dense Attention Unet main network utilizing attention and sparse sampling to further emphasize key areas. We put our model through rigorous testing on two publicly available datasets and the results demonstrate its superior tumor segmentation capabilities compared to other leading methods. Moreover, our model's efficiency is evident due to its minimal addition of parameters and computational requirements. Our team also conducted a detailed ablation study to evaluate the individual contributions of each network component and the effectiveness of different attention mechanism variations. Our model has been successfully applied in real-world scenarios and its code is available online for the benefit of the medical imaging community. 

The code for this project can be found at: https://github.com/zhengyuan888/DDAT-UNET-Segmentation. 

Highlighting key findings from our research:
- Our Dilated Dense Attention Unet model achieves outstanding performance in esophageal tumor segmentation tasks, surpassing the current state-of-the-art methods according to various evaluation metrics.
- Through ablation studies, we discovered that the integration of attention and sparse sampling techniques significantly enhances the model's performance and robustness.
- Our model exhibits superior performance when applied to other medical imaging segmentation tasks, including the segmentation of liver tumors from CT images and the segmentation of blood vessels from fundus images.
- We successfully applied our model to real-world esophageal tumor segmentation tasks and obtained promising results. 

Our research team believes that the novel architecture of our Dilated Dense Attention Unet model, combined with its efficiency and high performance, makes it an ideal choice for various medical imaging segmentation tasks and encourages further research into the integration of attention and sparse sampling techniques within convolutional neural networks.

In multilingual societies, effective information dissemination and consumption is crucial, and social media plays a significant role in this process. Social media platforms can be highly beneficial if they are accessible in multiple languages and provide relevant information to users. To achieve this, we need high-performance, multilingual natural language processing systems. To contribute to this goal, we focus on improving the performance of a crucial social media ranking system by developing a highly effective, multi-language neural model. Our primary objective is to enhance the ranking of posts based on their interestingness to users. To accomplish this, we created a rating prediction model that can handle multiple languages and produce highly accurate rankings. Our research involves two key components: a multilingual model that can rank posts based on their interestingness in any language, and a data collection process that gathers a large amount of high-quality post ratings in various languages. To train the model and gather more ratings, we designed a system that recruited university students in Malaysia to rate the interestingness of social media posts in three different languages. Our research resulted in a multilingual model that can rank posts in Malay, Chinese, and English, and a large dataset of rated posts in these same languages. Our findings demonstrate significant improvements in post ranking using a deep neural network model, and our approach provides a framework for collecting post ratings in multiple languages. To facilitate further research and development in this area, we are releasing our multilingual model and dataset of rated posts for free. Our hope is that this will contribute to various social media applications and services in multilingual societies. The rapid advancement of computer vision technology has led to a significant increase in visually impaired individuals who rely on image descriptions for navigation and understanding. Despite the progress made in generating image captions, the quality of these captions often falls short of human standards, necessitating more refined guidelines for machine-generated descriptions. This paper aims to address this challenge by developing a novel framework that utilizes a combination of natural language processing techniques and visual information to create detailed and accurate descriptions of everyday scenes. Our proposed framework, which incorporates a multi-task convolutional neural network and a generative adversarial model, demonstrates improved performance compared to existing methods, according to both automatic and human evaluation metrics. This research also explores the limitations of current image captioning datasets and highlights potential areas for future development. Our proposed framework is publicly accessible, providing a valuable resource for the visual language understanding community. Code is available at: \url{https://github.com/zhongyuyu1995/vl-descriptor}.

The growing physical and social segregation of communities, coupled with the homogenization of information platforms, has created an environment where the rapid dissemination of misinformation can occur within isolated social spheres. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in the United States, where demographic homogeneity is most pronounced. Our study examines the spread of fake news across geographically and socio-economically defined regions in the US, utilizing a combination of census data and Google's News Aggregation API to gather both the locations and topics of interest for a representative sample of Americans. We then employ a weighted random walk model to simulate the online spread of misinformation within these regions and find that the most segregated communities are more susceptible to the spread of false information about minority groups, while areas with greater social cohesion are more resistant to the spread of misinformation targeting their own demographic. Our findings are further supported by real-world data on the spread of conspiracy theories and vaccine misinformation. Our approach can be applied to understanding the online dissemination of various types of misinformation across different geographic and socio-economic boundaries. Our model's limitations and potential extensions are also discussed. Our research underscores the critical role of social cohesion in preventing the spread of misinformation within communities. To understand the underlying structure of semantic concepts in human speech during teaching tasks, it's essential to analyze the relationship between these concepts and various demonstration and instruction elements. Despite the complexity and open-ended nature of this task, a deep neural network can effectively identify key concepts in human speech. To explore the relationship between concepts and task variables, we employed a multimodal embedding method that integrates visual and auditory information from human actions and speech. In this approach, the network's concept embeddings are treated as semantic features, which are then analyzed using regularized linear models to study the relationship between concepts and variables such as demonstration type, audio instruction, subtasks, and errors. Our findings show that this method can capture distinct concept representations and explain the relationship between concepts and variables in our dataset. In particular, our results reveal that certain concept representations remain consistent across different demonstration types and that some concepts are associated with specific subtasks or errors. Our approach provides a versatile framework for investigating the relationship between semantic concepts and various factors in teaching tasks. To facilitate further research and applications, we have made our code and dataset publicly available. Our work has implications for areas like human-robot learning, where understanding the relationship between actions, speech, and environmental feedback is crucial for improving robot performance. Our findings and methodology can be extended to other human-robot interaction tasks, such as instruction following and feedback. Conversational system testing frameworks face numerous challenges in providing comprehensive automated tests, which can be attributed to the complex and dynamic nature of these systems. Our research addresses this issue by proposing an automated test generation method for API-based conversational systems using finite state machines as a framework. This approach differs from existing techniques by accounting for the unpredictability of user input and system responses, which we model as probabilistic transitions. We then develop an algorithm to identify testable system components and a subsequent test data generation method based on the Interaction Web Framework. Our approach enables the creation of automated tests that simulate user input and verify system output against expected behavior. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using a real-world example and evaluate its performance using existing testability metrics. Our approach and associated tools are available at https://github.com/ahmedeltamany/testable-api. This research focuses on examining various natural formulations for a range of integer and Boolean problems that can be solved using specific natural frameworks such as lattices, polymatroids, flow-cut, and bipartite cuts. We compare these formulations to their extended counterparts in terms of size, number of variables, and number of constraints. Our analysis reveals that some of these formulations have equivalent dimensions to their extended counterparts, indicating a special or "dual-blockade-free" property. We also propose an initial framework for categorizing these special cases based on their formulation dimensions. Furthermore, we explore the concept of "exotic-formulation dimension" as a measure of a problem's inherent complexity, and discuss the potential applications in solving and reconstructing exotic formulations. We also examine the relationship between this new measure and the more established "weak membership" property. Additionally, this study highlights several open problems and potential research directions in the field of integer programming. Some of these problems involve analyzing specific natural formulations, while others involve the relationship between the "exotic-formulation dimension" and other measures of a problem's complexity. This approach provides a new algorithm for solving the prize-collecting Steiner forest problem. A significant challenge in developing MRI analysis tools is addressing variability when combining different datasets for training and evaluation. This study investigates how combining datasets from different populations and with varying image quality affects the performance of deep learning models in analyzing MRI images. To examine this, a synthetic MRI dataset was created using 1000 brain MRI scans from healthy individuals and 2000 scans from individuals with Alzheimer's disease, with datasets separated into training, validation, and evaluation sets. Two models were developed: one analyzing MRI images based on their content and the other identifying features associated with Alzheimer's disease. When evaluating these models on unseen data, combining different population and image quality datasets was found to negatively impact performance. Specifically, increased variability in the training dataset led to decreased performance in both tasks, with the model distinguishing Alzheimer's disease features exhibiting a 12% reduction in accuracy after incorporating diverse population and image quality datasets in a large Alzheimer's disease study. Similarly, in a small Alzheimer's disease study, this model showed an 18% decrease in accuracy when combining datasets from different populations and with varying image quality. To mitigate this issue, the researchers proposed a new training method called domain-aware dropout that was found to significantly improve performance when combining diverse datasets, resulting in an 8% increase in accuracy when evaluating Alzheimer's disease features in a large Alzheimer's disease study and a 12% increase in a small Alzheimer's disease study. This method was further shown to improve performance in real-world Alzheimer's disease studies involving large and small datasets. This paper introduces a novel framework for solving network-based multi-agent optimization problems, which includes several significant applications such as load balancing, energy management, and transportation systems. Within this framework, optimization problems are reformulated as link-flow optimization problems that consider costs associated with links and nodes. We then develop a distributed algorithm to solve these problems, leveraging a primal-dual method and a gradient update based on local information. The algorithm's convergence properties are established, and we also explore two specific use cases: one for general costs and another for node-specific costs. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach through simulations involving a real transportation network. Our solution builds upon recent research by [D. Y. Liu, T. A. F. We introduce a decentralized decision-making model called Motivation Dynamics from a network perspective, expanding on previous single-agent theories. This multi-agent model assumes each individual's motivated action is influenced by the motivated actions of neighboring agents in their network, and it is formulated as a distributed system with observed and desired states. We prove that agents following this dynamic model and meeting certain connectivity requirements will reach a state of collective consensus, where the motivated action of each individual represents the average desired action of their community. As a specific application, we develop a decentralized strategy for agents to reach a common goal that is the average of their individual goals, given that the agents are positioned on a tree-like network. We demonstrate that this model's dynamics match those found in Motivation Dynamics, under the condition that the network structure satisfies a certain hierarchy. Furthermore, we show that this model's ability to achieve consensus is comparable to the ability of traditional centralized systems, under specific network configurations. Finally, we provide simulation results to illustrate the model's effectiveness in a linear network. This model's components can also be used in a broader context, representing a general framework for the dynamics of agents influenced by their social network and environment. This framework has implications for various social learning and diffusion phenomena, including but not limited to, the spread of ideas, cultural evolution, and epidemiology. To achieve this level of versatility, our framework employs a unique design with two key components: a Context-Agnostic Object Detection Network that serves as the foundation, and a Context-Specific Object Detection Network derived from it. To prevent overfitting, we implement a multi-task training approach that enables our model to capture general object detection knowledge and apply it across contexts. To evaluate our Context-Agnostic Object Detection framework, we conducted experiments on two challenging datasets, DeiT-50 and DeiT-T, and our results demonstrate that it is capable of adapting to new object detection tasks with a significant reduction in the required number of training samples. We introduce Incompatibility Markov Decision Processes (IMDPs), a framework that extends Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) to account for incompatibilities between actions in different states. IMDPs are then used to model a complex decision-making problem in kidney transplantation, specifically the challenge of making match acceptance decisions. In this application, incompatibilities represent the differing preferences of potential match acceptors, such as patients waiting for a kidney transplant. By analyzing the optimal policy for rejecting incompatible offers in the underlying MDP, we derive a more efficient algorithm for finding the optimal acceptance policy in the original problem. This algorithm consists of two parts: first, it identifies the most compatible offers in the underlying MDP; second, it applies a threshold-based dynamic programming approach to determine the acceptance threshold for each state in the original IMDP model. Notably, this algorithm allows us to bypass the computational challenges of solving multi-stage dynamic programming problems with general incompatibilities. As a result, we gain insights into the factors that influence the optimal acceptance policy, including the value function of the underlying MDP and the threshold levels for different states. We further validate our approach through numerical experiments and demonstrate its effectiveness in various scenarios. This paper examines the challenges that word2vec encounters when processing financial text, where antonyms like "profit" and "loss" are consistently represented as similar vectors. As a result, combinations of words like "profit margin" end up being inaccurately modeled as "vector sums with a zero middle part," undermining the predictive value of these models in tasks like stock price forecasting. To address this limitation, a modified word2vec algorithm is proposed that takes into account the inherent oppositeness of antonyms when learning embeddings, leading to more reliable models that better capture the semantic meaning of financial terms in complex equations and accurately represent antonyms as vector opposites. When put to use in estimating daily stock price fluctuations for Apple Inc., this new model shows noticeable performance improvements over traditional methods. Specifically, our research reveals that by accounting for antonym relationships, it's possible to extract more useful financial information from text, leading to a 20% boost in predictive accuracy when modeling Apple's stock price movements. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that this gain in accuracy is most pronounced in contexts with high levels of uncertainty, making it clear that the benefits of this approach are both robust and far-reaching. To facilitate further study and potential applications, the code and data used in this research are made publicly available. A key challenge in wideband waveforming lies in balancing data transmission rates across different frequencies and channels, particularly under dynamic and resource-constrained settings. This research focuses on finding optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput wideband waveforming strategies for single-user and multi-user DCS scenarios. Initially, we establish lower and upper bounds for the optimal fair-throughput in single-user DCS, extending previous results to include variable sampling rates. Next, we develop a discrete-state dynamic programming approach to determine the sum-throughput in single-user DCS, building on an algorithm that prioritizes channel allocation based on signal strength. Furthermore, we introduce a multi-user extension, incorporating user-specific priority channels and channel allocation strategies, and demonstrate the sum-throughput optimization algorithm's applicability to this expanded framework. Our research provides theoretical foundations for fair-throughput and sum-throughput waveforming strategies in various DCS settings, and offers practical channel allocation guidelines for dynamic and wideband waveforming. Experimental validation of our methods is conducted using real-world DCS data, and code is available online to facilitate further research and development. This work's results have been presented at the 2023 IEEE International Conference on Communications, Mobility and High Performance Networking. Our research extends previous fair-throughput waveforming studies, which were limited to narrowband settings, and offers a comprehensive framework for tackling the sampling and channel selection problems in dynamic and wideband scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyiwang/waveforming. A dimensionless, low-precision Navier-Stokes model is combined with a stochastic equation to capture the random fluctuations inherent in fluid flow. The Navier-Stokes component is solved using a high-performance, high-precision numerical method, while the stochastic component is solved using a fast, low-precision numerical method. The Navier-Stokes and stochastic components interact through a feedback loop that replicates branching behavior. We introduce a novel reinforcement learning framework that enables agents to swiftly discover and shun iteratively inferior actions, thereby achieving socially beneficial behavior in time, we demonstrate that it consistently produces superior outcomes to comparison methods, especially in scenarios with multiple players. Our approach, based on a dynamic action-value function, leverages action elimination knowledge and a two-player repeated game insights, and we prove that it converges to a socially optimal equilibrium, often surpassing existing benchmarks. Furthermore, our approach makes minimal assumptions about the environment, making it exceptionally versatile. We provide several compelling experimental examples to illustrate the efficacy of our method. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengwz/SAERL.

We've developed a probabilistic model to examine the dynamics of epidemics within complex networks that evolve over time. This model allows individual connections to change randomly, either permanently or temporarily, relative to a time horizon. We've determined the expected number of infected individuals at the end of the epidemic as either the minimum or the average of the minimum or average number of infected individuals in the temporary or permanent networks, respectively. Our findings show that the number of infected individuals at the end of the epidemic is non-decreasing as the size of the temporary networks is minimized or averaged, assuming these networks are edge-exchangeable. Furthermore, we have a formula to calculate the expected number of infected individuals in a specific dynamic network model, including one that mimics the behavior of a Yule process, in addition to providing conditions under which the minimum or average number of infected individuals remains unchanged over time. Our research also explores the application to a Yule process network, resulting in a formula that can be used in its own right. Our model can be applied to study the spread of diseases within dynamic networks that evolve according to a Yule process, no matter the tree structure. Our results demonstrate that the fraction of individuals infected at the end of the epidemic remains unchanged over time in such networks. Our study also offers a method for estimating the expected number of individuals infected at the end of the epidemic within a Yule process network, as well as providing an interpretation of this value as the proportion of the population that could become infected during an epidemic within the same time frame, conditional on a single individual being infected at the beginning. Our research was motivated by the analysis of mobile phone data from Rwanda, which revealed a unique pattern of dynamic network connections among individuals. Reinforcement learning using experience replay has experienced rapid development in recent years, and the variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework has been proposed to enhance policy gradient estimation by minimizing data waste caused by multiple uses of the same sample. Within this framework, the variance of the policy gradient estimator has been analyzed and found to be influenced by the variance of the gradient estimator and the difference in action probabilities. Based on this analysis, a new experience replay scheme has been designed to ensure that the variance of the policy gradient remains bounded, thereby improving the convergence rate to the optimal policy under linear function approximation. Furthermore, the proposed method has been applied to derive updated conditions for uniform stability and the growth condition, thereby broadening the applicability of existing policy gradient learning algorithms to linear MDPs. Numerical experiments have confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed experience replay scheme. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengxiaoyu1996/VRER. The research presented in this paper has been published in two separate articles: Xiaoyu Zheng, Zhiwei Tan, and Zhiyuan Liu, Variance Reduction Based Experience Replay for Policy Gradient Methods, Journal of Machine Learning Research, Vol. 20, 2020; Xiaoyu Zheng, Zhiwei Tan, and Zhiyuan Liu, Variance Reduction Based Experience Replay for Linear MDPs, Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, Vol. 63, 2021. In recent years, theory of mind has gained significance in the development of conversational AI, given its role in enabling machines to engage in meaningful dialogue that considers others' mental states and intentions. While initial studies focused on incorporating cognitive capabilities into dialog generation via neural networks, a more fundamental question remains unanswered: whether a better understanding of theory of mind through cognitive architectures can improve machine dialogue. To address this, we present a novel approach that leverages LSTMs in tandem with a cognitive architecture simulating theory of mind processes, and applies it to a generative dialogue task. Our findings, obtained through extensive experiments on a widely used dataset, indicate that this approach yields improved results when compared to various state-of-the-art baselines, and sheds new light on the relationship between theory of mind and generative dialogue. Furthermore, our research reveals the presence of an 'cognitive gap' that arises when integrating the architecture with deep learning models, and we propose a novel metric to evaluate the impact of theory of mind on machine dialogue. Our work paves the way for a deeper exploration of the relationship between theory of mind and machine learning through cognitive architectures, and provides a practical solution for developing more sophisticated conversational machines. We've developed MG-GLAM, a fast gravity library aimed at speeding up N-body simulations on supercomputers. Building on the success of GLAM, MG-GLAM employs a multigrid method to calculate the force interactions between particles, achieving a 2.5-fold boost in performance while using half the memory of its predecessor. By leveraging a combination of a hierarchical tree structure and multigrid, MG-GLAM excels in both short-range and long-range gravity simulations. In particular, it shows a 2.5 times increase in performance on a Cori HPC system, specifically on a Knights Landing architecture, and can handle up to 16 million particles on a single node with 64 GB of RAM. Furthermore, MG-GLAM's minimal memory requirements allow it to handle large-scale cosmological simulations on leading-edge high-performance computing platforms. As part of the evaluation process, we adapted the multigrid solver to adapt to various types of gravity laws, demonstrating its versatility. As a demonstration of MG-GLAM's capabilities, we conducted an N-body simulation of a Milky Way-sized galaxy with 13.75 billion particles on a single node of the Summit supercomputer within a 12-hour timeframe. As a result, MG-GLAM is now an integral part of the GADGET-4 code, used for a wide range of astrophysical applications. In its current form, MG-GLAM is available for download at https://www.mpa-garching.mpg.de/Code/GADGET-4.0. As the code continues to evolve, we invite feedback and suggestions from the community to further improve it. As a testament to MG-GLAM's performance, we also set a new record for the largest N-body simulation executed to date, as verified by the Guinness World Records. Notably, this achievement was recognized on November 29th, 2022. As of now, the record remains unbroken. As a side note, the record-breaking simulation was executed on the Summit supercomputer at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and it is worth highlighting that the code used for this record was an early version of MG-GLAM, prior to the introduction of the multigrid solver in the GLAM code. Nonetheless, this achievement remains a significant milestone in the history of N-body simulations. We introduce the chordal stretched Loewner equation, a natural extension of the standard chordal Loewner equation, and prove its equivalence to the chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution (CSE) with stretching parameter $\beta = 2$. The chordal stretched Loewner equation finds applications in describing the growth of CSE's "imaginary surfaces", specifically their complex time domains, and facilitates a stochastic interpretation of the CSE. Furthermore, we establish that the solution to the chordal stretched Loewner equation forms a Markov process, enabling us to derive boundary values of its solution and investigate its asymptotic behavior at its boundary. Along the way, we establish connections between the chordal stretched Loewner equation and the Schramm-Loewner evolution on the upper half-plane, and obtain bounds on the growth rates of its imaginary surfaces. These growth rate bounds have implications for the convergence of random maps under the combinatorial distance metric, and provide a criterion for the convergence to the Cardy's map in the thermodynamic limit. Finally, we prove that the solution to the chordal stretched Loewner equation retains its analyticity at the boundary if its initial condition does so, and that this analyticity can be characterized in terms of a certain growth condition on its imaginary surface. These findings collectively form the theoretical foundation for the study of random maps and their associated Schramm-Loewner evolutions in the thermodynamic limit. This work is relevant to ongoing research in the fields of stochastic partial differential equations, geometric probability, and statistical mechanics. A course on complex analysis and a basic understanding of stochastic processes are recommended prerequisites for understanding the material presented in this work. A more in-depth exploration of the topics covered can be found in the appendices. The main body of the text is divided into five sections. The first section introduces the chordal stretched Loewner equation and its standard Loewner chain interpretation. The second section delves into the relationship between the chordal stretched Loewner equation and the CSE. The third section examines the asymptotic behavior of the solution to the chordal stretched Loewner equation at its boundary. The fourth section explores connections between the chordal stretched Loewner equation and the Schramm-Loewner evolution on the upper half-plane. The fifth section presents applications of the chordal stretched Loewner equation to the study of random maps and their associated Schramm-Loewner evolutions. We've developed WorkingWiki, a customized wiki environment that streamlines the creation, editing, and management of complex documents and software projects. Built on top of a standard wiki platform, WorkingWiki enhances the typical wiki functionality by incorporating features that facilitate collaborative document development and source code management. These enhancements include a sophisticated version control system, the ability to create and edit structured documents, and tools for tracking and resolving issues. By leveraging the strengths of wikis and version control systems in tandem, WorkingWiki provides a flexible and efficient collaborative framework that can be applied to a broad spectrum of projects and document types. As a concrete demonstration of WorkingWiki's capabilities, we've used it to develop the MindTouch '09 tutorial series and the Darwin Information Typing Architecture, and have made the underlying code available online for community use and modification. Additionally, we're repurposing WorkingWiki as the foundation for the next iteration of MindTouch, a leading wiki-based knowledge management platform. Furthermore, we're exploring the potential of WorkingWiki as a pedagogical tool for teaching software development and documentation best practices. As an open-source project, WorkingWiki invites contributions from the community to enhance its features and broaden its applicability. To facilitate project participation, we're offering a $10,000 prize to encourage innovative submissions that demonstrate WorkingWiki's value in real-world software development and educational settings. These submissions can take various forms, including but not limited to, project case studies, educational curricula, and tool extensions. Notably, the MindTouch Corporation will be awarding a $10,000 cash prize to the individual or team that submits the most outstanding WorkingWiki-related project according to the criteria outlined on the project website. To be eligible for the prize, submissions must be received by October 31, 2009. The WorkingWiki project is hosted on Google Code at https://code.google.com/p/workingwiki/ where users can access the source code, project documentation, and community forums. The project's website at http://workingwiki.org/ provides additional information and resources. The underlying code for WorkingWiki is written in PHP, leveraging the MediaWiki framework, and employs MySQL as its database management system. The project's design emphasizes flexibility, extensibility, and ease of customization, and is intended to serve as a foundation for derivative projects. The WorkingWiki team encourages community involvement and invites project contributors to join the project's Google Group at https://groups.google.com/group/workingwiki-dev. The project's issue tracker is hosted on Google Code at https://code.google.com

This research develops a novel approach to analyzing turbulent reacting flows by combining a global DNS approach with a linearized combustion model, specifically the one-step irreversible Arrhenius reaction, and makes this analysis compatible with a linearized framework. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated through simulations of two distinct turbulent mixing layers with adiabatic and combustion scenarios. The findings of this study suggest that this model can serve as a starting point for more complex applications, including those with chemical equilibrium and heat release. The interconnection between neutrinos and dark matter of negligible mass, which oscillates at a similar frequency, could significantly impact early universe cosmology, particularly during the neutrino-dominated era. Depending on the strength of the interaction, this coupling may cause a shift from dark matter comprised of oscillating neutrinos to a system featuring a complex interplay between dark matter and neutrinos. In this scenario, a new component of hot dark matter emerges, whose influence on the standard cosmological model is then assessed. We examine the effects of this hot dark sector on the cosmic lepton asymmetry, the primordial abundance of helium-4, the cosmic microwave background, and the initial state of quantum fluctuations during inflation. Our research reveals that even a weak coupling between neutrinos and dark matter can lead to a suppression of the helium-4 abundance and lepton asymmetry, and may also result in distinctive patterns in the spectral indices of primordial fluctuations generated during inflation. Furthermore, this model predicts the formation of large-scale, gravitationally bound structures known as dark matter-neutrino bubbles, with sizes influenced by the neutrino mass and the strength of their interaction. These structures could potentially be detectable through future galaxy surveys and cosmic neutrino background observations. This model's minimal extensions also offer a possible explanation for the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. In summary, the interconnection between neutrinos and dark matter of negligible mass has a profound impact on the early universe, with far-reaching consequences for its evolution and cosmological outcomes. This research paves the way for a comprehensive study of this topic within the framework of standard model cosmology. This work can be found in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics of Year 2023. We develop a novel approach to describe nonlocal gravity based on an
observable-driven framework, where an observable-dependent metric is used
in place of the nonlocal metric. This new framework results in a constitutive
relation that non-trivially relates the nonlocal gravity's intrinsic
properties to observable quantities. We demonstrate that the nonlocal effect on
observable quantities can be viewed as a modification to the local gravity's
constitutive relation. Furthermore, we find that the nonlocal effect on the
stress-energy tensor's time derivative is unnecessary, leading to a reduced
set of constitutive relations that describe nonlocal gravity. Our approach is
applicable to both relativistic and semi-relativistic contexts. In the
relativistic case, our analysis yields a nonlocal, semi-linear second-order
covariant fluid dynamics equation. In the semi-relativistic context, our
constitutive relation framework matches the nonlocal fluid dynamics equation
found in previous research. Our method's flexibility is demonstrated by
reproducing previously established nonlocal fluid dynamics equations. Our
approach's generality is shown by presenting a nonlocal gravity's constitutive
relation in terms of a scalar field in both relativistic and semi-relativistic
settings. Our research also addresses issues related to nonlocality in
thermodynamics and thermoelectricity. We investigate the nonlocal effect on
thermoelectric heat flux and temperature gradient time derivative
dynamics. Our findings reveal that nonlocality results in an additional heat
transport channel, which we term the dissipative heat transport effect. We
predict that this nonlocal effect should be observable in experiments with
ultra-low temperature and high sensitivity. Our approach's applicability to
non-Abelian gauge fields in nonlocal gauge theory is also explored. We find
that nonlocality leads to a non-trivial modification to the gauge field's
stress-energy tensor's time derivative dynamics. Our research framework's
robustness is demonstrated by recovering previously established nonlocal
stress-energy tensor time derivative dynamics in both the semi-relativistic
and relativistic contexts. We investigate the nonlocal effect on the
thermoelectric heat transport in a one-dimensional lattice system using an
exact numerical method based on the Lanczos algorithm. We simulate the
nonlocal effect on the heat transport in a finite-sized system with periodic
boundary conditions. Our findings show that nonlocality results in an
oscillatory heat transport effect in finite-sized systems.

Our research focuses on measuring the yield ratios of strange particles, specifically $K^0_s$, $\Lambda$, $\Lambda^0$ bar, $\phi$, and $\Xi^0$, relative to charged pions in non-polar proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. These ratios are examined across various transverse momentum thresholds (0-1 GeV, 1-2 GeV, 2-3 GeV, 3-4 GeV, 4-5 GeV, 5-10 GeV) and mid-rapidity densities in the central rapidity region. Our findings are compared to previous experiments and theoretical predictions from the Wounded Nucleon Model and the Thermal-Statistical Model. The observed data is consistent with existing results and shows an increase in particle ratios with rising transverse momentum, although ratios for strange particles and the phi meson exhibit smaller growth compared to non-strange particles. Additionally, the measured ratios are within the predicted ranges from the Wounded Nucleon Model and the Thermal-Statistical Model. The most probable values for $K^0_s$ and $\Lambda$ production are found to be 0.73 $\pm$ 0.01 and 0.47 $\pm$ 0.01 per event in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The measured ratios also provide insights into initial state effects and the formation time of quarks in proton-proton collisions. The data collected in this research will contribute to ongoing and future studies aiming to understand strangeness enhancement in hadron collisions. The measured particle ratios can be utilized in current and future thermal models and serve as input for further investigations into initial state conditions and quark formation time in proton-proton collisions. The measured values for $K^0_s$ and $\Lambda$ production rates can be employed in studies of rare processes involving initial state collisions of proton-proton collisions. The measured particle ratios are compatible with existing data from the ALICE experiment in proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV and the LHCb experiment in proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV and 13 TeV. The measured particle ratios are also consistent with those obtained in heavy ion collisions at the LHC. We investigated the population of neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (LM XRBs) within the Milky Way by conducting a comprehensive search for these sources among the known X-ray binaries. Our analysis revealed 46 certain LM XRBs and 8 possible LM XRBs. By comparing their positions and orbital periods, we found that only 13% of LM XRBs with determined orbits have a companion with a short enough period to produce a millisecond radio pulsar. Within the Galactic disk, we found 69 confirmed millisecond radio pulsars (MSPs) and 17 likely MSP candidates. Considering the detection limitations, we estimate the total population of MSPs within the Galactic disk to be 1900 to 3500. We have computationally investigated the impact of rotation on hydrogen-burning marginally stable stars with masses less than the solar mass, and low-metallicity compositions, using full three-dimensional general relativistic hydrodynamics and a simplified treatment of surface temperature feedback. Our analysis focused on slow to moderately fast rotation rates and revealed how their shapes and stability are affected, particularly how critical curves are altered in response to their angular momentum. A key threshold exists at approximately 7.4 times $10^{49}$ erg s rad, below which their stable configurations resemble those of nonrotating stars. Notably, when stars rotate faster than this limit, their stability is compromised, leading to the loss of their hydrogen-burning stability and resulting in stars that are too cool to shine, similar to brown dwarfs. This threshold also explains the limited range of masses and luminosities within which main sequence stars reside, and it constrains the possible locations of low-mass stellar remnants in color-magnitude diagrams. Furthermore, this research provides the necessary tools for predicting the behavior of real stars and offers predictions for future missions that will study low-mass stars and their remnants. Lastly, we have also examined the characteristics of substellar objects with higher surface temperatures, and we found that they can be explained by the rotation of stars with masses similar to the solar mass. This phenomenon is expected to be observable in upcoming missions, and it will be crucial for testing our theoretical predictions. This study is relevant to ongoing and planned missions, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, the Giant Magellan Telescope, and the James T. Kirk Space Telescope, which will study the properties of low-mass stars and their remnants. This research is also significant for understanding the behavior of brown dwarfs and low-mass stellar remnants, and it has implications for the search for life on planets with masses similar to the Earth. To enhance the accuracy of hadron decay probability predictions, a novel approach using artificial neural networks is proposed for density estimation. This method involves training a series of regressors to estimate the probabilities of individual decay steps for different hadron types, taking into account their momenta, energies, and charges. The proposed framework, which can be applied to both particle and antiparticle decays, is demonstrated using a representative dataset of $\Lambda$-decay densities. The results indicate that compared to conventional neural networks, this multi-step approach yields improved performance, with a 2.5 times increase in precision when evaluating near the kinematic end-point and a 1.5 times increase in precision overall, when assessed using the same dataset. The method's effectiveness is further highlighted by the observation that the distribution of predicted probabilities matches the actual distribution of a reference dataset with similar characteristics, exhibiting improved agreement than the alternative approach. We present a comprehensive, five-parameter radiative jet model that accounts for both ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic afterglows, driven by a fixed amount of energy released during a jet. This model, which incorporates an observed radiative band, takes into consideration the effects of electron-proton scattering, synchrotron radiation from electrons within the jet, and the expansion of the jet itself. By comparing the model to various observations, specifically those of ultra-relativistic gamma-ray bursts, we find that the model effectively explains the spectral characteristics and temporal developments of these events, even when accounting for the impact of external radiation. Furthermore, we use the model to estimate the total energy released during each event, finding that this energy is significantly lower than previously estimated, with values ranging from approximately $10^{49}$ to $10^{51}$ erg. These findings support the conventional view that the majority of a burst's total energy is channelled into a radiative jet. We also utilize the model to investigate the effects of different jet properties on the observed phenomena, and to develop a method for estimating the total energy released during non-relativistic events, which could be applied to supernovae. A bipartite graph can be rendered planar if certain vertices are split into 2 parts, effectively breaking some edges into 2. We develop an algorithm that produces the minimum number of vertex splits required to make any bipartite graph planar, and we demonstrate that this number is equivalent to the minimum number of edge cuts needed to break the graph into disconnected parts, or to the number of vertex splits needed in a drawing where all vertices are on one side of a line. Additionally, we show that this number can be decreased by one if the graph contains a specific structure, and we provide an algorithm for drawing the remaining structure with the minimum number of vertex splits. As with previous research, we are able to achieve these results by utilizing a modified version of the Havel-Hakimi process, but with an added step to remove the structure that increases the number of vertex splits by one. We also explore generalizations to split graphs and list-coloring. Furthermore, we establish lower and upper bounds for the number of vertex splits required to make a bipartite graph planar, and we identify a specific pattern that is neither planar nor series-parallel, yet only requires two vertex splits to become planar. A generation method for random bipartite graphs is also presented, along with experimental data showing that the number of vertex splits is directly proportional to the maximum distance from a vertex to its furthest neighbor. As a result, we show that the power series field with a specified residue map has a computable model for first-order logic. Additionally, we determine the rank of its Boolean algebra of definable sets to be $\omega_1$ when the field is countably infinite. Based on these findings, we conclude that the power series field with a total residue map has a computable proof system of length $\omega_1$ for its first-order theory. Our approach to proving these results involves an extension of Wilie's algorithm, a modification of Herstein's method for computing the residue of polynomials, and an application of Rabin's decision procedure for weak first-order logic over ordered structures. Our research also introduces a new interpretation of the power series field as a structure of sequences of fields, which facilitates the use of its finite fragments in field-theoretic contexts. To address this issue, a new technique called HyperDegrade was developed, which reduces the necessity for system interactions and computational demands by over tenfold, and enables the recovery of precise system timing information from just one system interaction, and at a coarser time resolution of 50ms. Additionally, HyperDegrade's effectiveness was demonstrated across multiple system configurations, and it was discovered that various system anti-tempering mechanisms, including Intel's Software Guard Extensions, are susceptible to this attack. This outcome also enables us to create a bridge from any $(2,2n+1)$-twist bridge to a $(2,1)$-twist bridge. Additionally, our techniques allow us to transform any Whitehead link into a $3$-twisted Whitehead link and show that any twist knot can be created from a Whitehead knot using a $3$-twisted Whitehead link. Our approach to achieving these results involves employing diagonal moves, which we believe are novel, and comprise a part of our overall contribution to this field of study. Furthermore, our research reveals that any twist knot can be reconfigured into a twisted knot that has a specific type of rotation symmetry, and in doing so, we develop an algorithm for accomplishing this transformation. This algorithm, in turn, enables us to create a bridge from any $(2,2n+1)$-twist bridge to a $(2,1)$-twist bridge by first twisting the bridge while maintaining its core, and then proceeding to untwist the modified bridge while keeping its core. As a supplementary discovery, we find that any Whitehead link can be reconfigured into a twisted Whitehead link that has rotation symmetry, and in this case, we are able to determine the specific number of twists required for this transformation as $3$ or $6$, depending on whether the link has an even or an odd number of crossings, respectively. Both of these findings can be visually represented through diagrams. This research also includes an algorithm for creating a twisted Whitehead link from any Whitehead link, as well as a step-by-step guide for reconfiguring a twist knot into a twisted knot that exhibits rotation symmetry. This latter reconfiguration process is accompanied by an explicit diagram that illustrates the necessary steps involved. This diagram, in turn, is based on a specific, general approach that can be applied to any type of knot structure. We analyze the stability of the system's equilibria to understand how the distribution of task difficulties influences the decision-making strategies employed by the agents. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which the system's convergence to a specific equilibrium is guaranteed. These conditions are then applied to study several variations of the model. In a privacy-enhanced machine learning setting known as federated learning, users contribute to a shared model without revealing their individual data. We investigate two privacy breaches in vertical federated learning, where users collaborate by sharing data across different dimensions. The first privacy violation involves inferring missing data patterns, which the attackers use to reconstruct private information from a partially filled out dataset. The second privacy breach is information inference, where the attacker uses shared data to extract specific details. We developed two attack methods to achieve these breaches and tested them on vertical federated learning protocols. The results showed that our attacks successfully breached privacy in both cases. Furthermore, we proposed several security-enhanced vertical federated learning protocols and tested them against our attacks, finding that some of these protocols were vulnerable to our breaches, while others remained secure. The study also explored the design of secure vertical federated learning protocols, highlighting the significance of data dimensionality and data combinations in preventing information inference breaches. The research identified several challenges in vertical federated learning, specifically the difficulty in determining the relevance of data dimensions and the lack of guidelines for evaluating the privacy risks of these protocols. To address these challenges, we introduced a vertical federated learning evaluation framework that assesses privacy risks and provides guidelines for developing secure protocols. The study's findings and proposed framework can be applied to various real-world use cases of vertical federated learning. We present Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a method that refines the Random Fourier Features (RFF) approximation by incorporating the spectral density of the input data. PRFF systematically reduces the number of features required to capture the essential patterns and enhances the RFF's performance. Theoretical analysis and experiments demonstrate that PRFF achieves comparable results to kernel methods while utilizing Kernel Approximation techniques. In particular, it is shown that PRFF diminishes the dimensionality of RFF and other Kernel Approximation methods while improving classification accuracy. Our findings are supported by both synthetic and real-world data examples. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengwenguo/PRFF.

We introduce Cartesian Decomposition, a comprehensive framework that unifies various geometric structures on a manifold by combining regular group actions and diagonal groups. Specifically, we demonstrate how Cartesian Decomposition yields distinct components that reflect the manifold's invariants, including its equivariant and asymptotic properties.
