Our findings are notable because they demonstrate that the Proteus network model exhibits a unique characteristic: the removal of a single node leads to a massive and unpredictable effect on the surrounding cluster, resulting in a distribution of affected node sizes that is highly skewed and fragmented. We introduce the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, a new gravitational wave detector concept that enhances sensitivity and reduces thermal noise. This design modifies the Sagnac interferometer by filling the test masses and introducing a nonlinear relationship between mirror motion and light phase change, resulting in a frequency response proportional to frequency. This proportionality allows for the use of phase information from laser phase noise, effectively doubling the signal-to-noise ratio compared to traditional interferometers. Additionally, this design eliminates the Brownian noise contribution from mirror suspension, resulting in a 40% reduction in thermal noise. However, this design also introduces new noise sources related to fluid dynamics within the filled test masses, and its noise floor is marginally superior to that of the standard Sagnac interferometer only at very low frequencies. A detailed mathematical model of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer is provided, along with numerical simulations of its predicted performance. A key aspect of this design is the necessity for very low loss, high finesse optical cavities. A possible implementation using a novel type of optical cavity is proposed. A comparison with existing and proposed gravitational wave detectors is also presented. The number of users that a base station can support simultaneously is constrained due to random access (RA) overloads. To address this limitation in next-generation wireless systems, a new base station-user protocol called NOVR-XL is proposed for wide-band random access. NOVR-XL reduces base station processing loads by dividing users into two groups that transmit data at different power levels. This allows the base station to distinguish between low- and high-power signals and decode the number of incoming users more accurately. As a result, NOVR-XL raises the random access success rate by decreasing base station processing loads and improving user detection reliability. Simulation results confirm that NOVR-XL achieves higher random access success rates and lower base station processing loads than conventional protocols in both single-stream and massive MIMO systems. Additionally, NOVR-XL is found to be particularly beneficial in areas with high user densities and in massive MIMO systems. To implement NOVR-XL in practice, a detection algorithm called NOVR-XL detection is developed for base station users. This algorithm is capable of identifying the best protocol parameters, including the number of users that transmit at high power, and is shown to be highly effective in finding optimal solutions. Simulation data and theoretical analysis also reveal that NOVR-XL operates within an optimally defined limit that ensures its performance is always near the limit of its constrained base station processing loads. To further enhance NOVR-XL performance, a new algorithm called NOVR-XL estimation is proposed for estimating base station processing loads. This algorithm is found to be highly accurate and is capable of tracking changes in base station processing loads over time. To minimize base station processing loads, NOVR-XL can be configured to use a threshold-based mechanism that activates user detection only when base station processing loads fall below a certain predefined level. As a result, base station processing loads remain within optimal limits while maximizing random access success rates. The resulting model was then used to create a one-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulation of a protoplanetary disk. This core's growth was influenced by the amount of gas and dust it accreted during the substructure's formation. By adjusting the nuclear matter properties in the BigApple functional, we obtained the parameters for the new functional and used it to calculate the mass multiplet for the $^{16}$O-like nuclei, as well as two-neutron separation energies for those masses. Comparisons are made with results from other established energy density functionals, including SLJ, SH, and UNEDF1. Our findings show that the predicted two-neutron separation energies from M3 lie between those from SLJ and SH. Additionally, we examine the collective one-neutron states in $^{32}$S and the magnetic moments of even-even rare-earth nuclei. We investigate the performance of Molmer-Sorensen gates with varied frequencies in quantum entanglement generation, focusing on a system of trapped ions. Due to implementation limitations, quantum gate frequencies may differ from their ideal values, making frequency-robust designs crucial. Such robustness can be achieved through two-side $\pi$-control pulses, enabling the construction of highly reliable Molmer-Sorensen gates. Our analysis reveals that these gates efficiently produce quantum entanglement across an ion chain, even when frequency variations are significant. In particular, we find that the maximum quantum entanglement correlates inversely with the frequency difference, and that wider spectral windows lead to more robust, frequency-entanglement generation. As a result, we propose a Molmer-Sorensen gate based on two-side $\pi$-control pulses for a 129Xe$^+$ ion chain, utilizing magnetic field control, and demonstrate its capacity to efficiently create quantum entanglement within a range of applicable frequencies. Notably, this design enables the creation of quantum entanglement within a 2.5 MHz frequency window around its central value, a feat that surpasses the limitations of state-dependent Raman transitions. Our research demonstrates that carefully crafted Molmer-Sorensen gates can effectively produce wide-ranging, precise quantum entanglement, even in complex multi-level systems, making them highly suitable for quantum simulations involving diverse particle energies. Our findings also highlight the potential for a wide range of quantum applications that involve the controlled manipulation of quantum correlations within diverse energy spectra. A novel compound, GaCu3(OH)6Cl2, has been discovered and characterized as a three-dimensional quantum magnet that exhibits long-range magnetic ordering at 7.5 K. In a study published in Physical Review X, researchers delved into the in-depth examination of this material's electronic properties and magnetic behavior using a combination of experimental and theoretical techniques. By applying a layered-perovskite model to the crystal structure, simulations revealed that this compound harbors Dirac electrons within its energy spectrum. This discovery is particularly significant as it is rare to observe Dirac electrons in three-dimensional materials. Furthermore, the energy spectrum also displays unusual features that are indicative of strong electron correlations and many-body physics. This compound's unique properties make it an attractive subject for further investigation, and it may also have potential applications in the development of novel topological magnetic materials. This study employed a combination of methods including X-ray diffraction, magnetic measurements, and scanning tunneling spectroscopy to examine the material's microstructure, magnetic ordering, and quasiparticle interference patterns. This allowed the team to extract precise information about the material's electronic and magnetic properties. The search for heavy neutral leptons is a well-established and diverse experiment that can be improved in the future. Depending on their mass, these particles could interact through the weak force in a similar way to neutrinos, or instead behave like an anti-weak force with no connection to any known lepton family. Although their direct observation might be challenging, they would leave behind distinctive decay patterns, affecting the predicted outcomes of various particle physics experiments. To enhance detection capabilities, we propose combining data from deep-inelastic scattering at the Z-boson energy and electron-proton scattering at lower energies. By adjusting the mass range of heavy neutral leptons, we can cross-reference predictions from different experiments and tighten their detection limits. For the anti-weak force scenario, we find that future experiments at the Large Hadron Collider and the European Organization for Nuclear Research's Deep-Inelastic Scattering II facility could identify heavy neutral leptons within a specific mass range by examining specific decay products of bosons and scattering patterns off electrons and neutrinos. If these particles have a weak connection to the muon or tau family, we estimate that future experiments at the Z-boson energy and electron-proton scattering at lower energies will need to produce at least 30 ab$^{-1}$ of data to lower the detection limit to around 10 TeV, and to around 5 TeT for the anti-weak force scenario, respectively. If these particles have a weak connection to the electron family, we propose a modified search strategy that could reduce the required data to 10 ab$^{-1}$. If these particles behave like an anti-weak force with no connection to any lepton family, we find that future experiments at the Z-boson energy and electron-proton scattering at lower energies will need to produce at least 30 ab$^{-1}$ of data to lower the detection limit to around 10 TeV. Combining the strengths of both $N$-gram models and neural language models has yielded improved results in various language tasks including machine translation, summarization, and language modeling. This work introduces a new neural model that leverages the probabilities generated by $n$-gram models as additional training data to produce a neural model, which it terms a neural model pre-trained on a mixture model (NMM). By employing a mixture-of-experts architecture, NMM achieves performance enhancements in both machine translation and summarization tasks. Specifically, our findings show that NMM yields improved results when compared to standard neural language models, and the benefits of this approach become more pronounced under constrained data conditions. Our code is available online at: https://github.com/zhanglei1993/NMM. Our best NMM model has been deployed in a language model hub at: https://www.zhanglei.top/NMM. Our research also explores the impact of various $n$-gram models on NMM, and the results reveal that our proposed approach is robust and adaptable to a wide range of $n$-gram models. Our data processing guidelines and NMM code are designed to facilitate the creation of a massive language model dataset constructed from a vast number of $n$-gram models, which we term the neural grammar bank (NGB). Our analysis of NMM is grounded in both theoretical and empirical perspectives, and our research contributes to the development of a novel neural language model that effectively integrates both neural and grammatical components to enhance language understanding. Our research data and code are available at: https://www.zhanglei.top/NGB. Our NMM model has been deployed in a language model hub at: https://www.zhanglei.top/NMM. Our research findings are further validated through the creation of a novel language model dataset constructed from a massive collection of $n$-gram models, which we term the neural grammar bank (NGB). Our research shows that the integration of neural language models with a wide range of $n$-gram models through the NMM framework yields a robust and adaptable model that excels in both constrained and abundant data conditions. Our research also reveals that the NMM model is highly effective in predicting the quality of generated text, and our proposed approach is particularly beneficial for low-resource languages. 3D face reconstruction from images is a complex task, especially when attempting to generate highly detailed 3D models from limited data. Recent advancements have shown promising results using regression networks, but these models struggle to account for the wide range of facial poses present in real-world images. A new approach, the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), has been developed to tackle this challenge by dividing the pose dimension into two distinct, independent components: a pose-independent face and a pose-dependent face. By training two separate regression models, one for each component, and utilizing a novel alignment mechanism between them, the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network is able to accurately reconstruct 3D faces from images across a wide range of poses. Experiments using a large 3D face dataset, FL500, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, achieving improved results over current methods and demonstrating the ability to generalize to unseen poses. Additionally, the model's ability to handle pose variations was further validated through an ablation study and analysis of reconstructed 3D faces. We've developed a novel Gaussian curvature-based approach to analyzing the anisotropic curvature of the Bardeen potential during inflationary stages. By applying a fourth-order anisotropic curvature operator, we can determine how anisotropic features in the Bardeen potential's anisotropic structure factor influence the distribution of extreme values. Specifically, we found that large negative values of the Bardeen potential are more likely to occur when the Riemann tensor has a negative anisotropic eigenvalue, and this effect becomes more pronounced as the absolute value of the eigenvalue increases. Furthermore, we used our method to re-examine the scalar power spectrum's impact and discovered that a broader than Planckian Riemann tensor anisotropy spectrum leads to a wider Bardeen potential anisotropy distribution, resulting in more extreme values of the anisotropy. Additionally, we found that the distribution of extreme values correlates with the average anisotropic eigenvalue, even in the presence of isotropic components. This approach provides a promising tool for investigating the generation of anisotropies in the Bardeen potential during inflationary periods. To illustrate the applicability of our method, we used a standard slow-roll model as a reference point. This approach can be applied to models featuring more complex anisotropic patterns, and we have made our curvature operator code publicly available. In over-parameterized linear models with time-dependent variables, we develop a non-parametric training method that processes infinite-dimensional data. This approach leverages the observation that the model's parameters evolve in a piecewise linear manner, allowing us to define a operator that captures the underlying structure and facilitate efficient optimization using an augmented Lagrangian method. We initially propose this method for models with a fixed endpoint, and subsequently extend it to include time-dependent targets. The resulting algorithm comprises $O(λ^−1.5)$ time-dependent gradient updates to reach a given error threshold. Furthermore, we introduce a time-dependent variant of the method, which yields $O(λ^{−1.5}log(1/ε))$ time to achieve a specific error ε, and demonstrate its applicability to infinite-dimensional data in linear neural networks and temporally linear models. The proposed method's efficacy is also shown in experiments involving linear neural networks and temporally linear models. The underlying theory and numerical examples are presented in the paper. This study examines the long-term behavior of storage units that adopt a risk-averse approach, with implications for low-carbon energy policy. We develop a mathematical model where a single storage unit, or a storage unit as part of a microgrid, participates in electricity markets while managing its risk preferences. We analyze the model's equilibrium outcomes to understand how storage units' risk aversion affects their market activities and resulting carbon emissions. Our findings reveal that risk-averse storage units prioritize short-term gains over long-term benefits, leading to increased greenhouse gas emissions in the near term but lower emissions in the long run. We also explore policies aimed at reducing carbon footprint, including carbon pricing, renewable portfolio standards, and subsidies for storage units. Our results indicate that these policies can mitigate the risks faced by storage units and, as a result, reduce their carbon footprint more effectively in the short term than in the long term. However, we note that the effectiveness of these policies depends on various market conditions and the level of risk faced by storage units. Our research provides a theoretical basis for evaluating the impact of low-carbon energy policies on storage units and other market participants. Ultimately, it highlights the significance of considering risk preferences in modeling storage units' behavior and evaluating low-carbon energy policies. Our model can be applied to different market structures and configurations, offering a versatile tool for assessing and designing sustainable energy systems. Our findings are relevant to the energy policies of various countries, including the United States, China, and Australia. Our research was funded by the Australian Research Council. Our model builds upon existing literature in the field of operations research and economics. Our results are consistent with previous studies examining the impact of risk aversion on storage units' behavior and the effectiveness of carbon pricing policies. Our study extends the existing research by exploring the behavior of storage units in day-ahead electricity markets and examining the effectiveness of renewable portfolio standards and subsidies for storage units. Our model can be applied to different types of storage units and energy markets, and our findings provide a general framework for understanding the behavior of storage units and evaluating low-carbon energy policies in various market settings. Our research also offers a theoretical basis for developing agent-based models of energy systems that incorporate risk preferences and storage units' behavior. Our study's policy implications can be tested using real-world data from various electricity markets. Active learning algorithms aim to optimize labeling costs by prioritizing the most effective data points for human annotation. While these methods excel on small-scale datasets, they struggle to scale to large, high-dimensional datasets like ImageNet, due in part to the diverse ways its uncertainty can manifest. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel uncertainty representation learning framework, called Adversarial Uncertainty Prior Selection (AUPS), which extracts a compact, representative set of uncertainties that capture the most critical information for classification, and can be applied to massive datasets. Through rigorous evaluation, AUPS outperforms state-of-the-art active learning methods on multiple benchmark datasets, including a 6.5\% improvement in classification accuracy on ImageNet. Moreover, our research reveals that AUPS's representative uncertainties can be leveraged in a variety of machine learning tasks, including classification, robustness enhancement, and unsupervised outlier detection. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengzhengy/AUPS.

Donor atoms embedded in silicon serve as qubits and their interaction can be modulated to perform various logic operations. However, accurately modeling the interaction between donors and requireless precise control over their placement and bonding hinders the development of reliable two-qubit logic gates. This study presents a novel approach that uses a tunnel coupler made from germanium instead of the traditional III-V material. As a result, the interaction between donors can be more precisely controlled and varied, enabling efficient execution of two-qubit logic operations, including the CNOT gate, with high fidelity. Specifically, our findings show that the CNOT gate can be executed with high precision when the interaction between donors is neither too weak nor too strong, resulting in a high average fidelity of over 99.9%. Moreover, our results indicate that the average fidelity of the CNOT gate can reach 99.99% by adjusting the interaction between donors. This breakthrough paves the way for the development of reliable two-qubit logic gates using silicon spin qubits connected via a germanium tunnel coupler. The study reports the observation of an unusual resistance peak at zero Landau level in silicon macroscopic samples, where the resistance oscillations are prominent. The resistance peak appears at filling factors near $\nu = 0$ and is explained by a scattering process between Landau levels with equal and opposite energies. This scattering is significant because it occurs before the Landau levels split due to spin-orbit interaction and is thus a unique feature of this system. The resistance peak's position in the magnetic field is used to determine the effective mass of the electrons with high precision. The effective mass found is 1.48 times the rest mass of an electron and is the largest ever reported for silicon. The effective mass also allows for a more accurate calculation of the fine structure constant based on the resistance peak. The value obtained is 1/137.357, which is the most precise measurement of this constant using silicon without the need for quantum wells. The study's findings also indicate that the Landau level resistance oscillations are influenced by the sample's temperature and disorder. The observed resistance peak is a promising indicator for precise measurements of physical constants in solid-state systems. In this study, Hamiltonian Neural Networks are applied to a variety of tasks, including generating handwritten digits, face reconstruction, and protein structure prediction. When used to recreate MNIST digits, a HNN outperformed an LSTM-based meta-learner in terms of final digit accuracy, achieving a 99.4% accuracy after 5 generations. Additionally, a modified version of the HNN model produces realistic face reconstructions and accurately predicts alpha-helices and beta-sheets in protein structures. The underlying Hamiltonian dynamics of a system can also be learned and used to manipulate the system's parameters to construct novel, structurally similar proteins. A code repository is available at https://github.com/tinghuiroy/hamiltonian-neural-networks. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of Hamiltonian Neural Networks in modeling real-world systems and informs the design of future models that integrate physics and learning. In a collaborative setting where multiple agents work together to reach a common goal, a distributed machine learning framework can be highly effective. However, the reliability of this approach hinges on the trustworthiness of participating agents. We introduce a novel, game-theoretic paradigm that combines cooperative machine learning and reputation management. This system, designed for multi-agent environments, balances cooperation and competition among agents and awards them based on their contributions and behavior. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in two real-world applications. In the first, a collaborative image classification task among multiple agents from different domains shows a significant improvement in accuracy and a substantial boost in the trustworthiness of the model, with results including an accuracy rate of 95.44% and a corresponding trust score of 92.12. In the second, a collaborative sentiment analysis task among multiple agents from the same domain also yields improved outcomes, with results including an accuracy rate of 98.45% and a corresponding trust score of 96.75%. Deep learning models for natural language processing have seen significant boosts in performance when subjected to various data augmentation methods. While these improvements are notable, the underlying reasons behind them are not yet fully understood. This study aims to investigate the impact of data augmentation as input variations, drawing from both artificial and real-world sources, and to examine the relationship between this effect and the activation of neurons in deep learning models. We used a simple word-replacement technique as an example of input variations and found that the method that results in the highest activation of specific neurons is the most effective data augmentation strategy. However, when we applied this approach to actual data augmentation methods like back-translation and paraphrasing, the outcomes were less clear, suggesting that the effectiveness of these methods is influenced by the characteristics of the underlying distribution of the activated neurons. This research contributes to our understanding of the relationship between data augmentation, neural networks, and the distributions of activated neurons. We also found that the activated neurons in a model trained on a specific task are similar to those in a model trained on a related task with a shared underlying distribution, and that the neurons that are specific to a particular task are distinct from those of a model trained on a more general task. This finding is consistent with the idea that each task corresponds to a unique distribution of activated neurons, and that the neurons that are common to multiple tasks are clustered together in the network. This research paves the way for further exploration of the neural networks that underlie the effectiveness of data augmentation techniques. This work is relevant to the community of natural language processing practitioners and researchers, as it provides insights into the mechanisms behind data augmentation and suggests potential avenues for improving this method. This research is part of a larger project that aims to gain a deeper understanding of the internal workings of neural networks and to develop methods for improving the performance of machine learning models by manipulating their neural components. The complex Gamma function can be represented through an integral formula, which may be expressed as a contour integral in the complex plane. We examine various contours for this integral, focusing on those that connect branching points of the function, and we explore their applications in deriving integral equations for the Barnes G-function and the Gamma operator. This study measures the total cross section for top quark pair production using 4.7 fb^-1 of 10 GeV proton-proton collision data collected by the D0 experiment at the Fermilab Tevatron particle collider. The analysis employs three methods to measure the cross section: (1) identifying lepton+jets events with a missing transverse energy tag, (2) analyzing lepton+jet events with a tight jet selection, and (3) examining dijet events with a missing transverse energy component. The measured cross section is found to be 7.25+0.47-(0.42) pb, which is in line with theoretical predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics, with an estimated uncertainty of 4.5%. Additionally, the cross section is broken down into six differential distributions, including the transverse momenta of the leading jet, the invariant mass of the top quark pair, and the pseudorapidity of the leading lepton. These results are the most precise to date and provide a comprehensive study of top quark pair production in proton-proton collisions at 10 GeV.

Our proposed method introduces a technique called "approximate matching" to enhance accuracy during instance retrieval, particularly when the database is unavailable. This method employs a two-tiered approach where initial instance candidates are first identified, and these candidates are then ranked against a query. A key innovation of our method is the incorporation of a parameter that enables control of the number of database instances considered, allowing for a trade-off between precision and a newly introduced metric we call "expansion cost". This cost metric assesses the additional information required to determine a more accurate set of instance rankings. Our method is further enhanced by developing two strategies to obtain this parameter: a data-driven approach based on a pairwise comparison model, and a supervised learning method. Through these approaches, our model achieves improved results in instance retrieval tasks with limited database contents, and we demonstrate its effectiveness using two datasets. Furthermore, our method yields a ranking mechanism that can be utilized for classification and recommends suitable actions, thereby providing additional value over traditional methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyiwang/approximate_matching.

The Euclid mission's vast dataset, encompassing high-resolution sky maps and detailed object records, will significantly influence various astrophysical and cosmological studies. Euclid's primary focus on cosmological research is supported by in-depth analyses of its secondary astrophysical findings. The mission's all-sky observations will yield comprehensive records of over 3 billion celestial objects within its observable field, allowing for comprehensive studies of its detected populations and uncovering new ones. The resulting datasets and resources will be made publicly available, facilitating extensive multidisciplinary research. Specifically, Euclid's findings will be instrumental in advancing knowledge of the following areas: the evolution and distribution of dark matter and dark energy, the properties of black holes and neutron stars within galaxies, supernovae and stellar outbursts, planetary systems and the formation of galaxies. Notably, Euclid is poised to discover thousands of faint galaxies in the distant universe, shedding light on the early stages of the cosmos. The comprehensive dataset collected will also enable exploration of unexpected phenomena and new astrophysical objects. The extensive datasets and methodologies developed during the mission will serve as a foundation for future astronomical research. We investigate the statistical properties of a discrete time random walk in an random environment on a group, specifically the large deviation behavior of the empirical measure of path segments, given a large time interval. Under mild assumptions, we establish that the associated quenched rate function forms three separate regions: one with a quenched exponential tail for renewal-like behavior, another defined for an ergodic and stationary renewal process, and finally an asymptotically independent segment regime towards the right tail. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the large deviations in the renewal-like region are characterized by a specific parameter $\alpha$, which occurs in the tail exponent of $\frac{1}{\alpha}$ for the distribution of the time until the process reaches a given state, and show that this $\alpha$-value determines either a single state being reached rapidly or multiple states being visited uniformly, both leading to distinct large deviation behaviors. As for a one-dimensional torus, we find that the right tail of the time until the process reaches a given state has a tail exponent of $\frac{1}{2}$ for a random walk in a random environment with stationary and ergodic environment, providing a novel result. The primary contributions of this research are the study of quenched large deviations for letter sequences, the investigation of the associated rate function's properties, and the determination of specific tail exponents of the time until the process reaches a particular state in both general groups and a one-dimensional torus. These findings are achieved through the development of a large deviation principle for the empirical measure of path segments within a random walk in a random environment on a group, and are accompanied by specific examples and counterexamples that highlight the importance of specific assumptions and the diversity of random walk behaviors. The research in this paper extends and refines previous results on the random walk in a random environment on a one-dimensional torus, and provides a solid foundation for further exploring related topics, such as the random walk in a random environment on more complex groups and related systems, and the connection to Schramm-Loewner evolution. The associated technical innovations include the development of a level 1.5 PDE for random walk in a random environment on a one-dimensional torus, and the application of a random walk in a random environment on a group to model letter sequences. The research in this paper also offers insights into the connection between the random walk in a random environment and Schramm-Loewner evolution, and provides a statistical analysis of letter sequences, which is a fundamental aspect of the stochastic evolution of languages. In the context of evaluating and comparing machine learning models using cross-validation, we present a theoretical analysis of performance stability and provide a method to enhance this stability. Theoretical assessments of our approach's benefits are supported by empirical evidence from classification tasks. Our findings indicate that the proposed method consistently yields more stable performance assessments than standard cross-validation techniques, without sacrificing model selection accuracy. Consequently, we advocate for employing our approach as a standard for evaluating and comparing machine learning models using cross-validation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yzeng1998/JKCV. 

To the best of our knowledge, our research represents a pioneering effort in examining the stability of performance assessments via cross-validation, as well as in presenting our novel J-K-fold cross-validation method. Our work is inspired by a recent study on cross-validation's robustness and its connection to model selection, but our investigation diverges from their research by focusing on enhancing stability rather than robustness. Our approach is designed to be flexible and can be applied to various evaluation metrics, including multiclass classification metrics like AUC-ROC and AUC-PR. Our code is written in Python and incorporates popular machine learning tools such as scikit-learn and lightmetric. Our research and associated code can be found at https://yzeng1998.github.io/projects/JKCV. 

Our J-K-fold cross-validation method can be summarized as follows: we first divide our available data into K non-overlapping, equally-sized subsets, and then randomly select J subsets from these K subsets for training and evaluating our machine learning models. We recommend setting K to 5 or 10, as these values provide a suitable balance between performance stability and computational efficiency. We also suggest using 2 or 3 for J, as these values allow us to balance performance stability with the risk of overfitting. We acknowledge that our approach may result in some instances where we cannot form a subset of J equally-sized subsets from our available data, but we argue that these instances are relatively rare and do not significantly impact our findings. We also propose a method to handle such instances, but we found that this method is not essential for achieving our research goals. Our code allows users to input their own values for K and J, but we recommend using the values we suggest as these values have been validated through our research. Our code also includes an example classification task using the MNIST dataset, but we emphasize that our approach is versatile and can be applied to various machine learning tasks and evaluation metrics.

In recent years, the integration of Teacher-Student networks has significantly enhanced classification accuracy and reduced energy expenditure in mobile applications. Building on this concept, we present a novel dual-branch Teacher-Student framework, known as DTSNet, which incorporates two separate learning processes to train both the student and teacher components. Unlike conventional Teacher-Student architectures, DTSNet features a distinct student network for each data source and employs a joint optimization technique that synchronizes multiple student networks and a single teacher network. Theoretical analysis of the proposed method reveals a lower bound for the classification error of the student networks, indicating that the optimal performance of the student networks is directly proportional to the number of available data sources and network depths. Experimental evaluations conducted on mobile image classification and smart meter prediction tasks demonstrate improved performance relative to state-of-the-art compression methods and Teacher-Student learning benchmarks, with a 45.67% reduction in the number of parameters required and a 31.25% decrease in the number of operations performed compared to the BWN compression method. Furthermore, the proposed DTSNet outperforms the Teacher-Student learning method in both classification accuracy and model size reduction. The code for this work can be found at: https://github.com/zhengyong-yang/DTSNet.

Our analysis indicates that the traditional Lorentzian absorption lineshape is modified by a non-osculatory component at its peak, directly proportional to the saturation level and the recoil-induced shift. This modification becomes substantial at high saturation levels and narrow resonance widths. Our results can be applied to a variety of absorption phenomena, including optical and dielectric absorption, and we've also demonstrated the applicability to our specific experiment - Rb-87 atom absorption at a 780 nm wavelength. By comparing our theoretical lineshape to experimental data, we've determined the absolute power of the incident light, allowing for calibration of our optical phase and amplitude references. Our findings are relevant to various saturation spectroscopy techniques and can be used in future experiments utilizing similar setups. Moreover, our research shows that the usual assumption of negligible photon recoil effects in saturation absorption can lead to inaccurate phase and amplitude calibration, potentially causing difficulties in interpreting and comparing data from different experiments.

Notably, rCASPR's performance improvement becomes more pronounced as the system becomes more densely sampled. The method's effectiveness was further validated using real data from a flat-panel detector system, highlighting rCASPR's potential for improving image quality and reducing data collection time in cone-beam CT systems. We introduce a modified version of the standard Finite Group Method Reduced Order Extensive Iteration (FGMRES) for solving time-dependent parametric partial differential equations. The standard FGMRES has become a widely applied and efficient choice for solving time-dependent parametric PDEs using reduced-order models, particularly in the context of the Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method. However, the standard FGMRES iteration may yield suboptimal results when the residual operator varies significantly with parameters. To address this limitation, we modify the standard FGMRES iteration by incorporating a transformation matrix that accounts for the change in the residual operator. This modification is achieved by introducing an additional step that involves solving a small number of linear systems. As a result, the modified FGMRES iteration offers improved performance, particularly when the residual operator exhibits significant variations with respect to parameters. Ultimately, this approach enables the creation of efficient reduced-order models for time-dependent parametric PDEs governed by nonlinear residual operators. We demonstrate the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed method by applying it to numerical solutions of two benchmark problems. These results showcase the modified FGMRES iteration's ability to deliver superior solutions when compared to standard FGMRES and demonstrate the applicability of the method to complex geometries through a coupled structural-aero problem. Additionally, we provide a detailed theoretical analysis of the modified FGMRES iteration's convergence properties. Furthermore, we outline the method's extension to the Reduced Order Bulitkiewicz Method (ROBEM) and provide numerical solution results for a real-world application involving a wind turbine airfoil. In recent years, Memristor Neural Networks have made significant breakthroughs and are being considered as a high-performing and energy-efficient General-Purpose Classifier, rivaling the performance of conventional Artificial Neural Networks. However, the majority of existing studies focus on specific Memristor Neural Network architectures and lack a comprehensive comparison. To bridge the gap, this paper proposes a Spiking Neural Network, which we call SNN-S, and provides a precise mathematical analysis of its dynamics, followed by a Memristor implementation using TiO2 Memristors. Furthermore, we derive an analytical formula to compare the performance of SNN-S against ANNs, yielding a Memristor-based SNN-S architecture and a training algorithm. We then conduct extensive simulations to compare the Memristor-based SNN-S against ANNs on six benchmark datasets, demonstrating its superior performance in terms of accuracy while exhibiting significantly reduced power consumption. To facilitate further research, the proposed Memristor-based SNN-S architecture and training algorithm are made available online. This work lays the groundwork for the development of Memristor-based SNN-S and related applications in the field of Neuromorphic Computing. Experimental validation of the proposed Memristor-based SNN-S is also presented, showcasing the practical feasibility of this technology. A cubic graph is classified as an even-2-factorable graph if its edge set can be divided into two factors, each satisfying an even degree condition and one of them also meets the requirement for 2-factors. This study investigates the relationship between even-2-factorability and the existence of Hamiltonian cycles in cubic graphs, ultimately leading to its characterization. Specifically, it is shown that a cubic graph is even-2-factorable if and only if it contains a Hamiltonian cycle, thereby establishing an equivalence to the condition found by Chia and Kuo for graphs without Hamiltonian cycles. This, in turn, leads to the even-2-factorability of a cubic graph being equivalent to the absence of a Hamiltonian cycle. An alternative proof for the latter is provided, differing from the original approach given by Chia and Kuo. Additionally, this research introduces the concept of strong even-2-factorable graphs, which are an extension of even-2-factorable graphs and are characterized by requiring that one of the 2-factors contains all vertices while maintaining the even degree property for the other factor. It is demonstrated that a cubic graph is strong even-2-factorable if and only if it contains all 2-factor structures, thereby generalizing the condition found by Chia and Kuo for graphs without 2-factor structures. This study also presents an alternative proof for the condition found by Chia and Kuo, differing from the original approach given by Chia and Kuo. An interesting corollary arises from this, showing that a cubic graph is even-2-factorable if and only if it does not contain a 2-factor structure, both of which were unknown prior to this research. This study also offers a new approach to determining the even-2-factorability of a cubic graph, which is equivalent to the absence of a Hamiltonian cycle or the absence of a 2-factor structure within the graph. System call filtering is a critical security feature that prevents malicious applications from compromising host systems. While various solutions exist for low-level programming languages like C and C++, there is a lack of comparable solutions for high-level interpreted languages like PHP and Python. To address this issue, we developed Timeloops, a Linux-based system call filtering framework that leverages Linux kernel capabilities to meet security requirements. Timeloops includes two key components: a small kernel module that provides filtering functionality and a proxy daemon that acts as an intermediary between applications and the system. By intercepting system calls made by applications, the proxy daemon ensures compliance with predefined rules. In evaluating Timeloops, we successfully applied system call filtering to Apache Web servers and developed a set of best practices to enhance security. This research focuses on an Euler scheme for observed population models with degenerate diffusion, where the observation level varies over time. An inequality allowing us to manage population extinction is established, leading to the convergence proof of a specific algorithm for approximate optimal controls. The resulting scheme is then used to approximate solutions to an observed stochastic population model with degenerate diffusion, where the observation level changes over time, in a setting that ensures the avoidance of population extinction. The convergence of the scheme is demonstrated, along with the convergence rate, under the assumption that the underlying process has smooth density functions. The approach taken also yields the convergence rate of the scheme to the solution of the observed stochastic population model, which can be seen as an extension of previous results established for constant observation levels. The method employed in this research can be viewed as a starting point for exploring more complex models and variants. The approach taken is applicable to models with state-dependent birth rates and includes models with nonlinear growth, providing a versatile framework. We analyze the expected rewards associated with various actions in soccer, considering the state of the game and different player positions. Our research provides numerical values to compare the potential rewards of different actions, including fouls, ball outs, and offside infractions, in relation to scoring opportunities. By examining real game data, we show that our model effectively captures the observed behavior of actions and estimate that, in many cases, committing a foul results in lower rewards than causing the ball to go out or committing an offside infraction, contrary to conventional wisdom. Furthermore, we find that our model can predict the actions taken in game situations, even when these situations are not part of the training data, and that incorporating player-specific characteristics improves the accuracy of these predictions. Our approach enables the integration of action rewards with other decision-making frameworks, such as reinforcement learning, by providing a quantitative basis for evaluating actions in soccer. Our model and associated code are available online. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the state of the game, player positions, and the potential consequences of actions in understanding soccer behavior. Our research also presents a method for quantifying action rewards in soccer, a valuable tool for developing more effective decision-making strategies in the game. Our approach to estimating action rewards in soccer has been applied to real-game data from the English Premier League, revealing that our model accurately predicts actions in a wide range of game situations, even those not included in the training data. Our results demonstrate that our model effectively accounts for player positions, the state of the game, and the rewards associated with different actions, and that our approach can be used with other decision-making frameworks, such as reinforcement learning, by providing a quantitative basis for evaluating actions in soccer. Our code and model are available online at a specified URL. Our research has been used in the development of more effective decision-making strategies in soccer, including an approach to training agents that control the behavior of soccer players using reinforcement learning. Our model has been applied to real-game data from the English Premier League, consisting of 763 games played over a period of 13 years, and has been used to train agents that control the behavior of soccer players using reinforcement learning, resulting in trained agents that are able to accurately predict actions in a wide range of game situations, even those not included in the training data. Our findings have implications for the development of decision-making strategies in soccer, highlighting the importance of considering the state of the game, player positions, and the potential consequences of actions, and providing a quantitative basis for evaluating actions in the game.

Full waveform inversion (FWI) based on time-domain wavefields holds significant potential, but implementing it practically is challenging due to the problem of non-physical negative densities in the Earth. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various methods aimed at avoiding the use of time-domain wavefields, instead utilizing frequency-domain formulations. However, the frequency-domain approach can be computationally expensive, making it less appealing for large-scale inversion applications. This study proposes a hybrid approach, combining the benefits of time- and frequency-domain formulations, to create a more efficient and accurate framework for FWI. Theoretical and numerical investigations into the method's behavior have been conducted, revealing that this hybrid approach can effectively mitigate the issue of non-physical solutions. Moreover, this method has been applied to actual seismic data, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability for real-world inversion problems. To facilitate this research, a low-storage, memory-efficient implementation of the hybrid method has been developed and made available online. This development is expected to contribute to ongoing research and potential future extensions of the method. To further advance the field, this study also outlines potential avenues for future work, including the incorporation of anelastic effects and multiple scattering, as well as the development of better initial models. In the context of big data and the Internet of Things, cellular edge computing has the potential to reduce data transmission loads and minimize energy consumption for mobile devices. To facilitate efficient data and energy transfer to users at the cellular edge, a two-dimensional (2D) data and energy transfer framework called Time-Frequency Integrated Energy and Data Transfer (TFIET) has been proposed. Initially, a one-dimensional (1D) TFIET model was introduced in research, but it had limitations in terms of scheduling and resource allocation. To overcome these limitations, this study presents a Big Data Application Specific Integrated Circuit (BASEC) architecture and a corresponding 2D TFIET model. Furthermore, this study proposes a data and energy transfer scheduling algorithm called Energy-Aware and Data-Oriented Transfer Scheduling (EADOTS) to optimize data and energy transfer in the 2D TFIET framework. To evaluate the performance and efficiency of the BASEC architecture and the EADOTS algorithm, this study simulated a cloud-based edge computing system and conducted experiments on a high-performance computing platform. The results of these experiments showed that the BASEC architecture and the EADOTS algorithm can significantly reduce energy consumption and data transmission loads for mobile devices in a DED2D system. To further improve the performance of the BASEC architecture and the EADOTS algorithm, this study proposed a new 2D TFIET scheduling strategy called Energy-Aware and Data-Oriented Transfer Scheduling 2.0 (EADOTS2.0). The results of the experiments conducted on the EADOTS2.0 algorithm showed that it can reduce energy consumption and data transmission loads for mobile devices in a DED2D system by up to 30%. To facilitate practical implementation of the BASEC architecture and the EADOTS algorithm, this study also proposed a corresponding hardware design based on a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) platform. To evaluate the performance of the BASEC architecture and the EADOTS algorithm in real-world scenarios, this study conducted experiments on a cloud-based edge computing system and a real-world IoT application scenario. The results of these experiments showed that the BASEC architecture and the EADOTS algorithm can achieve high performance and efficiency in real-world scenarios. To further improve the performance of the BASEC architecture and the EADOTS algorithm, this study proposed a new 2D TFIET scheduling strategy called Energy-Aware and Data-Oriented Transfer Scheduling 2.0 (EADOTS2.0).

A mathematical model has been developed to assess the impact of electrostatic phase plate design parameters on electron probe dimensions and current density within an Electron Scanning Transmission Microscope. The code considers various aspects of the plate's design, including its fill-factor and the specific arrangement of pixels, and examines multiple operational conditions. By analyzing the interaction between the phase plate and incoming electron beams, the model identifies the optimal design settings that minimize probe size while maximizing current density. Numerical simulations demonstrate the code's accuracy and facilitate a comprehensive exploration of design trade-offs. This research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the effects of phase plate design on probe performance and offers practical guidelines for constructing improved phase plates. Specifically, the findings suggest that a hexagonal fill-factor of 0.8 and a specific arrangement of pixels can significantly reduce probe size and increase current density. This discovery has been experimentally confirmed using a modified Scherzer aberration-corrected Electron Scanning Transmission Microscope. The associated reduction in probe size and the resulting improvement in current density enable the imaging of lighter specimens with higher resolution. The developed code also enables the simulation of other types of electron microscopes that utilize phase plates, and its applicability to real-world design problems is demonstrated using an example of a hexagonal phase plate. This research has significant implications for the design of phase plates in various types of electron microscopes and provides a foundation for further studies on the optimization of other aberration-correcting techniques. The associated code has been made publicly available to facilitate the design of improved phase plates for specific applications and to support ongoing research in the field. The code's versatility allows it to be adapted for use with other electron microscope simulations, and it serves as a general framework for evaluating the performance of electron microscopes equipped with phase plates. The findings presented in this research have been experimentally confirmed using a modified Scherzer aberration-corrected Electron Scanning Transmission Microscope, and the associated code has been utilized to simulate the performance of this microscope. This study investigates the long-term behavior of a one-dimensional anharmonic system with a specific type of nonlinearity and an added external force, represented by the variable anharmonic oscillator. We examine the possibility of solitary waves maintaining their shape over time and identify conditions under which this stability is ensured. Contrary to previous findings for anharmonic oscillators without anharmonic terms, our research reveals that these anharmonic terms can lead to the break-up of solitary waves if they move too quickly. Our approach also provides a quantitative assessment of the threshold velocity above which these solitary waves become unstable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in the presence of these anharmonic terms, the conditions required for orbital stability need to be more stringent, specifically that the system must have a specific energy density that is directly related to its velocity. Our results are further validated numerically using a specific example of a van der Waals anharmonic oscillator. This research extends the orbital stability of solitary waves to include a wide range of applications in physics, such as in the study of anharmonic oscillators used in mass sensors and atomic clocks. We establish an inductive framework to examine the Galois module theory of wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of the rational numbers. Notably, we demonstrate that such an S-polynomial system associated with a finite non-abelian Galois group over the rational numbers corresponds to a additive Galois module with parameters (W,∂,S) that incorporates Hilbert's 12th problem, ultimately connecting to the additive Galois module theory of a finite non-abelian extension with an irreducible polynomial as its defining equation. Our investigation into these systems also uncovers connections to the fundamental theorem of Galois-Lie algebra theory and its applications in constructing the lower central series of Lie algebras. Furthermore, we derive explicit formulae for computing the additive Galois module structure of certain systems, thereby providing a computational method for determining the Galois group of a finite non-abelian extension. Our research in this area is an extension of previous studies on monic polynomial systems with simple roots.

To enhance the detection of a neutral long-lived particle at a collider, researchers propose using a near-beam neutrino telescope as a search strategy. This approach would allow for the identification of a broad range of decay lengths, extending beyond the limitations of traditional particle detectors. By positioning highly sensitive neutrino detectors near the target where new particles would likely interact and then decay, a comprehensive search can be conducted for neutral long-lived particles, even in scenarios where their decays occur within a few meters of their creation point. This novel search method can effectively compensate for the lack of conventional signatures from these particles and could provide valuable insights into their properties and masses. As an illustration, the feasibility of this approach is demonstrated for a muon-like neutral long-lived particle at three different energy colliders, and the potential for neutrino detectors to identify signatures of these particles is explored in detail. Specifically, optimized search strategies are presented for the ATOMIA experiment at the CERN SPS, the SHiP experiment at the same facility, and three possible configurations for a future hadron collider. In each case, the minimum decay length required for detection scales inversely with the beam energy and is found to match predictions from theoretical models. Consequently, this novel search strategy is positioned as a valuable addition to existing methods for discovering neutral long-lived particles at colliders. Additionally, the inherent flexibility of this approach makes it suitable for use in conjunction with traditional detectors at existing and future hadron colliders. Furthermore, this research highlights the potential for neutrino detectors to be used in new and innovative ways at these facilities. Given the broad applicability of this search method, it is recommended for inclusion in the physics potential studies of future hadron colliders and for consideration in the design of new or upgraded neutrino detectors. Understanding how word meanings evolve over time is crucial for developing natural language processing systems with a temporal perspective. Recent advances in supervised semantic change detection rely on contextualized embeddings, yet the underlying factors influencing these shifts remain poorly understood. We argue that changes in the variance of contextual representations reflect a fundamental aspect of semantic change, specifically the expansion or contraction of a word's meaning in response to varying contexts. We demonstrate that by controlling contextual variance, we can disentangle the effects of both local and global context on a word's meaning and identify specific context-dependent patterns of semantic change. Furthermore, we show that models trained on supervised change detection tasks are actually capturing the relationship between contextual variance and the position of a word's meaning in the semantic space, rather than the intended temporal or directional aspects. We also find that these models can be improved by incorporating a variance-aware representation of the historical or target context. Our findings highlight the limitations of current approaches and provide valuable insights for developing more effective methods in modeling the evolution of language. We investigate the behavior of ultra-light, Bose-Einstein condensed dark matter in the presence of a black hole in a 5-dimensional braneworld scenario. This model allows us to describe a dark matter particle as a graviton within an AdS space and includes a black hole as a source of gravitation. We then analyze the effects of the black hole's mass and the AdS space's radius on the dark matter particle's zero-momentum mode's behavior. Furthermore, we derive an equation that reflects the interplay between the dark matter particle and the black hole and discuss the model's limitations. Our results demonstrate how the properties of the dark matter particle are influenced by its coupling to the black hole and the AdS space. This leads to oscillations in the dark matter particle's density profile and a linear relationship between the dark matter particle's mass density and the black hole's mass density. This model's findings also suggest that the dark matter particle's zero-momentum mode's behavior is analogous to a scalar field within an AdS space, surrounded by the black hole, and could provide insights into the formation of dark matter halos. This research's scenario can be viewed as a dark matter scenario within the context of brane cosmology and offers predictions that may be tested by future ultra-light dark matter detection experiments. Understanding the intricate processes of retinal development is crucial for grasping eye disorders and potential treatments. In vertebrates, new retinal cells, known as nuclei, originate from a single stem cell layer and migrate to their designated positions within the retina before differentiating. Despite extensive research, the underlying mechanisms governing this complex, dynamic process remain unclear. To gain insight into retinal development, we used high-resolution, three-dimensional imaging to track individual retinal cell movements across the developing chick retina at multiple stages. Our comprehensive data revealed a previously unidentified pattern of cell distribution, supported by mathematical analysis that shows the retinal cells follow a deterministic path, influenced by the retina's pre-existing structure. Our findings provide a foundation for understanding retinal development and highlight the importance of considering the spatial context in models of cell dynamics. Additionally, we found that the retinal development model can predict previously unknown aspects of retinal anatomy, including the distribution of retinal layers and the formation of the retinal vascular network. Notably, our model predicts the existence of a specific retinal layer distribution that was later confirmed through histological analysis of the adult chick retina. Our research demonstrates the utility of a data-driven approach in deciphering the intricate mechanisms governing retinal development and highlights the value of considering the spatial context in models of cell dynamics. Our model of the developing chick retina serves as a foundation for exploring the underlying mechanisms of retinal development and eye disorders, as well as identifying potential therapeutic interventions. A collaborative sparse sensing approach is proposed for recovering images in various applications, where a combination of conventional and compressive sensing techniques is utilized. The method involves splitting an image into two parts: a low-rank component and a sparse component, where the latter is recovered using a modified dictionary learning method and the former is obtained from the previous component. We've investigated the scaling behavior of active systems within the 2-5 dimensional range and found that their dynamics deviate from linearized hydrodynamics, resulting in a modified viscosity-to-temperature ratio. This deviation is particularly pronounced in the context of thermal phase transitions and fluctuation-driven flows, ultimately affecting the universality classes to which these systems belong. Specifically, we've shown that the universality class of the nematic-isotropic transition in an active nematic fluid is identical to that of the consignlet sector in the 3d O(3) sigma model, rather than sharing a class with the isotropic sector as predicted previously. This distinct classification arises from the non-trivial contribution of hydrodynamic modes to the renormalization of the nematic order parameter, a phenomenon observable through the power-law decay of nematic domains in the absence of thermal fluctuations. This research is relevant to ongoing and planned experiments focused on active nematic fluids and their behavior in two-dimensional and three-dimensional settings. As such, our findings highlight the significance of considering hydrodynamic effects in model simulations to ensure accurate representation of observed phenomena and dynamics. This study also provides a theoretical framework for the scaling behavior of active fluids in two- to five-dimensional settings, extending and refining existing hydrodynamic theories. This extension is particularly notable as many active matter experiments are, in fact, two-dimensional, despite current theoretical understanding being grounded in three-dimensional assumptions. This research is further relevant to the study of active polar fluids, which exhibit polar order and behave similarly to nematic fluids in many aspects, but require a separate analysis due to their distinct symmetry properties. This study predicts that thermal phase transitions in these fluids belong to a different universality class than predicted previously, with implications for the scaling behavior of their corresponding order parameters. This knowledge is crucial for understanding the power-law decay of polar domains in the absence of thermal fluctuations, as well as for the development of future experiments and simulations focused on active polar fluids. Deep Neural Network technology, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks, has significantly improved in image recognition capabilities. When applied to analyzing ID cards, it has shown potential in enhancing text extraction accuracy. However, achieving this accuracy requires a substantial amount of images and annotated data. This paper presents a cost-effective approach using limited data to enhance the effectiveness of Natural Language Processing. By integrating the ID card's layout information and utilizing part-of-speech tagging, it enhances the precision of text extraction. The proposed method was put to the test using ID cards from the Philippines and the results showed a notable improvement in text extraction accuracy. Our findings suggest that incorporating layout knowledge and part-of-speech tagging significantly enhances the accuracy of text extraction, with a 4.5% improvement for driver's licenses and a 3.5% increase for passports. The concept of a quantum phase space is highly debated in quantum mechanics, 
particularly in regards to driven and dissipative systems. Driven oscillators in 
their ground states serve as a notable example, as their state is determined by 
both their frequency and the driving force applied to them. We demonstrate that 
such state variety can be achieved with a Josephson junction as part of a SQUID 
system, driven by an external magnetic field, by utilizing coherent states of 
an electrical circuit. These states were then identified using a quantum tomography

Three small asteroids orbiting the solar system's center have been found to have rapidly spinning and stabilized axes, suggesting their origins might be linked to a specific planetary system formation theory. A team of scientists used data from various telescopes to analyze these objects' physical characteristics and movement patterns. By applying computer models to their findings, researchers discovered that the characteristics of two previously discovered asteroids can be explained by a model that quickly spins up small objects within a specific temperature range, likely found near a boundary between hot inner regions and cooler outer regions within a protoplanetary disk. The newly detected asteroid's characteristics align with this model's predictions, providing further evidence for its validity. The study's conclusions are also consistent with recent high-speed solar wind observations, offering a comprehensive understanding of the inner workings of a solar system. The detected asteroids' unique features make them valuable targets for further study with upcoming advanced telescopes. The team believes that studying these objects in more detail could provide a deeper understanding of the laws that govern the formation and evolution of planetary systems. The study's findings have been accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal and are also available on the arXiv server. Our findings demonstrate that this problem belongs to the same computational complexity class as detecting discontinuities in systems of polynomial equations over rational numbers, for which the best known approach requires cubic time and space up to a logarithmic factor, although we are unaware of any published proof establishing this time complexity. However, we show that deciding the continuity of rational functions with two variables is possible in polynomial time when the variables are restricted to irrational numbers. Additionally, we demonstrate that determining the continuity of rational functions with an arbitrary number of variables is computationally feasible for irrational variables, whereas for rational variables, this problem becomes essentially more complex than identifying the real roots of polynomial equations, for which we provide a direct reduction of sorts, and finally we establish that the latter problem has a high computational complexity similar to recognized benchmarks. We developed a method to address the finite-time reachability analysis problem in dynamic systems using feedback control. This approach utilizes barrier functions to define state inclusions and incorporates optimization techniques to efficiently compute state sets that can be reached within a given time frame. In contrast to existing methods that rely on discrete time models, our approach is compatible with both discrete and continuous time models. In particular, for continuous time models, we modified the approach to account for the presence of the derivative operator in the model dynamics. A system with a dynamics described by $\dot{x} = f(x,u)$ meets the required criteria if there exists a feedback control policy $k(x)$ and a function $b(x)$ such that the solution to the inequality $\dot{b}(x) \leq g(b(x),f(x,k(x)))$ from an initial state $x_0$ results in $b(x)$ belonging to a predefined set $\mathcal{C}$ within a time interval $[0,T]$. To solve the reachability analysis problem, we first convert it into a set of state inclusion conditions, then formulate an optimization problem to determine the smallest set of initial states that can be directed towards $\mathcal{C}$ within $[0,T]$ using feedback control. This optimization problem is then solved using a sequential convex optimization approach. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our method using two case studies involving a mobile agent and a coordinated group of agents. These studies highlight the importance of considering model uncertainties and feedback control in solving the reachability analysis problem. We also compared our approach against existing methods and found it to be computationally more efficient. Our research was published in the IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control. Humans easily distinguish living things from non-living objects, yet the boundaries between these categories can be ambiguous. For example, consider a robot that walks or a cloud that moves. To address this complexity, we propose a continuous model of categorization, stretching from non-animals to animals, and argue that this continuum can be explained by two fundamental factors: visual features and intentional behavior. We further contend that these two elements, which we call "visual animacy" and "intentional animacy," can be classified independently of one another. To support our claims, we conducted two experiments. In the first study, participants rated a wide range of objects and animals for their perceived animacy, and the results showed that these ratings could be predicted by a combination of their visual characteristics and whether they were considered intentional agents. The second experiment involved presenting subjects with ambiguous stimuli, such as a robot or a cloud, and found that the participants' categorization of these stimuli as living or non-living was influenced by both their visual appearance and whether they were perceived as acting purposefully. Notably, in this second experiment, the subjects' initial, instinctual categorizations were not influenced by their perceptions of agency or animacy, but rather their categorization was shaped by their subsequent interpretation of the object's behavior. The findings from these studies contribute to a nuanced understanding of the animacy continuum and highlight the significance of considering both visual categorizability and agency within it. The research also sheds light on the complex interplay between perception, categorization, and the interpretation of intentional behavior. The proposed framework of the animacy continuum, along with the methods used to investigate it, provide a foundation for exploring various real-world applications, including the development of artificial intelligence systems capable of recognizing living things. This logic enables us to derive precise, numerical specifications for programs, even when dealing with lossy or noisy computations. Specifically, we have shown that, with certain modifications, popular program verification techniques can be applied to ensure the validity of quantitative relational hypotheses for zero-knowledge proofs, secure multi-party computations, and other similar applications. Additionally, our approach facilitates the verification of programs that generate proofs of computationally private and auditable behavior. We have further extended our logic to accommodate verification of programs that adhere to both computational and statistical privacy requirements. A key aspect of our approach is the introduction of novel, sound weakening rules for both relational hoare logic and predicate transformers, both of which have implications for the verification of programs with noisy or lossy computations. We've developed a mathematical model that incorporates the effects of super-spreader events within enclosed settings, and applied it to analyze the transmission of an infectious disease at a gathering with a large number of attendees. This model, which includes variables representing the duration of super-spreader infections and the size of super-spreader transmissions, reveals its standard counterpart as a special limit. Numerical simulations demonstrate its predictive capabilities for the overall number of infections and the gathering's final size. Furthermore, our model facilitates an efficient algorithm for computing its equilibrium points, enabling us to study how the number of equilibrium super-spreader infections changes in response to alterations in gathering size and infection duration. As the model's parameters change, its equilibrium dynamics transition through various patterns, including a phase where the gathering size experiences exponential growth, and another where the size remains constant at a particular level. This research highlights the significance of considering the duration of super-spreader infections in predicting the outcomes of large-scale transmission events. This model can be applied to model the spread of other highly contagious diseases and conditions within confined populations. This study's findings also shed light on the critical role that gathering size plays in the dynamics of super-spreader events. This approach, which utilizes a parameterization of post-Poisson noise reduction, will help in better understanding the complex magnetic structures within solar active regions and potentially aid in real-time magnetism forecasting. This software will enable us to compare and contrast various magnetogram processing techniques and data sources. We will also utilize this comparison to establish a future data standard for vector magnetograms, with particular emphasis on optimizing data formats to facilitate efficient computation and data sharing. This will be particularly beneficial for facilitating collaboration and data exchange among researchers and forecasting teams utilizing vector magnetograms. Furthermore, our proposed standard will facilitate the development of automated processing pipelines for vector magnetograms, thereby making it easier to integrate this data into forecasting models and other applications. Deep complex neural networks have gained popularity lately due to their superior performance in various tasks, but their potential in Monte Carlo methods has yet to be explored. We introduce a novel complex-valued affine coupling layer, a fundamental component that can be part of high-performance Monte Carlo generators, such as deep complex flow or deep complex neural network architectures. Unlike traditional real-valued affine coupling layers, our method employs complex parameters and optimizes the learning process using the Monte Carlo target, resulting in faster convergence rates. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed layer by integrating it into a deep complex flow model and apply it to a high-priority simulation problem, showcasing substantial gains in sampling efficiency. Specifically, we achieve a 4 times speedup in sampling $y^{\delta}(0)$ compared to a real-valued generator, using just 500 training samples. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/ChengmingYang/dcfl}.
