Numerous machine learning tasks involve a sensitive feature that requires special care due to privacy concerns. This study focuses on optimizing performance on private data without directly accessing it, instead utilizing publicly available data from related tasks. We establish a theoretical bound for the optimal expected performance on private data in comparison to performance on public data. This is further expanded into a generalized framework where the expectation of performance on private data is shown to be related to the expectation of performance on public data, with a key component being a measure of similarity between private and public data. This framework is then applied to generate hypotheses for evaluating and improving several specific models, including those utilizing transfer learning and semi-supervised training. This research is relevant to machine learning models that incorporate side information and sensitive features. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for improving performance on private data without directly accessing it, with the aim of advancing the field of privacy-preserving machine learning. In this paper, we demonstrate the presence of a specific kind of walk within the group's structure that allows us to determine the number of spheres in a particular arrangement associated with it. As a result, we find that this number can be equivalent to the size of any given set of generators, which includes a subset consisting of right-handed generators. In addition, we establish a connection between the number of spheres in this arrangement and the volume of its associated root system. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which the Coxeter group exhibits no spheres in its structure, effectively characterizing those systems with this property. Finally, we provide examples of Coxeter groups that do and do not satisfy the property of having no spheres. As a related discovery, we find that the number of spheres in a Coxeter group's structure is unaffected by the addition of redundant generators. Based on the work presented in this paper, we establish a formula to calculate the volume of any given root system, which can be either irreducible or not. In the case of an irreducible root system, this formula yields the well-known result from Bilu and Lannes. Moreover, we introduce the concept of a Coxeter group's $k$-spherical aspect and investigate its properties. Additionally, we demonstrate that the volume of a root system can be determined from the super-spherical aspect of the corresponding Coxeter group. This leads to an alternative proof of the result established by Bilu and Lannes. Furthermore, we establish connections between the $k$-spherical aspect of a Coxeter group and various related geometric and combinatorial structures, including the Bruhat order, the weak order, and the strong order. Finally, we provide a formula to calculate the number of elements in the $k$-spherical subset of a Coxeter group, which allows us to recover the results established by Brink and Howlett, and by Dyer. This formula also enables us to investigate the asymptotic behavior of the $k$-spherical subset as $k$ approaches infinity. This behavior is found to be influenced by the geometry of the associated root system. In particular, we find that the ratio of the $k$-spherical subset's size to the total number of group elements converges to a value that can be determined from the root system's parameters when $k$ becomes sufficiently large. We examine the Bezier curves defined by four control points in three-dimensional space and investigate their classifications within the Bezier curve family. In Euclidean space, we find that only straight lines correspond to the Bertrand curve category. However, in both spherical and spherical-like spaces, we identify specific curve types that satisfy the Bertrand relationship conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that curves satisfying the Bertrand relationship in these spaces share the same geometric properties as their Euclidean counterparts. Additionally, we establish that a curve in these spaces can be determined using a single control point, and we provide a set of algorithms for constructing spherical-like Bezier curves from given control points. Finally, we explore the characteristics of curves that maintain the Berzzarella relationship in both spherical and spherical-like spaces and analyze their applications in computer graphics and geometry. Keywords: Bertrand curves; Bezier curves; spherical space; spherical-like space; curve construction; curve properties; computer graphics; geometry.

Training neural networks with loss functions that accurately reflect real-world labeling errors is crucial for achieving superior performance on classification tasks. This paper investigates the impact of KL Divergence, a fundamental loss function with significant applications in Generative Adversarial Networks, when used as the classifier loss. Surprisingly, we found that using KL Divergence as classifier loss results in subpar performance, significantly inferior to cross-entropy loss. To address this issue, we propose a novel distribution estimation method based on a regularized mixture density network. This approach allows us to transform the intractable optimization of KL Divergence loss into an efficient and scalable problem with a computationally attractive solution. We further develop a unified framework that combines the proposed method with the GAN framework, effectively bypassing the need to sample fake data and estimate discriminator's parameters. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on synthetic data and outstanding performance on real-world classification tasks. Specifically, our classification model surpasses top performance on SuperResolution, CrowdCounting, and PanopticSegmentation, demonstrating the versatility and efficacy of our approach. This research develops a thermomechanically coupled constitutive model for polymer materials that exhibits strain-induced crystallization. Building upon existing thermodynamic frameworks, we employ a dual formulation that accounts for multiple phases of crystallization and incorporates the effects of temperature and stress. Key features of the model include an internal variable approach, using the Gibbs free energy of crystallization as a driving force, and a rate-dependent crystallization kinetics equation. Additionally, we integrate the model into a finite element framework using a consistent linearization method for numerical stability. The model's capabilities are demonstrated through computational simulations of uniaxial tension and compression tests, and a thick-walled cylinder experiment. The results show that the model effectively captures the crystallization kinetics, temperature effects, and pressure-induced crystallization phenomena observed in real-world experiments. Our research focuses on the magnetic susceptibility of superconducting materials near a nodal ring, a type of Fermi surface with rotational symmetry in three-dimensional space. We examine the moment generation function of the magnetic field in these materials and derive a universal expression for their susceptibility in the superconducting state. When the energy of the magnetic field is low, we find that the susceptibility of these materials is determined by their superconducting energy gap and range of pairing, rather than their superconducting critical temperature. Our results also show that point nodes in a material's energy spectrum do not contribute to its magnetic susceptibility. Furthermore, we find that a material's Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction is related to its magnetic susceptibility and anti-ferromagnetic coupling, and can be inferred from this relationship. Our study is relevant to the materials Sr$_2$RuO$_4$, NbSe$_2$, and Cd$_2$As$_2$ and suggests that these materials's nodal ring energy spectra could make them suitable for magnetic field-induced quantum critical points. To enhance the connection between speech features and linguistic data within a neural network for speech recognition, a bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) is proposed to be part of the encoder's architecture. Initially, a convolutional neural network is used to encode speech patterns and generate a fixed-dimensional representation. This representation is then fed into a bi-directional attention module that produces weighted vectors of linguistic context based on their semantic similarity. These weighted vectors are then used in a recurrent neural network to project the speech feature to a linguistic space, allowing for a more precise alignment. Experiments conducted on the Librispeech corpus demonstrate the effectiveness of BiAM, achieving a 6.3% reduction in word error rate compared to a standard attention-based approach and a 2.4% decrease when compared to a neural network that utilizes convolutional layers alone. Furthermore, BiAM is found to outperform state-of-the-art models such as the Neural Conditional Random Field and the Neural Expectation Maximization algorithm by 2.4% and 2.1% respectively in the clean condition of the medium difficulty level of the Librispeech dataset. In addition to this improvements, BiAM also exhibits a more stable performance when training on noisy data. The proposed bidirectional attention mechanism is a flexible and efficient method to incorporate linguistic context that can be applied to various neural network architectures for speech recognition. Unlike the common gradient norm, this $p$-norm-based regularization allows us to trade off smoothness for computational cost, given that larger values of $p$ lead to a decrease in computational expense. Our approach can be combined with dropout techniques to further improve performance. Moreover, I prove that this $p$-norm-based regularization formulation is equivalent to an optimization problem involving an infinite number of convex miniprisms, which provides a theoretical foundation for this novel method. Our approach is applied to a range of tasks, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and a game-based control problem, and the resulting models are found to achieve comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate that the choice of $p$ significantly influences the performance of neural networks and that our method can be used to obtain neural networks with a bounded Lipschitz constant, which is particularly valuable for safety-critical applications. This study investigates how contextualized word embeddings influence the effectiveness of neural coreference resolution and highlights the limitations of current models in capturing structural dependencies specified in centering theory. To validate the potential for improvement, we introduce a novel neural coreference resolution model that integrates structural dependencies from centering theory and employs multi-task learning to enhance performance. Our experiments using the DTREG tool on the MUC-7 corpus show that, without incorporating our framework, the model struggles to adhere to basic centering theory constraints but exhibits significant gains when our framework is added. To further analyze the impact of contextualized embeddings, we conduct an experiment using the BERT base model on the same corpus and MUC evaluation metrics, resulting in a notable improvement but also revealed model limitations due to its inability to capture long-distance structural dependencies. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Contextualized Structured Memory Network that effectively leverages both contextualized embeddings and a learned graph-based structured memory to capture long-distance structural dependencies, leading to a significant improvement in coreference resolution accuracy. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MUC-7 corpus with MUC evaluation metrics. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhanglei1993/CSMN.

Understanding indoor environments through WiFi fingerprinting has become increasingly popular, yet estimating the distance between geospatial points often relies on impractical, manual methods, such as Euclidean distance or path-based algorithms, which don't account for real indoor obstacles. To address this limitation, we propose an indoor distance estimation framework leveraging Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). By training CNN on a set of 2D WiFi vectors, it learns the shape of indoor spaces and their corresponding distance metrics. Our experiments using a large, real-world indoor dataset at a university campus show that this method outperforms traditional distance estimation techniques and accurately captures the layout of previously unseen areas. Furthermore, by integrating CNN with Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), we enhance its performance when dealing with sequential data from WiFi scans. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of deep learning in modeling indoor spaces and distance estimation, paving the way for more complex applications, such as routing and optimization, within such environments. Source code for this project is available at https://github.com/zhongyuan-liu/DeepIndoorDistance.

A multi-pass energy recovery linac can overcome the beam-RF breakdown limitation by fully or partially recovering the energy lost in the beam, but the impact of filling pattern design on beam-RF interactions and the minimum required RF power remains unclear. This paper investigates the impact of filling pattern design on beam-RF interactions and the minimum required RF power in a multi-pass energy recovery linac using a numerical method that considers beam-RF interactions in various sections and compares simulated beam patterns against measured data. The results show that the threshold current can be lowered by adjusting the filling pattern, allowing for the use of smaller RF power. For example, in a 325 MHz, 4-pass energy recovery linac, reducing the beam current by a factor of 2.5 is possible without beam-RF breakdown by optimizing the filling pattern, and this can be particularly beneficial for future energy recovery linacs with high repetition rates. The paper also presents an analytical model to estimate the beam-RF interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs and the required RF power to prevent breakdown, and this model is validated against numerical simulations. The limitations of the model are discussed, along with the need for further research into the impact of beam emittance and filling pattern design on beam-RF interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. Our analysis is applicable to surfaces of any given curvature and our findings are verified through numerical simulations of a random walk model mimicking polymer chains. We discover that the free energy linked to chain stretching is directly proportional to the surface's mean curvature. This relationship holds true regardless of whether the surface is locally curved or if the surface is shaped into a cone or a cylinder. Notably, the proportionality constant includes the mean radius of the surface and the persistence length of the polymer chains. Our study's implications are relevant to polymer brushes found on the surfaces of vesicles, membranes, and nanotubes. Moreover, our work's underlying mathematical framework is extendable to higher-dimensional surfaces and provides a valuable theoretical foundation for understanding the behavior of polymer brushes in various curved geometries. Schematically, our results can be represented as follows: any variation in surface curvature $\Delta C$ results in a corresponding change in free energy $\Delta F$ according to the ratio $\Delta F / \Delta C = \kappa$, where $\kappa$ represents the surface's mean curvature, the free energy linked to chain stretching, the mean radius of the surface, the persistence length of the polymer chains, or the angle of the cone or the length of the cylinder. Our research also reveals that the distribution of chain end-to-end distances is shifted towards longer distances when the surface curvature increases, while the distribution's width remains unchanged. Specifically, we establish an inequality that shows the reduced metric dimension of a truncated graph is less than a predetermined value, in proportion to a smaller value, when the graph's geodesic distance is limited to a certain range. This research extends previous findings related to graphs with unbounded metric dimension and provides individual proofs for particular cases, including linear trees, certain types of toroidal graphs, and graphs based on circulant connectivity, each with unique properties. Additionally, we provide an illustrative example highlighting the tightness of the inequality, and we outline potential directions for further study.

Applying this method, we found that the entropy of light curves distinguishes periodic from aperiodic components and differentiates objects with similar luminosity but distinct variability patterns. Furthermore, we used a non-parametric method to identify periodic components and calculated the duration of their cycles, finding that they tend to increase with the time elapsed since the big bang, particularly at $z\sim1.7$. We also observed a positive correlation between entropy and redshift, likely resulting from the viewing angle effect, and a positive correlation between entropy and black hole mass, possibly due to the growth of supermassive black holes. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of differential entropy in uncovering the physics of AGN variability and support the co-evolution hypothesis of black holes and their host galaxies. Our research also presents a large dataset of 10,000 variable quasars with measured component periods, offering a valuable resource for further investigation. Our study's findings are consistent with the idea that massive black holes grow in tandem with their host galaxies. In settings with multiple agents making collective decisions, effective mechanisms require approximate welfare maximization to ensure fairness for all participants. Unfortunately, achieving optimal welfare is computationally challenging, and we must rely on algorithms that find acceptable substitutes. To evaluate the quality of these solutions, we examine valuations based on matching in bipartite graphs and on directed cuts, which provide upper and lower bounds on the true welfare values. We then utilize these benchmarks to establish performance guarantees for various greedy and approximate optimization methods in combinatorial domains, including market equilibrium, network flows, and facility location. Our research reveals that these benchmarks offer valuable insights, enabling the development of efficient algorithms that for bipartite matching and directed cuts, can solve problems to different levels of approximation in polynomial time. Our work also highlights the limitations of these benchmarks in other contexts, demonstrating that we cannot achieve certain approximation ratios, and by doing so, we establish a fundamental understanding of the relationships between these valuations and the performance of corresponding combinatorial optimization problems. Our results build upon our earlier findings and provide a comprehensive framework for evaluating the quality of solutions obtained from various greedy and approximate algorithms in a range of applications. Our research has implications for the design of efficient mechanisms in settings with multiple agents, highlighting the value of bipartite matching and directed cut valuations as general frameworks for designing and analyzing mechanisms that prioritize fairness in decision-making scenarios. Our work also offers a fundamental understanding of the relationships between these valuations and combinatorial optimization problems, demonstrating that we can achieve different levels of approximation in polynomial time for specific domains, and that we cannot achieve certain approximation ratios in other domains. The detection of small binary asteroids from wide-field surveys like Pan-STARR1 poses a challenge due to limited positional data. A statistical approach to assess the likelihood of asteroids being part of a binary system has been developed, leveraging the point spread function analysis techniques similar to those used in binary asteroid identification from high-resolution imaging. This method considers the distribution of light within an object's detection and estimates the binary fraction as a function of an object's size, by comparing observed sizes of detected secondaries to those predicted by a binary fraction model. Based on Pan-STARR1 observations of 1839 near-Earth asteroids, the binary fraction was found to vary with orbital energy and orbital period, and estimates of the Earth-crossing binary asteroid population were made for different size ranges. The study also found that the ratio of binary asteroids to single ones decreases as size increases, and a previously reported size-dependent binary fraction trend was confirmed. The estimated fraction of binary asteroids with a primary component in the size range 0-1 km is 0.8 plus/minus 0.2, and the estimated time required to form a binary asteroid through gravitational disruption following a close approach to Earth is 10 to the power 4 years. The study suggests that many small asteroids that experience close approaches to Earth may break apart into binary or even ternary systems, and eventually merge into larger bodies. The estimated fraction of binary asteroids in the total population of 100 to 500 meters in size is 0.5 to 1.0, and the estimated time required to form a binary asteroid through gravitational disruption following a close approach to Earth is 10 to the power 4 years. The paper presents a theoretical model of binary asteroid formation based on gravitational disruption following close approaches to Earth, and uses this model to estimate the size distribution of secondary components and compare it with observations.

The task of analyzing network peer effects through variable interactions has been made more accessible by recent advancements in econometric methods. Our research further refines these developments by introducing a generalized framework that can capture multiple interactions between variables and a diverse range of network structures. This streamlined approach eliminates the need to specify separate models for each variable's peers and enables estimation via semi-parametric techniques. We demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of this generalized framework through simulated data and real-world examples, including an analysis of voter behavior in the 19th-century US House of Representatives. This historic dataset presents both methodological and empirical challenges, including limited control variables, missing data, and complex network dynamics, yet our model successfully extracts meaningful insights from the data. Our findings indicate that our methodological approach can accurately capture peer effects within the context of these challenges, thereby expanding the range of possible research questions that can be explored. Our framework is available for use through an online repository, allowing for further customization and adaptation by interested researchers. Our empirical discovery that voting in accordance with constituents' wishes is associated with increased re-election chances, in turn fuels further investigation into peer effects within this dataset, in addition to contributing to the existing literature on peer effects and providing a methodological tool for future research. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/andrewc-wang/network_peer_effects. Our empirical discovery is also featured in a related policy brief that can be found at https://www.hamiltonproject.org/policy_briefs/how_voting_with_constituents_influences_election_outcome. In our research, we developed a theory-of-mind based cooperative multi-agent learning framework that enables agents to effectively collaborate and achieve their shared objectives in complex dynamic environments. This approach allows agents to accurately infer each other's mental states and goals, and adapt their behavior accordingly. We tested the effectiveness of our method in two challenging scenarios: a competitive game where an agent must outsmart a rival, and a cooperative problem-solving task where multiple agents work together to overcome an obstacle. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating a theory-of-mind component into our previous successful cooperative learning algorithm enhances the agent's performance and ability to adapt to changing situations, even when the other agent is using a different learning approach. Specifically, this approach leads to improved performance in both the competitive game and the cooperative task, and allows the agent to recover from failures more effectively. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ChengxiangPan/TOM-CAML.

Deeper analysis of protein folding pathways is crucial for comprehending the evolution of complex topological structures within proteins. This study focuses on "shallow knotted" proteins that contain a single trefoil knot and limited crossings, examining their folding routes in comparison to more intricate "deeply knotted" proteins. Through a comprehensive assessment of 13 "shallow knotted" proteins, researchers discovered that their folding pathways diverge significantly from those of deeply knotted proteins. A proposed model, supported by molecular dynamics simulations and NMR structures, suggests that the formation of trefoil knots within these proteins occurs through distinct mechanisms that involve either a loop that closes back on itself or interactions between two separate chains. Notably, the protein "thaumatin" stands out from the rest, as its unique folding route involves a distinct trefoil knot formation that is unprecedented in known protein structures. This study's findings highlight the importance of considering a protein's topology when predicting its three-dimensional structure, and it also provides a framework for classifying the complex structures found within "shallow knotted" proteins. Furthermore, the research revealed thaumatin's unique folding route, which could serve as a reference for understanding the dynamics of protein structure and evolution. This knowledge may also be applied in the creation of novel biologically active compounds, as thaumatin is an example of a protein with a highly stable and trefoil-knotted structure that is resistant to degradation. As a result, this study's findings have far-reaching implications for various fields, including molecular biology, biochemistry, and pharmacology. This research was conducted by a team of scientists from Japan and Poland. This study's findings were published in the scientific journal Nature Communications on July 17, 2020. Given a symplectic form on an oriented, closed $2n$-dimensional manifold $M$, an irrationality condition can be imposed by stating that the symplectic form's $n$-fold power has full measure with respect to a certain $SU(n)$ invariant measure. We demonstrate that for symplectic forms satisfying this irrationality condition on a $2n$-dimensional manifold with a specific topological characteristic, $H^{2}(M,\mathbb{Z})$ generated by the symplectic form, there exists a modified irrationality condition such that its fulfillment implies the form's topological invariance is unaffected. This result can be applied to control the topological characteristics of certain symplectic transformations and their associated domains. Additionally, we provide a modified version of the Reeb variational principle, which enables the determination of a form's topological characteristics when these characteristics are preserved under a specific class of variations. This approach can be viewed as an expansion of the ideas presented in the works of W.K. Alves, M. Corberi, and A. De Nicola, and A. Panazzolo, and A. Salazar. This research was motivated by the study of Hamiltonian flows within the context of surface homeomorphisms. As a result, we establish the topological invariance of the first return map associated with a class of Hamiltonian flows defined on surfaces. This invariance is linked to the topological characteristics of the flow's associated measure, which is derived from the measure induced by the first return map. Our research introduces Counterfactual Sensitivity Analysis through Guided Counterfactual Generation (CSG) to examine the behavior of machine learning models when exposed to counterfactual data. Counterfactuals represent hypothetical scenarios that could have occurred but didn't, and we utilize a method called Discriminative Counterfactual Selection (DISCO) to generate high-quality counterfactuals for a specific dataset. By incorporating a sensitivity component into the loss function of a guided adversarial framework, we develop a way to produce counterfactual instances that a model is likely to misclassify and which are consistent with the data it was trained on. We find that using a counterfactual dataset generated through DISCO to train models increases their robustness and enhances their ability to generalize to new data. Furthermore, we observe counterfactuals generated by this method to be of high quality and find that they align with human-conceived counterfactuals. Our research demonstrates the utility of CSG in evaluating model behavior through counterfactuals, analyzing model robustness through adversarial counterfactuals, and providing a method for counterfactual data augmentation. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhongyuan-liu/CSG. Our results also shed light on the limitations of current counterfactual generation methods and the challenges of evaluating the quality of counterfactuals. Our research paves the way for further investigation into the quality assessment of counterfactuals. Our findings are validated on multiple classification tasks using real-world datasets, and we believe they are applicable to unsupervised counterfactual generation settings as well. Our approach to training models on counterfactual data demonstrates improved model performance in both robustness and generalization according to model loss and results from human evaluation. Our research reveals that the quality of counterfactuals has a significant impact on their effectiveness in enhancing model behavior and that the best counterfactual generation method varies depending on the characteristics of the dataset in question. Our analysis of the issues surrounding counterfactual quality assessment is accompanied by our attempt to develop a set of guidelines for future research in this area. Our findings are expected to contribute to the advancement of counterfactual generation and evaluation methods. Our code for generating counterfactuals using DISCO is available at https://github.com/zhongyuan-liu/DISCO. Researchers synthesized epitaxial materials on a graphene substrate using chemical vapor deposition and observed the formation of distinct regions within the material. Depending on the growth temperature, the material's epitaxial relationship with the graphene changed, resulting in four distinct $K$-point locations within the Brillouin zone. Notably, temperatures between 1000°C and 1050°C led to the coexistence of two different epitaxial configurations within a single material layer, creating an Moiré pattern. By varying the growth temperature from 950°C to 1100°C, the material's epitaxial relationship evolved from the edge of the Brillouin zone to the center, and finally back to the edge, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between lattice mismatch, surface energy, and graphene's influence on material synthesis. The temperature-dependent transformation also enabled the creation of a superlattice with a 1.5 nm periodicity, potentially useful for applications in nanotechnology. The versatility of this method was demonstrated by synthesizing epitaxial materials from both transition metals and main group elements, including a 10 nm thick layer of silicon on graphene, a material combination previously thought incompatible. The findings of this research provide a foundation for the large-scale synthesis of epitaxial materials on graphene, offering a high degree of control over the material's structure and enabling the creation of novel nanoscale patterns and superlattices. The method developed in this study also enables the synthesis of graphene-based nanomaterials, including nanotubes and nanosheets, and allows for the controlled transfer of epitaxial materials to other substrates. The resulting materials exhibit unique properties, including a 10-fold increase in carrier mobility compared to traditional silicon, and demonstrate great promise for use in high-performance electronics and energy applications. We introduce a novel sampling approach called single-to-multi (S2M) that generates supplementary multi-label data without a significant increase in annotation expenses, drawing on the principle that people often assign multiple labels to a single piece of text without explicit guidance. Our analysis reveals that when annotating text for a single task, annotators frequently assign additional labels to the same text in an unstructured and often inconsistent manner. To capitalize on this phenomenon, we developed the S2M sampling technique for data collection, which involves instructing annotators to label the same text for multiple, unrelated tasks. Our experiments with multiple datasets showed that training models on these additional labels, even when considered noisy, can yield substantial gains in performance on multiple tasks with only a minor increase in data requirements. To maximize the benefits of S2M data, we introduced a semi-supervised learning framework that incorporates techniques such as label noise reduction and knowledge distillation to enhance the efficacy of this data in reducing the need for annotated data and improving overall performance. Our findings demonstrate that S2M data can be particularly valuable in low-data scenarios and that our proposed framework effectively leverages this data to achieve notable gains in multiple tasks. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/zhongyuan-liu/single-to-multi.

We introduce a new notion of weak naturality in categorical settings, which is essentially a relaxed version of the concept of weak adjunctions. This involves two functors, F from the category C to universal objects within a category E, and G from the category C opposite to universal objects within a category E bar. We show that a pair of functors F and G satisfy weak naturality if and only if there exists a weak adjunction between the category C and the category C opposite. As a result, we derive a universal property for weak adjunctions, which extends the existing properties of adjunctions. This new property has implications for the study of monads within categorical theory. Furthermore, it enables us to investigate weak adjunctions in connection to distributive laws, specifically the star Kock-Zanella monad. This analysis paves the way for exploring the properties of weak adjunctions within the context of tracts, which are collections of endofunctors equipped with specific structural properties. As an example, we examine the weak adjunction associated with the monad for propositional logic, which in turn allows us to investigate the properties of the monad itself. This investigation reveals that the weak adjunction associated with the star Kock-Zanella monad determines the properties of cartesian closures of the category of proofs for propositional logic. This, in turn, provides a categorical explanation for the properties of the lambda term equality theorem proved using the Barendregt's development of the Curry-Howard correspondence. This includes an analysis of the properties of the monad for lambda calculus, which was not previously part of the lambda calculus Curry-Howard correspondence. This extends the existing correspondence from typing and equality of lambda terms to showing that the lambda terms themselves form a cartesian closed category, which in turn yields the strong normalisation of lambda terms as a consequence of the cartesean closure induction. This outcome was not previously derivable from the original formulation of the lambda calculus Curry-Howards correspondence. This new understanding also enables us to establish the connection between the monad for lambda terms and the cartesian closure of the category of proofs for propositional logic at the categorical level, which in turn provides a formal explanation for the fact that lambda terms form a cartesian closed category. This outcome was not previously achieved using the lambda calculus Curry-Howard correspondence. The MAD model's ability to accurately explain the gamma-ray observations at GeV energies, particularly those from Fermi-LAT, relies on an assumed electron heating rate within the galactic bulge. However, this rate isn't directly supported by local observations of the ISM. An alternative approach is proposed, replacing the MAD model's standard assumptions with a more general model that incorporates the spatial distribution of the electron heating rate based on the 21cm hydrogen line mapping. By adjusting the parameters of this extended model, we can match the gamma-ray spectra from Fermi-LAT, but find it requires an unusually high electron heating rate within the bulge, exceeding the energy input from OB stars by an order of magnitude. Furthermore, this rate is found to be inconsistent with the local gas density and temperature profiles, and may also be incompatible with the observed gamma-ray spectra above 1 GeV. An analysis of the spatial distribution of the gamma-ray emission within 1 kpc of the galactic center also reveals an unexpected feature - a ring-shaped structure that isn't accounted for by the standard MAD model. This feature is, however, mirrored in the distribution of the electron heating rate inferred from the 21cm hydrogen line mapping, and could be indicative of a bar-shaped dark matter distribution within the galactic center. Ultimately, we find that the standard MAD model struggles to accurately explain the gamma-ray observations at GeV energies, and that a more nuanced understanding of the particle physics within the galactic bulge is necessary to fully capture the gamma-ray emission within the central kiloparsec. We propose a novel deep learning technique that utilizes a residual connection-based convolutional neural network for detecting cardiac abnormalities from noisy heart sound signals. This method leverages a multi-task approach by simultaneously analyzing sound signals and their denoised versions, thereby enhancing the robustness of its ability to identify cardiac issues. The introduction of a cardiac abnormality classification sub-network and a transfer learning-based feature extraction strategy further improves the method's performance. We tested this approach on two distinct datasets and obtained promising results, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately identifying cardiac abnormalities across various noise levels. Compared to existing techniques, our method shows improved results in terms of both performance metrics, according to leave-one-out cross-validation. Moreover, this approach exhibits a high level of consistency in performance across multiple datasets and variations in model size, thereby highlighting its potential for real-world cardiac sound analysis applications. Machine learning models on wearable devices for activity recognition require significant data and computational power for training, which poses a challenge for their development, particularly for certain user groups with limited access to resources.  A new collaborative learning framework called FedHealth aims to address these difficulties by combining federated learning with transfer knowledge and multi-task training.  FedHealth surpasses traditional approaches by allowing the fusion of health-related data and activity recognition on wearable devices, using a mixed-regularization approach to prevent overfitting and ensuring the security and privacy of user data.  The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through simulated and real-world experiments, showing that FedHealth achieves activity recognition accuracy on wearable devices that is 10-20% higher than conventional federated learning methods.  Additionally, FedHealth yields a robust model capable of identifying falls from wearable data, outperforming baseline models by 30-40%. This research focuses on solving backward stochastic differential equations with
two underlying diffusions, denoted as $X$ and $Y$, where the payoff function $f$ is
philanthropic in the sense that it benefits from the underlying $Y$. We derive an
integral expression for the solution component related to the diffusion $Y$ and
determine the optimal payoff as being directly proportional to the square root of
the underlying $Y$. Furthermore, we establish a connection between our solution and
previous results involving a single diffusion, and we also provide a numerical method
based on a Monte-Carlo scheme. Additionally, we provide an empirical study on the
performance of our solution in a real-world application involving electricity prices.

We calculate the exact size of the largest intersection between two metric balls in a Cayley graph, using Hamming distance as the metric, for binary codes of a specific length and error rates of 1 and 2. Our analysis applies to random key generation and a related problem, and provides a lower bound on the size of the largest intersection for arbitrary error rates 1 and 2. For error rate 1, the largest intersection corresponds to the set of all binary strings with at most one incorrect position, which can be represented as the edge set of a Hamming graph. We identify the vertices of the largest intersection for error rate 2, which involves checking the parity of up to two positions. Both cases have implications for random key generation and a problem involving secure group communication. We also discuss an optimization problem to minimize the size of the largest intersection for arbitrary error rates. Our approach can be generalized to other metric spaces and random protocols, and we outline an application to combinatorial geometry. Finally, we provide a solution to the optimization problem for a family of polynomial codes, known as Reed-Muller codes, offering insights into their structure. Our approximate analytic expressions for the variance of gravitational wave backgrounds due to continuous gravitational waves from neutron star glitches have been validated against numerical simulations for different pulsar timing array experiments. By comparing our results to existing studies using closed-form equations, we found our alternative approach provides similarly accurate representations of the variance, with average discrepancies of $0.01$ or less. These approximate expressions can efficiently handle large datasets and realistic noise levels, and we suggest using either set of equations interchangeably. Our research also highlights the importance of correctly accounting for the distribution of glitch amplitudes and their correlation over time, and we propose a novel method to simulate these properties based on the Vela pulsar's observations. Ultimately, our work supports the use of approximate models to forecast the detectability of GW glitches from Vela and other pulsars with similar characteristics. Given the computational intensity of current PTA data analyses, our efficient approach could serve as a valuable tool for exploring different scenarios and detecting GW glitches, with one optimized code run taking approximately 15 minutes to complete. Our code is available online for public use.

We present a new computational approach for estimating model parameters in differential models based on observed data, incorporating constraints that ensure the model's trajectories fall within a specified region. This method, which utilizes a mixture of parametric and non-parametric elements, is particularly suited for applications in epidemiology, such as modeling epidemic spread and vaccine effectiveness, and managing mobile populations, such as studying the spread of diseases in urban environments. Unlike traditional optimization methods, our approach enables the incorporation of biological feasibility constraints that prevent model components from becoming negative or unrealistic, even when fitting to incomplete or inaccurate data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to synthetic and real-world datasets, and compare it to existing optimization techniques. Our results show that this method provides accurate and biologically plausible parameter estimates, and can be more reliable than existing methods, especially when constrained models are partially misfit. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be efficiently applied to large models and complex problems, and offer guidelines for optimizing model size to balance accuracy and computational efficiency. A sample implementation of the method is available in the form of the EpiModel Python package, which is designed to estimate model parameters from observational data, and includes pre-built models for studying the spread of diseases within mobile populations. This package is accompanied by a companion paper that presents a detailed analysis of a specific application, namely the estimation of vaccine effectiveness in a real-world measles outbreak. This application, which is based on a previously published study, is used to evaluate and refine the approach, and includes a description of the model, methods, and results, as well as guidance on how to apply and extend the methodology for other purposes. Our research involves studying a one-dimensional Bose-condensed gas that undergos atom-molecule conversions, driven by an oscillating potential. By developing an "effective non-rigid pendulum model", we've created a simple, yet dynamic framework that captures the intricate, bidirectional coupling between the atoms and molecules. This model reveals the emergence of an internal degree of freedom, allowing us to analyze the system's behavior through a combination of analytical and numerical approaches. By applying this method, we gain insight into the complex, atom-molecule interactions and their resulting instabilities. Furthermore, we find that the model's pendulum-like behavior can lead to complete atom-molecule conversion, facilitated by initial conditions and the duration of the driving potential. Additionally, we observe the onset of oscillatory behavior and the formation of molecule-rich domains within the system. Notably, the model demonstrates that the system can become "trapped" in a state of partial conversion, resistant to changes in the driving frequency. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the intricate dynamics governing atom-molecule interactions and offers a versatile framework for studying analogous quantum systems. It also highlights the system's propensity for complete atom-molecule conversion and its resilience in the face of frequency changes. This study is relevant to current quantum technology aimed at generating and controlling long-lived molecules within Bose-Einstein condensates. It is also applicable to other analogous systems, including coupled optical resonators and spin-oscillations in chemical physics. In DNA data storage systems, retrieving stored data is a complex and time-consuming process due to the non-linear relationship between sequence queries and data retrieval. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various methods that pre-process data before storage. One such approach, using primers to break down large data sets into manageable storage units called DNA molecules, has shown promise. However, managing storage partitions poses a significant computational problem, as it requires identifying optimal primer pairs. To tackle this difficulty, two strategies have been developed: one that divides data sets, and another that divide sequences. Both of these approaches rely on primer pair design, which is a challenging task on its own due to the interplay of multiple factors including primer specificity, data fragmentation, and storage efficiency. To address this challenge, we developed a design framework called Efficient Fragmentation through Primer Selection (EFPS), which takes into consideration the characteristics of sequencing machines, primer pair design, and storage management. By leveraging a novel representation of data fragmentation patterns, EFPS employs a linear model to predict fragmentation costs and a greedy algorithm to find optimal solutions. Through extensive simulations, our results showed that EFPS achieves better storage efficiency, reduces the number of required molecules, and shortens retrieval time compared to existing methods. To facilitate further research and practical applications, we have publicly available the code and evaluation tools for EFPS. Furthermore, we outline potential research directions and discuss the limitations of our proposed framework. Understanding and modeling river systems relies on combining remote sensing and in-situ data, and developing efficient statistical methods to analyze these combined data sets.  For many applications, geostatistical methods are widely used, but they can be computationally intensive due to the need for multiple iterations between modeling and interpolation steps.  To address this challenge, we have created a fast and efficient geostatistical algorithm called Principal Component Geostatistical Algorithm (PCGA), which leverages the principles of dimensionality reduction and matrix operations to optimize performance.  By applying PCGA to a study of the Rio Iguacu, we successfully estimated the riverbed bathymetry using flow velocity measurements from acoustic Doppler current profilers, and the results showed that the method accurately captured key features of the riverbed terrain.  Compared to traditional geostatistical approaches, PCGA significantly reduced computational costs while producing comparable or better estimates of bathymetry, demonstrating its potential for efficient modeling of large river systems.  As a testament to the method's flexibility, we have also made PCGA available as an open-source tool for the community to use and adapt for various hydrodynamic applications.  To facilitate further development, we have made the code available on GitHub at https://github.com/igaucu-group/pcga.  We encourage researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us in refining and expanding the capabilities of PCGA in modeling complex river environments.  To support reproducibility, we have also made available the data and code used in this study at the following link: https://doi.org/10.7910/dev/3223915.  Future directions for PCGA include incorporating additional variables and non-stationarity in the model, and exploring its potential for modeling estuarine and coastal systems.  We believe that PCGA has the potential to revolutionize the way we analyze and model combined data sets in hydrodynamics, and we look forward to collaborating with the community to realize its full potential.  We have also made available the code for a related algorithm called Riverbed Bathymetry Estimation using Geostatistical and Machine Learning Techniques (RBEST), which combines PCGA with a machine learning model to improve the accuracy of bathymetry estimates.  We hope that PCGA and RBEST will contribute to a new era of efficient and accurate modeling of river systems. The challenge of creating High Dynamic Range (HDR) images has been a persistent issue in photography, particularly in outdoor settings where the difference between light and dark areas is most pronounced. To address this, camera exposure settings are adjusted to capture a wider range of brightness levels, but this often results in over-exposed or under-exposed areas in single exposure images. To counter this, various methods have been developed to select optimal exposure settings, leveraging both technical and visual principles. In the quest to improve these techniques, a new approach is proposed that utilizes a single HDR image as a training dataset, extracting a decision tree from data that allows for the prediction of optimal exposure settings based on image features. Unlike existing methods that rely on complex algorithms, this approach is more straightforward, yielding a clear understanding of the factors that influence exposure setting decisions. Experimental evaluations reveal that this method compares favourably to existing approaches, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing the quality of HDR images. To facilitate further research, a dataset of 1,000 HDR images is made available, along with the associated exposure settings, on the project website. This new perspective leverages the recent application of the degree-theoretic form of the Riemann-Hurwitz relation, yielding a set of equations that map surface symmetries to outline graph symmetries. We develop a non-singular coercive BDDC operator for $n\times n$ complex matrices with respect to a non-overlapping subdomain partition of type one-way, based on a set of minimal face constraints. The operator acts on pairs of subdomain matrices, producing a consistent local component and an interdomain component that form a pair whose sum equals the original matrix. The interdomain component is defined by solving a small linear system with a coefficient matrix given by the collection of constraints on faces of the subdomains. Theoretical coercivity and singularity estimates are established, along with an $O(n^3)$ setup procedure and $O(n^2)$ application procedures for the operator. We examine the interplay between cross-phase modulation and self-phase modulation in a loop resonator with identical counterpropagating light modes. Analyzing the strength of these non-linear effects under identical conditions, we find that cross-phase modulation significantly exceeds self-phase modulation by a factor of at least 4, reducing to 2 when the loop is partially filled. This distinction holds true regardless of the light's polarization state. Our study also reveals that the peak intensity of the self- and cross-phase modulation signals occurs at different points within the loop, and we provide explicit expressions for the induced phase shifts in both their uniform and peak forms. These findings have implications for the use of loop resonators in nonlinear optical applications. Reinforcement learning algorithms are frequently evaluated using a static evaluation environment, but this approach doesn't account for how settings typically evolve in real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose a method to assess the performance of a reinforcement learning agent by examining its ability to adapt to a dynamically altering curriculum, which is representative of a broad spectrum of changing settings. In contrast to traditional metrics, this approach measures an agent's proficiency using a benchmark that assesses progress through a sequence of progressively more challenging settings. We argue that this assessment is more relevant to real-world applications and provide a theoretical analysis of how well it correlates with measures of performance in specific dynamic environments. To support large-scale RL research, we introduce a systematic framework for controlled curriculum modification and leverage it to investigate several key findings about the performance of various RL baselines and three representative learning agents, including MAX-Q, MAX-A, and MAX-H, by examining their performance in a comprehensive set of evaluations spanning 21 distinct settings. Our results demonstrate that the majority of RL agents are capable of adapting to dynamic settings, but many struggle with a common pitfall: overgeneralizing from easy settings and failing to leverage the information provided by harder settings. To address this challenge, we outline potential solutions and propose future research directions. Our work is accompanied by publicly accessible code and evaluation data at the following repository: https://github.com/chenhao9999/rrc. Our research framework is also applicable to the study of other dynamic learning environments, such as meta-learning and few-shot learning. Our findings and methodology are expected to contribute to the advancement of RL research and provide a valuable assessment tool for the evaluation of various RL baselines. The Riemann-Hodge problem seeks to extend the compactification of the moduli space of smooth, projective algebraic varieties to include singular and irreducible varieties with Shimura properties. To tackle this issue, we focus on the compactification of the moduli space $\mathcal{A}_g$ and examine its relationship to the compactification of the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{g,1}$ for curves with one marked point. Specifically, we investigate how geometric and cohomological compactifications of $\mathcal{A}_g$ relate to the compactification of $\mathcal{M}_{g,1}$ and provide evidence for a proposed conjecture regarding this relationship. Additionally, we explore the connection between these compactifications and the Griffiths criterion for extension, as well as its connection to the cohomological compactification of $\mathcal{A}_g$. Furthermore, we establish that the cohomological compactification of $\mathcal{A}_g$ is equivalent to the geometric compactification defined by Mumford's compactification of $\mathcal{M}_{g,1}$ with level $\Gamma^{\text{geometric}}_1$, and demonstrate that this geometric compactification does not extend the moduli space to varieties with non-trivial automorphisms, thereby confirming a prediction made by Deligne and Mumford. Finally, we outline the steps required to solve the Riemann-Hodge problem for the moduli space $\mathcal{A}_g$ and discuss the related issues that arise when considering the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{g,n}$ for varieties with $n$ marked points.

To mitigate the challenges of large sample complexity and uneven negative sample distribution in Visual Relationship Detection, we introduce Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling, a method that leverages proposal balancing techniques commonly applied in classification problems. By assigning varying weights to negative samples based on relationship class frequencies, our approach ensures that the model is optimized with equal frequency for all relations. We further develop a novel data selection strategy that prioritizes training data assignment according to both proposal confidence and weighted sample importance. Experimental evaluations on the Visual Relationship Detection dataset demonstrate improved performance, with an increase in the mean AP score of 3.4% relative to the baseline model. The impact of accretion streams on the development of galaxies is a subject of growing interest and debate. To investigate this effect, we utilized a state-of-the-art hydrodynamic simulation with a galactic halo stream and a galaxy with a mass similar to that of the Milky Way. Unlike previous studies, this simulation modeled the interaction between a galaxy and a stream through high-resolution, three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations. It revealed that accretion streams can lead to the formation of bars, as they inject angular momentum into the galaxy's disk. However, this process is short-lived (less than 1 billion years) due to the disruption of the bar by tidal forces from the stream. As a result, the galaxy's central bulge grows more rapidly than expected. Furthermore, the distribution of elements like alpha-to-iron abundance ratios is not uniform across the galaxy's disk and bulge, as matter is transported from the central bulge to the outer regions through spiral arms. This research demonstrates that accretion streams can significantly influence a galaxy's evolution, particularly in its central regions, and its chemical composition. It also highlights the importance of considering the interplay between the galaxy's central bulge and its disk in the interpretation of spectroscopic data. Ultimately, it shows that the Milky Way's history might resemble that of Andromeda Galaxy, and that the accretion of small galaxies is crucial for explaining the observed abundance patterns in the solar neighborhood. Finally, it suggests that the detection of the galactic stream in the solar neighborhood might be hidden, and that future high-resolution, high-speed spectroscopy might be necessary to reveal it. It also implies that the accretion of the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy is insufficient to explain the observed abundance patterns in the solar neighborhood, and that the search for the progenitor galaxy of the Milky Way should focus on finding a galaxy with a mass similar to that of the Large Magellanic Cloud. A comparison of the gamma-ray and X-ray light curves revealed a delay of approximately 20 minutes between the peak gamma-ray emission and the peak X-ray emission, and the shape of the gamma-ray spectrum was found to be consistent with acceleration of relativistic particles over a period of several hours. KIC 9267654 is a solar-type star with an unusual rotation rate that differs between its equator and poles. To investigate this phenomenon, we used asteroseismology to analyze data from the Kepler space telescope and a stellar rotation profile model that incorporates differential rotation. Our analysis considered various input parameters, including the star's mass, radius, age, and internal structure, and applied Bayesian inference to evaluate their probabilities. We found that the most plausible explanation for the star's behavior is its relatively young age, approximately 480 million years, which is consistent with a rapid rotation period of about 4.5 days. However, we also discovered that KIC 9267654's characteristics fit the expectations for pre-main-sequence stars with conservative core contraction. Consequently, our results challenge the initial assumption that this star is a main-sequence star with differential rotation. Instead, we propose an alternative scenario in which the star's rotation is influenced by its internal dynamics rather than surface meridional circulation. Additionally, our analysis revealed that the star's core contraction could lead to variations in its oscillation pattern over time, and we expect these changes to become more pronounced within the next 10 million years as the star evolves towards the main sequence. As a result, KIC 9267654 presents a unique opportunity to observe the early stages of a star's life cycle through asteroseismology.

The rapid dissemination of information across social media platforms has made detection of fabricated news and rumors more pressing than ever. Given the vast amount of data involved, deep learning methods, specifically attention-based graph neural networks, have shown significant progress in this area. Our proposed MetaFEND model builds upon existing research by integrating a meta-learning framework with attention-based GNNs, yielding a more effective and adaptable approach. Unlike previous work that focuses on detecting specific types of misinformation, our model is designed to detect fabricated news in a general sense. Our results show that the MetaFEND model outperforms current state-of-the-art methods for both small and large-scale datasets. Furthermore, our model's adaptability to detect specific kinds of fabricated news is demonstrated, and our findings highlight the significance of incorporating visual information when detecting fabricated text. Text-based detection of fabricated news typically involves multi-task learning to leverage the semantic meaning of words and phrases. This research investigates a one-dimensional transport equation with nonlocal flow and no dissipation within a periodic framework. Contrary to similar nonlocal equations without transport components, we find that initial data with odd symmetry, smoothed to a certain degree, ultimately result in solutions with solutions composed of infinitely many sharp shockwaves that develop in a finite amount of time. To support this finding, we provide a key example of an odd function whose corresponding solution includes a sequence of shocks at regular intervals, occurring at specific time points, and affecting an ever-expanding portion of the domain. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even a single initial discontinuity will lead to a pattern of infinitely many shocks within the domain over time. Both of these results can be generalized to certain nonautonomous variants of the same equation. Additionally, we observe that a related partial differential equation, characterized by a specific nonlocal flux with no transport component, exhibits similar behavior, with the added feature that even odd data will yield solutions composed of infinitely many shocks. On the other hand, a variant of the transport equation with a nonlocal flux that is both anisotropic and anisotropically periodic, and no transport component, results in solutions composed of infinitely many shocks for both odd and even initial data. Both of these variants can be generalized to include time-dependent components. A quaternary Golay complementary array (QCA) consists of 4^7 arrays from G(4,7) such that any two have a Hamming distance of 2^7, and there are two distinct ways to group the arrays into pairs with complementary autocorrelation functions. We investigate the existence of QCA pairs and find them for dimensions 4^3 and 4^5, but determine that there cannot be QCA pairs for the dimensions 4^1, 4^3, 4^9. Additionally, we outline an approach to constructing QCA pairs for 4^7, and also provide a framework for quaternary complementary arrays with Golay complements in 4^7, but note that these arrays are distinct from QCA pairs. Furthermore, our research reveals that arrays with Golay complements in 4^7 can be used to construct balanced quaternary tight-knee-knee metric designs, extending the previous availability of these designs for dimensions up to 4^5. Moreover, our method for constructing arrays with Golay complements in 4^7 enables the creation of a balanced quaternary tight-knee-knee metric design from any linear code over the finite field F_4 with a dimension of 4^6 or 4^7, and a dual code with a dimension of 4^1 or 4^7, and without loss of generality, a trace function that is non-zero. This allows us to extend the range of balanced quaternary tight-knee-knee metric designs from dimensions 4^5 to 4^7. This research also presents an algorithm for constructing arrays with Golay complements in 4^7, utilizing a random and exhaustive approach to search for suitable linear codes and their duals over F_4. This algorithm was utilized to construct arrays with Golay complements in 4^7 from 22 random linear codes and 49 random dual codes, and also from 18 specific linear codes and 7 specific dual codes. This resulted in 22 distinct arrays with Golay complements in 4^7. These arrays were used to construct a balanced quaternary tight-knee-knee metric design Do(4^7,4^3) and an optimal quaternary linear code C_(4^7,4^3), and also provided the autocorrelation functions for these arrays. This research was partially presented at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics

Quantum computing using spin-exchange interactions in a silicon crystal lattice is a highly promising approach. Despite being a primary component of this method, the Heisenberg exchange interaction's variability with impurity placement remains poorly understood. To address this, we used a multi-orbital model to calculate the exchange interaction for different dopant configurations, specifically focusing on phosphorus and boron replacements. Our findings, which account for both valence and conduction bands, show that the exchange interaction can be either positive or negative, and even fluctuate in response to changes in Fermi level, due to filled and empty energy levels within the band. Furthermore, we discovered that the exchange interaction's dependence on the Fermi level can be explained by a balance between filled and empty energy levels, and that it is influenced by both valence and conduction bands. Our research also reveals that the exchange interaction's magnitude is more stable for deeper dopants, and that it is unaffected by the presence of either n-type or p-type dopants. Our work paves the way for a comprehensive understanding of the exchange interaction's behavior in silicon crystal lattices. To facilitate experimental verification, we provide a simplified expression for the exchange interaction based on dopant placement, and discuss potential device designs that could exploit the variability of this interaction. Our findings have significant implications for the development of quantum processors using silicon spin-exchange interactions. To facilitate further research, our multi-orbital model is compatible with both tight-binding and k.p methods. To facilitate verification of our results, we made our code publicly available. In this research, we develop an approach to reconstruct a complex system's probabilistic model using probabilistic inference, based on time series data from a similar system. This method enables the recovery of a probabilistic structured model for a new system instance, assuming access to a structured model and associated generative parameters for a comparable system. We extract a key component from our approach, a generative neural network that can sample continuous variables, and incorporate it into a structured model through a variational reinforcement learning framework. This results in a generative model that produces masked data variables, which are then used in a neural collaborative filtering method to predict variables in the target system. This prediction is shown to improve with increasing model complexity, measured by the number of structured variables. Our approach is tested on three real-world datasets, demonstrating improved performance over existing methods. The code for this research is available online. In addition, we observe an improvement in predictive accuracy with larger model complexity, as well as a study on the impact of different mask methods on variable prediction. In particular, we find that our approach generalizes the concept of knowledge graph embedding, as it employs node and edge embeddings similar to Knowledge Graph Embedding, but with distinct effects on variable prediction. In particular, node embeddings contribute more significantly than edge embeddings in predicting variables from the generative part of the model, whereas both node and edge embeddings contribute equally when predicting variables from the shared part of the model. This finding is consistent across all three datasets used in this research. In contrast, Knowledge Graph Embedding models treat node and edge embeddings equally. This discovery highlights the potential for further research into the distinct roles of node and edge embeddings in this type of model. In addition, we release a new dataset containing 10,000 instances of a generative model, along with associated time series data, for the purpose of evaluating the performance of our approach and potential variants in the future. This dataset is available online for research purposes. In the course of this research, we encountered difficulties with existing generative models that prevented us from utilizing them with our approach. This led to the development of a new generative model, which we call Graph Attention Variational Autoencoder (GAVAE), in order to overcome these challenges. GAVAE is a novel generative model that integrates the strengths of Variational Autoencoder (VAE) and Graph Attention Network (GAT) in order to improve performance. This model is specifically designed to tackle the limitations of existing models by utilizing a variational reinforcement learning framework to learn node and edge embeddings

This paper introduces a concept of graded power series in the setting of stable homotopy theory, establishing an isomorphism between graded polynomial rings and these power series. This isomorphism enables the interpretation of certain cohomology theories as graded power series. Specifically, it shows that the cohomology theory $H^n(X,R)$ is equivalent to the coefficient $R$ applied to the power series corresponding to $X$. This framework also facilitates an analysis of the structure of the stable homotopy category's ring object $SH(B)$, where $B$ represents a connective Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $B$. This involves demonstrating that the power series associated with $X$ and $Y$ being additively conjugate is equivalent to $X$ and $Y$ being homotopy equivalent, and revealing the connection to the Cauchy product of power series. Finally, this leads to an examination of the structure of the power series for the Moore spectrum $M_n(B)$, yielding a recursive formula that can be solved to obtain a combinatorial interpretation for the sequence of power series indices, mirroring the structure of partitions. This partitions-based representation serves as a foundation for a deeper exploration of the relationship between graded power series and the stable homotopy category's ring object $SH(B)$. This study's initial results have implications for a broader investigation of graded power series and their connection to the homotopy theory of superalgebras. This research's underlying ideas also lay the groundwork for a forthcoming study on the relationship between graded power series and the structure of the stable homotopy category's ring object $SH(B)$, specifically with regard to its relationship to the homotopy theory of superalgebras. A newly proposed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture is designed to enhance the accuracy of Regions of Interest (ROIs) in medical imaging by streamlining the image segmentation process. This optimized framework precludes the need to train separate classifiers for various medical conditions, instead focusing on a general classifier that identifies specific patterns indicative of abnormalities. A subsequent step involves training a generator using a ROI and the output of the classifier to produce a synthetic image that matches the desired characteristics. This technique, known as Adversarial Medical Image Synthesis (AMIS), leverages the classifier's feedback to refine the generator, and through extensive testing, demonstrates substantial improvements in both naturalness and diagnostic accuracy when compared to existing methods. Our team's findings also indicate that this approach can be applied to various medical applications, including the segmentation of tumors and organs, and showcases the versatility of CNNs in medical imaging by reducing the gap between real and synthetic images to less than 16%. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications for the field of medical imaging analysis, and our team is eager to explore the potential of this method in real-world clinical settings. Deep neural networks have achieved superior performance in various tasks, yet their complex nature and extensive training data requirements limit their practical applications. To address these challenges, a novel End-to-End Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction framework is introduced, which leverages Residual Neural Tee structures to combine non-linear feature extraction methods with multi-task optimization. This framework enables the selection of both unsupervised and supervised learning techniques to enhance the representation of input data. Specifically, it utilizes the t-SNE algorithm for unsupervised learning and an end-to-end optimization of classification losses for supervised learning. The proposed framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its ability to improve the representation of input data and achieve state-of-the-art performance in classification tasks. Evaluations of the framework's components also highlight the benefits of integrating supervised learning to improve the representation of input data. The code for this research is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ali-khassid, where users can access the proposed framework's source code and experiment with it using their own datasets.

We create an infinite number of distinct graph species that belong to either the $AC$-bridgeless or triangle-free categories, possessing cubical symmetry and alternating Hamiltonian properties. These graphs possess a $V$-shaped or right-angled structure and their vertex labelling can be defined using integer sequences that adhere to specific arithmetic patterns. A key aspect of our findings is proving that the proposed graphs possess a particular type of automorphism group classified as nilpotent of rank two. This achievement supplements our earlier success in generating a infinite variety of graphs with cubical symmetry and alternating Hamiltonian cycles, but now within the more restrictive category of triangle-free graphs. Our methods for achieving this also yield new insights into the structure of nilpotent automorphism groups. To produce these graphs, we develop an approach that leverages the properties of the integers modulo a specific prime number, namely 2, and apply this approach to a set of vertices labelled as the integers modulo 2, resulting in a subgraph with cubical symmetry that can be expanded into a larger graph meeting our criteria. Notably, this technique allows us to construct graphs with cubical symmetry and alternating Hamiltonian cycles among the integers modulo any given prime number, providing a solution to a problem initially proposed by Albertson in 1971. Our method also enables us to investigate the characteristics of nilpotent automorphism groups in more detail, revealing that they are equivalent to the groups associated with the integers modulo a given prime number, and can be extended to the ring of integers modulo a given integer, resulting in a new class of nilpotent automorphism groups referred to as the Galois groups.
