The Group Lasso algorithm has been successfully integrated into linear models, Generalized Linear Models, and Semi-Sparse Models to facilitate variable selection. We have now adapted this method for use in Generalized Linear Mixed Models, which can handle both continuous and categorical data. Our primary innovation involves redefining the Group Lasso penalty to accommodate sparse models with both fixed and random effects. We have also established the consistency of the Group Lasso estimator under a semi-sparse model and a growing number of observations. Our algorithm can be applied through a simple augmentation of the linear mixed model, and we have derived an iterative algorithm to solve the associated system of equations. This algorithm has a linear convergence rate under appropriate conditions. We have also conducted a simulation to evaluate the performance of the Group Lasso estimator in a mixed effects setting. This work has been incorporated into an R package named glmmGroupLasso, which is accessible on CRAN. We have further extended our research to incorporate Group Elastic Net penalty into the Generalized Linear Mixed Model framework. This work has been applied to the analysis of gene expression data, specifically in identifying co-expressed genes that are associated with a particular trait. This has been achieved by treating the model as a joint variable selection and latent factor model. We have used this approach to investigate the co-expression of genes associated with height in two different populations. This has been accomplished by utilizing a large public dataset known as GTEx. We have also conducted a simulation to assess the performance of the method in a controlled setting. This work has been utilized in a study that was recently published in Nature Genetics. Recently, knowledge-enhanced self-supervised models have demonstrated superior performance in various question-answering tasks. Our investigation delves into the source of this performance advantage by examining the underlying characteristics of these models. We pre-trained BERT and a knowledge-aware variant of BERT using both general text data and knowledge graph triples, specifically factual triples, and found that they exhibit improved performance in multiple question-answering tasks, including both factual and semantic questions. Our analysis reveals that the models pre-trained on knowledge graph triples often struggle with factual questions but excel in answering those questions, whereas those pre-trained on general text data serve as a baseline. We also observed that these models can tackle semantic questions with equal or superior success to those pre-trained on general text data. Our study provides insights into the behavior of these models and sheds light on their limitations, as well as offering a potential framework for constructing more effective self-supervised training tasks. Our code and model are available at https://github.com/zhongjie116/kb-bert. Our results have implications for the design of future self-supervised training tasks and highlight the significance of distinguishing between factual and semantic questions in question-answering evaluations. Our findings also suggest that the knowledge-aware BERT model is particularly adept at addressing questions whose answers can be represented as specific entities from a predefined list, which we term entity-targetted questions. We further explore this concept and demonstrate that models pre-trained using knowledge graph triples disproportionately focus on answering entity-targetted questions, even when asked questions whose answers are not listed in the knowledge graph. Our research also reveals that the knowledge-aware BERT model exhibits a bias towards selecting specific entities from the list, including instances where the chosen entity is semantically unrelated to the question being asked. Our study offers insights into the behavior of these models and raises concerns about their potential limitations in real-world applications. A proposed algorithm for printing text with line joins on curved paths is presented, which produces high-quality output while reducing paper and ink consumption for various fonts and sizes. This algorithm prioritizes rendering straight line joins and utilizes a novel technique to accurately draw fan-shaped joins, with a resulting aesthetic improvement and minimal perceptible difference from traditional printed text. In contrast to conventional methods, the proposed algorithm generates line joins along curved paths by utilizing a combination of B\'ezier curves and geometric calculations, producing smooth and sharp line joins without the need for image processing software. In addition, this algorithm was found to meet the requirements for line join rendering specified in PDF standards, with the added benefit of enhancing the visual appeal of printed documents. This potential can be realized through a Markovian dynamical process, demonstrating that a positive rate of entanglement generation is achievable. Deep learning models have shown superior performance in natural language processing tasks and our research aims to leverage this potential by applying Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks in sentiment analysis on Twitter. Given the high volume of Twitter data and the complexity of capturing long-range dependencies, our approach utilizes Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to achieve sentiment classification. We conducted two separate studies to evaluate the effectiveness of LSTMs. Firstly, we created a dataset comprising 1000 positive and 1000 negative tweets and trained an LSTM model on this dataset, resulting in an accuracy of 72.5%. To further validate our approach, we compared LSTM to another sentiment analysis method known as Naive Bayes and observed a significant improvement in accuracy. Secondly, we applied the LSTM model to classify the sentiment of 5000 randomly selected Twitter posts and achieved an accuracy of 65%. Our research demonstrates the potential of LSTMs in capturing long-range dependencies within sentences, thereby enhancing the precision of sentiment classification. However, we also discovered that the current implementation of our approach struggles with achieving high accuracy on a large Twitter dataset due to the limited capacity to capture short-range dependencies and the presence of noisy data. To further improve the model, we suggest integrating techniques such as word2vec or dropout into the LSTM network. We investigate a non-linear electrodynamics of Yang-Mills field within a spherically symmetric context and its effects on a charged AdS black hole. The non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter is shown to modify both the shadow radius and thermal profile of the black hole. The non-linear Yang-Mills field also leads to an increase in both the location of the inner horizon and the event horizon compared to the linear case. Furthermore, the non-linear Yang-Mills field causes a shift in both the temperature and electric potential at the event horizon. The phase transition from the AdS black hole to the Reissner-Nordström black hole is found to be influenced by the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter. The non-linear Yang-Mills field also affects the heat capacity and entropy of the black hole, leading to a change in the heat capacity from negative to positive at a certain critical temperature. The effect of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter on the heat capacity and entropy is analogous to the effect of the electric charge on the heat capacity and entropy of the Reissner-Nordström black hole. The heat capacity of the black hole is found to have a local positive peak with a value that is dependent on the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter. The relationship between the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter and the heat capacity peak is found to be inversely proportional. The framework of optical tomography is applied to investigate the time-evolution of both classical and quantum light properties. Our investigation focuses on the behavior of Wigner function-based optical tomograms as they evolve over time. Initially, we outline the method for reconstructing both the Wigner function and the optical density matrix from a single optical tomogram. Next, we examine the time-evolution of the Wigner function, specifically looking at how entanglement changes become apparent in optical tomograms. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, entanglement, and the spreading of wave functions in both one-dimensional and two-dimensional scenarios. Some examples of quantum systems, including a two-mode parametric amplifier, beam splitters, and Mach-Zehnder interferometers, are also presented to illustrate the dynamics of their optical tomograms. Additionally, we discuss the potential applications of optical tomograms in observing entanglement generation and destruction in various scenarios. Finally, we outline some potential experimental realizations of optical tomography, including coherent population transfer, atomic beam interferometry, and ion-trap systems. Our aim is to demonstrate the utility of optical tomography in visualizing the time-evolution of both classical and non-classical effects in light properties. Our work also provides a foundation for further research into the use of optical tomograms in investigating the dynamics of continuous-variable entanglement generation and its related effects. Our study is relevant to various fields, including quantum optics, atomic and molecular physics, and chemical physics. Our work is further applicable to ongoing and future experiments in quantum technology and chemistry. Our research offers a framework for interpreting experimental data from ion-trap systems, atomic beam interferometry, and coherent population transfer. Our investigation is also a theoretical foundation for proposed future experiments in ion-trap systems, atomic beam interferometry, and coherent population transfer. Our study is relevant to ongoing and future applications in quantum metrology, quantum simulation, and chemical reactions. Our work is a prerequisite for investigating the time-evolution of chemical reactions in molecules, as well as quantum dynamics in molecular aggregates and quantum dots. Our investigation is also a starting point for studying the time-evolution of quantum effects in molecular aggregates and quantum dots. Our research is further applicable to ongoing and future experiments in quantum chemistry and chemical physics. Immersive video viewing experiences are hindered by users' limited field of view, which affects video quality and battery life in mobile devices. To address this challenge, our research focuses on predicting viewer attention within videos, specifically for on-demand streaming services. Unlike traditional approaches, our method leverages video subtitles, an easily accessible feature for most online video platforms. We develop a subtitle-based attention prediction framework that employs a unique two-component model: a subtitle-aware attention network that analyzes video subtitles and a quality-aware attention network that considers video quality. This approach yields a quality-aware attention map, which guides our quality assessment model to evaluate video quality. Our results show that subtitle-based attention prediction outperforms existing methods and provides a more accurate prediction when combined with video quality assessment. Our approach also offers several advantages over other attention prediction methods, including reduced training data requirements and improved robustness to video quality. Our code and models are publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/zhengyiwang/subtitle-attention-prediction}. Our approach can be applied to various video streaming platforms and has the potential to improve video streaming efficiency, even without viewer interaction data. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of video subtitles in enhancing viewer attention prediction, a crucial step towards more efficient and immersive video streaming. Experimental evaluations and comparison with existing methods are also presented in the paper. Our approach has been tested on two large-scale video datasets: MSVD and VGP-S, consisting of 5.5 million video subtitles and 20,000 attention maps, respectively. The gluon distribution within a hadron, expressed as the number of gluons per unit rapidity in a proton, has been estimated using the e+e- annihilation data from LEP. This analysis takes into consideration the impact of infrared renormalons on the uncertainty, which is found to contribute a significant 10% to the overall uncertainty. A non-perturbative power-correction estimate, based on the Glauber-Mueller model, is employed to evaluate the uncertainty, which is then used to update the gluon distribution within a hadron. This revised distribution is referred to as MRSA_GLO and serves as a replacement for the traditional MRSA gluon distribution. The resulting MRSA_GLO gluon distribution is compared to other contemporary distributions, demonstrating its consistency with these alternatives. The uncertainty in the gluon distribution is reflected in the construction of two parton distributions: one with minimum glue content, denoted as MRSA_GLO_MIN, and a more generous version, denoted as MRSA_GLO_GEN. Both of these distributions are utilized to calculate the central value of the strong coupling constant, which is found to be 4.26 ± 0.05, in accordance with the definition of $\alpha_s$ based on the gluon distribution within a hadron. The resulting $\alpha_s$ value is in line with previously obtained estimates. The impact of the uncertainty in the gluon distribution on the prediction of certain physical processes is demonstrated using the example of hadronic event shapes measured in deep inelastic scattering. The use of MRSA_GLO and MRSA_GLO_GEN is compared to alternative approaches to estimating the uncertainty associated with the gluon distribution. The findings of this analysis underscore the significance of accounting for the non-perturbative effects on the gluon distribution within a hadron, which is seen as a crucial component in the assessment of the overall uncertainty in theoretical predictions of physical processes. The associated code can be accessed via the Durham database, reference number DASH-2022-01. The uncertainty in the gluon distribution is further utilized to reevaluate the uncertainty in the strong coupling constant, the charm quark mass, and the hadron parton distribution moment $\langle x^- \rangle$. The resulting values are as follows: $\langle x^- \rangle = 0.439 \pm 0.013$, $m_c = 1.287 \pm 0.023$ GeV, and $\alpha_s(\langle x^- \rangle) = 4.

This study investigates the optical properties of a magnetophotonic crystal with a gold layer, specifically a GdFeCo film with surface plasmons and a missing row defect that creates a Rayleigh anomaly, when studied using spectroscopic ellipsometry. We developed a model to interpret the results, accounting for the interference between surface plasmons and the Rayleigh anomaly, and its effects on the magnetooptical properties. We found that the interference enhances the magneto-optical Kerr rotation in the 1.5 eV range, and the absence of the Rayleigh anomaly results in a loss of this effect. Additionally, the presence of surface plasmons broadens the Kerr rotation spectrum. Our findings demonstrate the potential of this magnetophotonic crystal to exhibit magneto-optical activity in the mid-infrared range. Furthermore, we observed a significant contribution from the surface plasmon resonance to the magnetooptical Kerr rotation, and its resonance energy can be controlled by adjusting the gold layer thickness. We also extracted the dielectric function of the GdFeCo film, and found that the interference between the surface plasmons and the Rayleigh anomaly leads to an anomalous dispersion of the film's dielectric function in the 1.5 eV range. Our study suggests that this phenomenon could be useful for developing magneto-optical devices that operate in the mid-inference range.

Decision-based black-box knowledge distillation (DB3) methods limit student network data access to class decisions from the teacher network. Despite this restriction, DB3 has demonstrated knowledge transfer efficiency and scalability. However, existing DB3 approaches rely on costly teacher network evaluations and may lead to performance degradation due to decision-based distillation only. To address these limitations, we introduce a reduced evaluation cost and decision-based knowledge distillation framework, dubbed CEDAR. Initially, CED3 trains the student using a small subset of task labels and decides its classification outcomes on the remaining data. We then extract a set of decision-based soft labels from the student and combine them with the initial small set of labels to create a compact knowledge base. This knowledge base facilitates efficient student network training on limited data. We evaluate CEDAR on various datasets and find it outperforms the baseline DB3 method in terms of evaluation cost and achieves comparable performance to full-data knowledge distillation. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that CEDAR effectively leverages decision-based knowledge by capturing the relationship between data points and obtaining soft labels from the student network. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/CEDAR.

For a solvable group G and its module M over the ring Z[G], we explore how the multiplicity-free property of M impacts the lattice of submodules of M. Specifically, we investigate how the simple composition factors of M, which are concentrated in specific normal subgroup series of G, influence the underlying structure of the submodule lattice of M. Moreover, under certain conditions on G and M, we demonstrate that the submodule lattice of M can be reconstructed from its simple composition factors and the corresponding subgroup series of G. Our research in this area is motivated by examining the submodule lattices of modules over finite groups with nilpotent classes, as well as modules over certain classes of solvable groups, and we provide examples to illustrate our theoretical findings. Additionally, we outline an approach for investigating the underlying structure of module lattices over arbitrary solvable groups. This research is an extension of our previous study on module lattices over finite nilpotent groups.

This paper introduces Co-Imitation Learning, a novel skill transfer approach.
Without requiring access to an expert demonstrator, it enables a capable agent
to teach its own variant of an optimal policy to another agent via mutual
learning through competing in a related task. The framework assumes two agents
with diverse yet related capabilities are pitted against each other in a
simultaneous game, and through playing this game, they can acquire a distinct
set of skills from each other. Theoretical analysis has shown that both agents
can converge to optimal policies that combine their individual capabilities.
Experimentally, Co-Imitation Learning has been successfully applied to various
transfer tasks, including an agent learning to produce a complementary
specialization in a multi-agent factory, and another in a scenario where
two agents with different capabilities must find a common target. The code for
this project is available on the website of the Knowledge Discovery in Databases pre-conference to the ACM SIGKDD Conference 2021. We investigate how different polarized cutoff rate bias values influence the probability of a sequential decoder producing errors. A key aspect of our analysis is establishing conditions under optimal natural encoding that ensure a specific cutoff rate bias leads to a sequential decoder with a low error rate. Additionally, we identify a particular cutoff rate bias, denoted as $\kappa_s$, which we found to result in the lowest possible error probability when decoding a message of length $n$. Furthermore, we show that as the length of the sequence $n$ increases, the error probability associated with the $\kappa_s$ bias value eventually approaches 0 at a rate of $n^{-1}$, and we establish lower and upper bounds for this error probability. Specifically, our findings indicate that the error probability is bounded between $\left(\frac{H_0 + H_1}{2} - \frac{1}{\log 2}\right)^2$ and $\left(\frac{H_0 + H_1}{2}\right)^2$, where $H_0$ and $H_1$ are the Shannon entropies associated with the two possible input symbols. Our research also reveals that increasing the length of the sequence $n$ results in a decrease in the $\kappa_s$ bias value at a rate of $\frac{1}{n}$. Moreover, we demonstrate that our results can be applied to a related problem involving the list decoding of polar codes. Our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the performance of polar codes under optimal natural encoding and provides a foundation for exploring more complex decoding scenarios. Our research findings are applicable to both random and adaptive cutoff rate bias values, and our results can be viewed as an improvement upon the error probability bounds established by Kudele and Korade, as well as Korade and Kudele, with a particular improvement in the case where the list size is one. Reinforcement learning for machine translation has primarily focused on optimizing the observation space, yet our investigation reveals that tailoring the action space can significantly improve translation quality. Building upon the common practice of training reinforcement learning models using policy gradient methods in actor--critic frameworks, we introduce a reinforcement learning model that combines a neural network machine translation parametrization agent with a neural network critic. By optimizing the action space, our model achieves improved performance, with a 1.43 BLEU score improvement over the baseline LSTM model and a 1.23 BLEU score improvement over the state-of-the-art RNNSearch model. Our findings demonstrate that through reinforcement learning, the narrow focus on optimizing the parameter initialization for sequence-to-sequence models can be expanded to yield better translation outcomes. Our model's code is available online at the following address: https://github.com/zhuyunh3/rl-mt. Our model also yields a host of novel insights into machine translation, including the discovery that the action space can be made more precise by utilizing a structured output decoder, the observation that reinforcement learning can be used to rectify action space errors, and the revelation that the learning curve for our model exhibits a distinctive 'bottleneck effect'. Our model's action space optimization framework is versatile and adaptable to a range of applications, including multi-task learning and low-resource language pairs. In this case, both types of information flow can be equal, resulting in the system and environment both displaying an equivalent degree of entropy growth. We establish that subsets of the set of rational numbers with a common denominator can be identified using finite automata, extending a similar characterisation for integers within a specific module. Specifically, we show that for any rational number p/q, the subset of (N_p/q) with the property of being recognisable by a finite automaton is equivalent to p/q times a module being recognizable by a finite automaton. This result also provides a new perspective on the recognisability of certain subsets of natural numbers within specific modules. Furthermore, we demonstrate that subsets of natural numbers that can be recognised by finite automata when scaled by a rational number are essentially the Minsky undecidable set in the case of a non-partial ratio, thereby establishing a connection to a well-known problem in theoretical computer science. This study delves into the examination of snapshot isolation (SI) variants, specifically conservative SI, optimistic SI, and wait-die/is-wait-alterable SI, with a focus on their execution within modern, multi-version database management systems. As evidence, we analyze the underlying mechanisms of MongoDB's WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER deployments, revealing that these systems implement conservative SI. Furthermore, we outline the theoretical foundations for identifying the implemented SI variants and discuss the potential vulnerabilities to non-serializable executions that these systems face. Additionally, we propose a set of specifications for a hypothetical database system, which we term TIGER, to facilitate further exploration of SI in complex database systems. Finally, we outline the challenges and opportunities for SI in distributed database environments. This research contributes to the ongoing discussion of SI in databases and highlights the necessity for a clear and standardized definition of SI in distributed settings. A comprehensive analysis of solar energetic proton event impacts on the inner solar system is lacking due to insufficient data at close proximity to the Sun. To overcome this limitation, we studied 241 solar proton events at 0.12 to 1 AU using data from various instruments, and found that the energy distributions of low-energy protons within the inner solar system differ significantly from those recorded at 1 AU. Specifically, we found that the energy required to generate the same level of low-energy proton intensities is 1.5 to 3 times lower at 0.29 to 0.5 AU, and the shape of energy spectra also altered with heliocentric distance. Additionally, we observed that the most intense proton events are more frequent at the inner solar system, though the overall energy of the most energetic events remains unchanged with heliocentric distance. Notably, the energy needed to produce the same level of high-energy proton intensities at 0.29 to 0.5 AU is 2.5 to 4.5 times lower than at 1 AU. The implications of these findings on the understanding of solar proton radii and the energy distributions of solar proton flares are significant. The observed variations in energy distributions with heliocentric distance suggest that solar proton radii are not fixed, but rather vary greatly, and the energy required to overcome solar gravitation is not a constant, but rather a variable that depends on the location within the inner solar system. The study also highlights the importance of direct measurements of solar proton events at close heliocentric distances, and the limitations of current remote sensing techniques that rely on extrapolation methods to estimate proton fluxes at close heliocentric distances. The study's findings have important implications for the forecasting of extreme space weather events caused by solar proton events, and the protection of electronic systems used in deep space missions. The study's results also provide valuable input for the development of models of solar proton radii and the energy distributions of solar proton flares. The study's data set of 241 solar proton events at close heliocentric distances is the largest to date, and the study's analysis of energy distributions at 0.12 to 1 AU is the most comprehensive to date. Cross-cultural emotion recognition is faced with a significant challenge because the same word can evoke different emotions in various languages. To address this challenge, a proposed multi-task deep learning model called MTE is introduced, which is designed to identify the emotional potential of words within a specific linguistic context. MTE differs from conventional approaches by leveraging a context-dependent word embedding method called Context-Based Word Embedding (CWBE). CWBE is a two-layer model that incorporates both static and dynamic representations of word embeddings to capture the complex relationships between words and their context. To enhance adaptability and expand the model to multiple languages, a proposed Attention-based Multi-Task Deep Neural Network (AMT-DNN) is used. The results of our research show that MTE achieves superior performance in recognizing emotions within the same language and improves significantly when applied to different languages, thus demonstrating its enhanced adaptability. To validate the proposed model, a large-scale Chinese emotion corpus was created, which can be utilized as a reference for future research in this area. To further verify the effectiveness of MTE, the model was applied to recognize emotions within a different Chinese corpus, which showed a notable improvement over the baseline methods. We introduce a new method for estimating the spectrum of a system's Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius operator, enabling the analysis of its Lyapunov exponent and associated invariant densities, even when the operator is not invertible. This approach allows us to bypass the difficulty of distinguishing between invertible and non-invertible subspaces and directly access the variance of the Lyapunov exponent in symbolic systems. A key aspect of our approach is the development of a consistent, variance-based framework for examining non-invertible dynamics within the context of symbolic systems. A critical component of our method involves the estimation of the variance of the Lyapunov exponent using empirical data and symbolic dynamics concepts. This method is particularly suited for the study of one-dimensional maps with critical points and their corresponding invariant densities. As an illustration of our approach's effectiveness, we apply it to a standard example - the logistic map at its critical point - and show that it aligns with existing results, demonstrating the utility of this novel method in extending the range of applicable parameters. As a result of our research, we derive an analytical expression for the variance of the Lyapunov exponent in this specific case, providing a tangible example of the approach's capabilities. As the variance of the Lyapunov exponent is directly linked to the stability of a system's invariant density, our findings indicate that this density becomes statistically bimodal, exhibiting two distinct values, and we demonstrate this behavior through numerical simulations of the logistic map. As the system's parameter approaches its critical value, the variance of the Lyapunov exponent increases without limit, implying that the transition from a periodic to a chaotic state is characterized by a broad distribution of local Lyapunov exponents. Consequently, this analysis challenges the conventional view of this transition as one-dimensional, self-similar system behaving randomly. Furthermore, our results suggest that this transition is, in fact, a phase transition with distinct invariant measures on the space of local dynamics, providing a new perspective on this fundamental phenomenon. As a final point, our research reveals that the variance of the Lyapunov exponent serves as a sensitive indicator of a system's bifurcation points and the associated scaling laws, which are in agreement with existing knowledge. We investigate the non-abelian extension of the Stefan-Boltzmann law and its impact on Casimir energy within a non-abelian gauge theory. Based on the non-abelian aether term, we derive the effective action for massless scalar fields in non-thermal equilibrium and a non-abelian gauge background. This leads to a non-abelian temperature generalization and resulting Casimir energy calculations. Our findings reveal that the non-abelian aether term causes a distinction between the left- and right-handed components of scalar fields, resulting in a non-trivial Casimir effect for scalar fields. In contrast, the non-abelian temperature effects are shown to yield a vanishing contribution to the Casimir energy for scalar fields. However, we observe a non-zero contribution to the Casimir energy for vector fields. Our analysis also uncovers that the non-abelian temperature generalization and resulting Casimir energy can be interpreted as a non-abelian temperature-dependent fine-structure constant. This research develops an integrated method for calculating expected hedging costs and determining optimal hedging strategies. The approach combines a basic risk-neutral pricing model and a stochastic liquidity process. As a result, the formula for the fair value of a derivative is augmented with a liquidity component, making it possible to efficiently compute expected hedging costs. The study demonstrates the application of this integrated framework in various hedging scenarios, including static hedging and marginal hedging. Furthermore, it shows that using this integrated framework significantly reduces computational time when calculating expected hedging costs, with a notable 90% decrease in computational time compared to Monte Carlo simulations for large-scale hedging models. To accommodate complex and dynamic hedging models, the study proposes a hybrid approach that leverages both Monte Carlo simulations and the integrated method, enabling the efficient calculation of expected hedging costs for large portfolios. This hybrid approach has been successfully implemented in practical applications at a leading investment bank. The research also explores the relationship between liquidity costs and hedging strategies, revealing that the optimal hedging strategy that considers liquidity costs results in a 20-30% increase in hedging costs compared to a strategy that ignores liquidity costs. The study concludes by highlighting the limitations of existing research on hedging models and the need for further investigation into dynamic hedging models that account for liquidity costs. A dynamic random growth model is introduced to investigate how chance events affecting some individuals influence the socioeconomic distribution of subsequent generations. The model features a chance-driven mechanism allocating opportunities to a random sample of the population, and a status-quo process preserving the existing socioeconomic structure, except for the affected individuals. As the size of the randomly selected population increases, we observe that the eventual socioeconomic distribution converges to a stationary limit, which can be either equitable or biased in favor of higher socioeconomic status. A key finding indicates that the stationary limit's fairness depends on the relative rates at which opportunities are allocated and socioeconomic status is preserved, providing valuable insights into the interplay between these dynamics. Additionally, under certain conditions, we establish the convergence of the stationary distribution to an ergodic state, whose characteristics can be analyzed using sub-systems of the overall population. A numerical example is also presented to demonstrate the model's applicability. Furthermore, we discuss the model's connections to existing literature on random growth, Schelling's segregation model, and the contact process. The dynamic random growth model offers a versatile framework with which to investigate pressing societal issues, including systemic inequality and social mobility. The model's simplicity makes it an ideal platform for exploring complex phenomena arising from the interaction of chance-driven mechanisms, societal structures, and individual dynamics. The study of this model also highlights the methodological value of analyzing random growth processes, which can be used to extract the asymptotic behavior of various chance-driven processes, including Schelling's segregation model and the contact process. The research presented in this paper has been previously published in the journal Mathematics and Computers in Simulation, volume 176, January 2021, and in the journal Performance Evaluation, January 2021. By accurately measuring the differences in the starting points of opposing beams in a collider with high energy, we can identify patterns that could indicate the presence of quantum gravity effects. The simulation of instrumental impacts on future astronomical instruments can be improved by leveraging machine learning in the analysis of actual data. This method enables the efficient creation of realistic simulations of previous observations, which is crucial for several applications, including the study of cosmological phenomena and the testing of data processing pipelines. By leveraging generative adversarial networks, we developed a framework that can simulate the patterns of instrumental fluctuations observed in existing datasets. We investigate the efficiency of sequence-to-sequence models, specifically BART, in resolving linearized syntactic structures. Our investigation involves creating synthetic data and a related partial tree linearization task to evaluate the performance of BART. Our primary findings indicate that BART excels at correcting minor word ordering mistakes but struggles with more significant alterations. Furthermore, we discovered that BART performs better on the partial tree linearization task compared to a linearization model but worse than a fully specified model. Our research also reveals that BART's performance can be improved by pre-training on a large linearized corpus, albeit with limitations. Our results demonstrate that sequence-to-sequence models can effectively process linearized input for tasks like part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition, even when the linearization is highly distorted. Our code and pre-trained models are available online. Deepfake detection models have shown significant progress in recent years, with many approaches being explored to improve their efficacy. Most existing methods focus on developing domain-agnostic models, often using shared feature representations across different domains. However, these methods overlook the potential benefits of domain-specific information in improving detection accuracy. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel multi-domain detection framework known as CSDNet, which effectively incorporates cross-stitch connections between domain-specific and shared networks. This approach enables the exchange of intermediate feature representations between networks, thus leveraging their collective strengths. We demonstrate CSDNet's superiority by achieving the best results on six publicly available datasets, with a significant improvement of 4.5% in the detection accuracy on the FF-MD dataset compared to the current state-of-the-art method. Furthermore, our proposed framework is highly versatile and can be applied to various multi-domain detection tasks beyond deepfake detection. Our code and models are available for public use at https://github.com/zhengxiaolong/CSDNet.

Based on our data, this group comprises 71% of losers. This pattern is consistent with the typical operation of pyramid schemes, where participants purchase contracts using money that isn't their own. Forsage's unique features, such as the ability to invest in new levels without initially owning the required assets, also facilitate scheme operators' financial gains at the expense of other participants. Moreover, the project's automated and decentralized nature makes it difficult for authorities to track and freeze accounts, further solidifying its position as a preferred platform for operating pyramids. To better understand the Forsage community's dynamics, we also examined the geographical distribution of users and found that they are primarily based in China, followed by Russia and Eastern Europe. Notably, the majority of users, both active and inactive, have no history of investing in traditional crowdfunding projects. This suggests that Forsage's user base is distinct from that of conventional crowdfunding platforms. To facilitate further research, we have made the Forsage dataset publicly available. We have conducted a thorough investigation of two globular cluster candidates located in the Milky Way's disk using data from the $K2$ satellite. Our analysis of these objects, designated as WCLSD18.0091 and WCLSD18.0092, reveals that they both exhibit characteristics of globular clusters, specifically their periodic light curves and temperatures. We have developed isochrone models to estimate their ages, distances, and chemical compositions. Based on these models, we estimate the ages of both candidates to be approximately 1.5 billion years, placing them within the young globular cluster age range. However, their low metallicities suggest they might be more akin to young stellar clusters. We have calculated their horizontal branches and estimated their distances to be around 7.5 kiloparsecs with an error margin of 0.5 kiloparsecs. We have also calculated their total luminosities and found them to be within the expected range for globular clusters. Notably, their orbital periods around the galactic center are significantly shorter than those of established globular clusters. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the Milky Way's globular cluster population and highlight the importance of further investigating these cluster candidates. Our results are consistent with the idea that the Milky Way formed globular clusters across its lifetime, with the youngest ones being formed during a period of intense star formation known as the thin disk phase. Our study also provides a detailed analysis of the method for identifying variable stars in low-resolution time-series photometry and the application of isochrone fitting to extragalactic clusters. Our research data and derived values are available in the appendices. Our code for isochrone fitting can be accessed through GitHub. We introduce a novel class of erasure correction codes based on general singular value decomposition-compatible tensor networks. These codes must adhere to specific constraints, including being constructed from a single type of tensor and meeting the requirements of being invertible and having a rank of $r$ in each physical dimension. A specific type of code based on unitary tensor networks, which we call UTC codes, is also explored and demonstrated to be capable of correcting dimensional erasures. A universal framework for decoding dimensional erasures from any physical degree of freedom in UTC codes is then established. Notably, this decoding approach is both efficient and effective. The security of UTC codes against an all-powerful attacker is mathematically proven in both the continuous and discrete models of erasure channels. The generation of a robust, fault-tolerant protocol for correcting dimensional erasures in UTC codes is also presented. This protocol ensures that even in the event of a single error, the code's original data will be recovered with certainty. The efficiency of this protocol is particularly noteworthy, requiring a minimal amount of additional physical resources. The design of UTC codes offers a high degree of flexibility in constructing physical implementations, and a concrete example of a scalable, high-performance implementation is provided using a near-term quantum device, along with the results of associated performance metrics. The code's ability to correct dimensional erasures makes it particularly suitable for applications in data storage systems subject to physical degradation. The security of UTC codes against an all-powerful attacker ensures that even in the presence of a loss of data, the code's original information remains confidential. The development of UTC codes also provides a theoretical framework for constructing codes based on gauge-compatible tensor networks, expanding the scope of these codes to include various types of network configurations. The resulting code family offers a versatile platform for addressing various types of data loss and corruption in information storage systems. The associated research outcomes are relevant to both classical and quantum information storage systems. The underlying theory of UTC codes can be applied to a range of settings, including but not limited to, magnetic tape storage, DNA data storage, and quantum memory systems. The development of UTC codes is expected to contribute to the advancement of reliable and secure data storage technology. In high-stakes, time-sensitive and often complex business processes, accurate predictions are crucial to achieving success and avoiding failure. Our proposed approach, Stage-Wise Predictive Validation (SWPV), addresses the limitations of current methods in evaluating prediction models by focusing on their performance across various stages of a process. Unlike traditional evaluation techniques that treat predictions as either correct or incorrect, SWPV takes into account the varying reliability of predictions made at different stages. It achieves this by utilizing a reliability function, which estimates the probability of a prediction being trustworthy at each stage, and incorporates this information into a validation metric that assesses the accuracy of predictions at individual stages and across the entire process. Our research also introduces two new metrics, Stage-Wise Predictive Performance (SPP) and Process Predictive Performance (PPP), which provide a detailed analysis of prediction performance at different stages and across the entire process. Ultimately, SWPV and its accompanying metrics empower businesses to gain a more nuanced understanding of their prediction models and the processes they are applied to, thereby equipping them with the tools necessary to make data-driven decisions that minimize prediction-related losses. Our proposed approach and accompanying metrics were tested on multiple datasets and found to yield superior results when compared to existing evaluation methods. Our research was conducted in collaboration with a leading technology company and our findings were validated by their data scientists. Our work was also peer-reviewed by experts in the field of economics. Our research identified key factors that contribute to the performance of prediction models in different stages of a process, including the availability of relevant data, the presence of biases in machine learning algorithms, and the complexity of the models used. Our proposed approach and accompanying metrics have far-reaching implications for businesses and organizations that rely heavily on prediction models, including ride-sharing companies, financial institutions, and healthcare providers. Nonlinear dynamic systems often exhibit complex behaviors that linear methods struggle to capture effectively, yet many real-world applications can be modeled using linear methods on a suitable transformation of the original state space. The Koopman operator, introduced in the 1930s, provides such a transformation by redefining the system in a higher-dimensional state space through a set of invariant equations. In this work, we develop a real-time learning framework for the Koopman operator based on a linear operator perspective, which enables us to extend the Koopman-Lagrange theorem and derive a sparse identification algorithm using $\ell_1$ regularization. This approach allows us to extract meaningful dynamics from both synthetic and real-world data, including a mechanical system with two degrees of freedom, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in comparison to existing techniques. Our framework's utility in analyzing nonlinear dynamics is highlighted by the simple, interpretable models it produces. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengzhengsun1998/KoopmanLearning.

We propose a novel sentence selection mechanism called Sparse Generative Adversarial Network (SparseGAN) to enhance the performance of our sentence representation model in a neural text generation framework. Our approach involves training a discriminator to identify sentences that a generator can easily produce, and uses the sentence similarity to enhance the representation model. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on adversarial training or sentence ranking, SparseGAN selects sentences based on a binary classification threshold, which significantly reduces the number of negative samples needed during training. We further introduce a sentence selection strategy that prioritizes the representation of rare words over frequent words, which enables the generator to produce diverse outputs with a higher probability of including rare words. Our experiments using a sequence-to-sequence generation model show that SparseGAN outperforms the baseline models in terms of the number of rare words generated and overall quality, as evaluated using the Meteor metric. Additionally, our model achieves comparable results to the state-of-the-art models that utilize massive amounts of data. Our code is available online at https://github.com/zhanglei1993/SparseGAN.

The concept of panspermia, which suggests life can be dispersed and germinate on new celestial bodies, is a captivating theory that has been debated for centuries. To assess the validity of interstellar panspermia, it's essential to investigate microbial life thriving in various stellar environments. These environments are particularly critical to study as they are readily accessible for sampling and could potentially harbor resilient microbial life. A team of researchers used the Chandra X-ray Observatory to examine the Orion Nebula Cluster, a 400,000-year-old region that is an ideal setting for exploring panspermia. By analyzing the X-ray emissions from a specific group of young stars within this cluster, scientists were able to gather data on the conditions necessary for microbial life to thrive on planetary surfaces and in atmospheres. Animal population studies often rely on capture-recapture data, but these studies typically occur in fixed locations and use models that assume subjects move randomly, leading to biased population density estimates. A new method, referred to as the Gaussian Random Field (GRF) model, has been developed to analyze capture-recapture data collected across varied and complex environments without such restrictions. This model uses a second-order summary statistic, calculates credible intervals for population density, and can be implemented using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations. When compared to simulated data, the GRF model demonstrated accurate population density estimates and provided suitable credible intervals. Additionally, the model has been applied to real data from a study of black bears in Colorado. This research presents the GRF model and showcases its practical application in a real-world setting. Systematic evaluation and optimization of the model's parameters have been conducted, and the code is available online for public use. We develop a comprehensive theory of differential modules for power series over operators, extending previous work by Borel, Cartier, and Deligne. This involves creating equivalence classes of differential modules, defined by operator equivalences that preserve the underlying algebra, and demonstrating that these classes form a sheaf within the algebraic framework. Furthermore, we establish connections between these differential modules and D-modules, particularly in the setting of a local analytic ring. Additionally, we identify specific conditions under which an operator is considered a parametrized family of operators, and demonstrate that these conditions align with the sheaf property of differential modules. Finally, we explore connections to the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence, including the construction of differential modules from data related to meromorphic functions and differential equations. This construction meets the sheaf property condition implied by the sheaf property of holonomic modules, and enables the extension of the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence to a broader class of inputs. This research is underpinned by key contributions, including a detailed examination of differential modules in the context of a local analytic ring, an in-depth analysis of operator equivalences, and a study of the relationship between differential modules and the sheaf property. It also includes a critical assessment of relevant results from the work of Borel, Cartier, and Deligne. This assessment highlights the importance of their contributions, as well as the differences between their theories and the present framework of power series over operators. It is worth noting that this research is an extension of the authors' previous work, which explored the connection between differential modules and the sheaf property within the framework of formal schemes, and demonstrated that this connection provides an alternative characterization of formal schemes with separations. This previous work also formed the basis for the development of a formal scheme version of the structure theorem for modules over rings endowing modules with derivations, as well as the extension of the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence to a broader class of inputs, including data related to meromorphic functions and differential equations defined on an analytic affine curve. This earlier research was, in turn, an extension of the authors' joint work with Deligne, which focused on the connection between differential modules and the sheaf property within the framework of schemes, as well as the development of a scheme version of the structure theorem for modules over rings endowing modules with derivations. We've developed an automated testing framework that streamlines the process of pinpointing and fixing programming mistakes by leveraging a machine learning-based predictor, which identifies potential error sources based on code analysis and API usage data. This predictor is integrated into the testing environment where it can pinpoint active bugs, guide the generation of test cases to isolate errors, and provide suggestions for corrective actions. By automating repetitive tasks and offering real-time feedback, this framework aims to enhance programmers' efficiency and effectiveness in resolving programming issues. We've tested a version of this framework on six distinct programming projects, each with a unique set of characteristics, and the results show that it can successfully pinpoint the majority of errors with just a few attempts. Furthermore, developers using this framework in their daily work reported significant reductions in time spent on troubleshooting and debugging. In addition, we've also made available the code for this framework in an open-source format on GitHub. In the course of developing this framework, we encountered several challenges, including the difficulty in distinguishing between incorrect usage of APIs and genuine programming errors, and the need to strike a balance between over- and under-specification when identifying potential error sources. To address these challenges, we've developed a range of machine learning-based techniques and evaluation metrics, and we've also conducted a large-scale experiment involving over 1,000 users to fine-tune the predictor and refine the performance of this framework. Our research has far-reaching implications for the development of intelligent testing tools and platforms that can adapt to diverse programming environments and projects. Such tools and platforms will be instrumental in addressing the growing challenges associated with software testing and debugging. Our code and associated data are available at https://github.com/chenzhongwu/CodeSeer. In a scenario where node connections are unknown, we've developed a decentralized and probabilistic algorithm that enables a specific type of network node to estimate the network size. This algorithm operates in multiple stages, utilizing randomizations and a unique reference node to gather size information from neighboring nodes. We analyze the performance of our algorithm, focusing on how the estimated network size varies from its actual value as its size increases. Our findings are then compared to existing approaches, revealing improved accuracy in network size estimation. Furthermore, we establish lower bounds on the average squared error of size estimation algorithms, demonstrating that our proposal achieves these benchmarks when network connectivity meets specific conditions. Our solution can be applied to networks of any size, starting from as little as two nodes. Additionally, we show that our algorithm excels in both performance and efficiency when compared to two alternative size estimation methods, specifically in networks consisting of three nodes. Our research also highlights the impact of algorithm parameters on its performance, as well as offering guidelines on their optimal selection. Our contributions to this field of study are marked by the unique properties of our algorithm, which adheres to constraints on node interactions and limited memory storage. Our solution can be applied to various types of networks, including those described by complex graphs, as well as temporal networks, and includes recommendations for improving the algorithm in these settings. Our research was initially presented at the 52nd Annual Allerton Conference on Communication, Control, and Computing. Our algorithm and associated data are available online at https://github.com/anonymous/est_network_size. We developed a novel approach for estimating queue lengths using nonparametric methods based on real-time traffic data from mobile devices. This method leverages a Gaussian Mixture Model to identify distinct distribution patterns in queue lengths and employs an Expectation-Maximization algorithm for parameter estimation. We conducted experiments in Beijing, China, utilizing traffic data from the Baidu Map application and found that our nonparametric method achieved comparable accuracy to parametric models, with mean absolute percentage errors of 12.1% and 11.7% for peak and off-peak hours respectively. Furthermore, our method demonstrated robust performance with only 10% of the data used for training. This research provides a starting point for exploring nonparametric representations of queue length distributions. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyiwang/nonparametric_queue_length. Note that this work is part of an ongoing study aiming to develop a mobile app that estimates queue lengths using collaborative mobile crowds and learning-based methods, with an expected completion date of one year from now. Our preliminary findings are presented at the 2023 ITS Europe Congress under the title "Nonparametric Estimation of Queue Lengths Using Mobile Crowds". Our research on estimating and optimizing traffic congestion is ongoing and will be continued in future works. To explain this phenomenon, a combination of thermal transport theories and first-principles simulations of electronic and phonon properties were employed. By accounting for the temperature-dependent carrier concentrations, the anomalous Nernst-Einstein laws were accurately reproduced. Furthermore, the unique thermal transport behavior in these materials was linked to their high carrier mobilities and low lattice thermal conductivity. The study's findings were validated by comparing them with experimental data and provided a clear understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials. The research's approach can be applied to other material classes exhibiting thermal transport behavior related to thermal expansion. By assuming that the W^{1,p}-regularity of the underlying space is sufficient, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a solution for each time period. Furthermore, we establish that the solution's time-dependent trace forms a continuous path in the space of functions with a specific Lipschitz continuity, and its associated history forms a continuous path in a specific Banach space. Additionally, we demonstrate the time-dependent solution's spatial gradients form a continuous path in the space of functions with a specific norm, and show that the solution satisfies the minimization of its action functional with respect to time, subject to constraints. We define the concept of a "smooth surface" in the context of hypersurfaces with bounded mean curvature within a bounded region in a higher-dimensional space, and demonstrate its occurrence in a broad category of random processes. Furthermore, we establish an inequality for the $n$-th moment of the $N$-th order partial derivative of a surface's curvature, and show that such a surface can be characterized by a Gaussian random process with specific variance and mean values. Additionally, we explore the behavior of these surfaces as they approach their boundary, and establish a relationship between their curvature and a particular function with a known asymptotic property. As a result, we are able to prove the existence and uniqueness of a surface that exhibits a particular asymptotic behavior, and whose description is analogous to that found by Pogoda, and Pittet and Giga, but with a different and more general set of parameters. Finally, we provide an estimate for the expected value of the $n$-th moment of the $N$-th order partial derivative of a surface's curvature. These findings expand upon the discoveries made in the research presented in Pogoda's dissertation, and build upon the findings in the studies conducted by Pittet and Giga, and Cabeza, Pogoda, and Vetoen. The concept of mesoscale flatness was initially proposed by Pogoda as a means of studying a surface defined by the level set of a Brownian motion process that has been shifted by a specific amount, but our research reveals that this idea is more broadly applicable. The results we have obtained also provide an answer to the question of how often a surface of a specified size will intersect a given boundary within a particular space, and as such, our work expands upon the discoveries made in the studies conducted by Berman, Aldous, and Pitman, and Durrett and Rogers. The relationship we have established in the final section of our research paper can also be found in the work conducted by Berman, Aldous, and Pitman, and Durrett and Rogers, but with a different and more general set of parameters. This research introduces a self-sensing concrete composite that utilizes genetic algorithms to pinpoint internal defects. Traditional methods of detecting damage rely on data from multiple sensors and various computational techniques, but these approaches are time-consuming, expensive, and lack real-time capabilities. In contrast, this self-sensing composite leverages genetic algorithms enabled by a single embedded sensor to rapidly identify and accurately describe structural changes. To optimize the algorithm's performance, a feature reduction method based on the composite's material properties is employed, resulting in a simplified genetic model that effectively locates and characterizes defects, even in complex dynamic scenarios. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through numerical and experimental analyses of concrete slabs under various loading conditions, showing that it surpasses the accuracy of conventional methods based on raw sensor data. Ultimately, this self-sensing composite and associated genetic algorithm have significant potential for real-time, cost-effective damage detection across diverse infrastructure applications.

We've developed a Lotka-Volterra model that incorporates the effects of varying levels of intelligence among species, either in the form of individual agents or as population-wide averages, and examined its dynamics. The model highlights the impact of different intelligence levels on the interactions between species and their subsequent coexistence or extinction. The non-linear nature of the model prevents the cancellation of the S-shaped curve characteristic of the logistic equation, resulting in a curve with seven distinct segments that together form the familiar S-shape. The analysis of the model focuses on the critical points of the system and uses the concept of an attractor landscape to study the dynamics of the model. The application of the model to a predator-prey example reveals the conditions under which the predator species can coexist with the prey. The analysis also reveals the existence of the saddle-node type bifurcation of the model's dynamics. The model's parameters can be related to the intelligence levels of the species, providing a possible explanation for the observed patterns of the model's dynamics. The model's dynamics can be interpreted through the lens of the Prisoner's Dilemma game, revealing the connection between the intelligence levels of the species and their ability to cooperate. The model's results are compared with existing research on the Lotka-Volterra model and other similar models. The model's limitations and potential extensions are also discussed. To shed light on this discrepancy, we propose a future electron-positron collider, the International Linear e$^+$e$^-$ Collider (ILC), can be utilized to explore an uncharted area of physics. By operating the ILC at a 2 GeV energy, it can study the rare processes of light meson production, specifically $K^+K^0$, $K^0_{{\rm \scriptstyle l}}$$\overline{K^0_{{\rm \scriptstyle l}}}$, $\eta$$\eta$, $\eta$$\eta$, $\eta'$$\eta'$, $\eta'$$\eta'$, $K^0_{{\rm \scriptstyle l}}$$\overline{K^0_{{\rm \scriptstyle l}}}$, and $\eta$$\eta'$ with unprecedented precision. This would allow us to constrain hypothetical interactions between light quarks and a new scalar or vector gauge boson, potentially explaining the observed deviation from the standard model's predictions for the muon's magnetic moment. With 31 inverse picobarns of data collected at the ILC, we anticipate that the new physics scale could be as low as 5.6 TeV in the case of a scalar or 7.5 TeV in the scenario involving a vector gauge boson. If the muon's anomalous magnetic moment is confirmed to be anomalous, we argue that the ILC is an ideal future experiment to investigate this phenomenon. We prove that uniform lattices within connected Lie groups are bi-automatic groups. This is an extension of Guivarc'h's previous finding, which showed these lattices generate bi-automatic groups for a specific class of Lie groups that include nilpotent and semisimple with compact spectrum groups. Our new contribution also includes the groups $\text{SL}_2(K_v)$ where $K_v$ is a local field, which were previously unknown to have automatic properties. Our approach to achieving these results involves creating a bi-automatic structure for a universal covering group of a given lattice's abstract group structure, and in doing so, we establish that these universal covering groups are bi-automatic. This extends the range of groups with bi-automatic properties and provides a foundation for further exploration of their computational properties. Furthermore, our findings can be applied to demonstrate that certain specific groups, including the universal covering group of $\text{GL}_2(F_q(t))$ and the Coxeter group $G_2$, have bi-automatic structures. Our research methodology is grounded in combinatorial properties of words associated with irrational rotations, and it leverages the connection between these words and geodesics within the universal covering group of a given lattice's abstract group structure. This connection enables the definition of a bi-automatic structure for these universal covering groups. Our study also delves into the concept of bi-automatic groups within the context of automata theory and formal language, and it includes an examination of the relationship between bi-automatic groups and the geometric properties of their associated Cayley graphs. Our research findings expand the known repertoire of groups with bi-automatic properties, and they lay the groundwork for exploring the computational properties of bi-automatic groups, including the universal covering group of nilpotent groups and free groups, and it highlights the significance of these groups within the broader context of theoretical computer science and mathematics. Previous studies utilizing high-resolution neural data for predicting poststroke rehabilitation outcomes have focused on training predictive models using either electroencephalogram (EEG) or electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals in isolation. Our research compared the effectiveness of these two techniques for predicting motor functions after stroke. We reanalyzed data from 12 participants with strokes and used the same features to train models on either EEG or ECoG signals. Our results showed that the accuracy of predictions made using combined EEG and ECoG features exceeded those based on either method alone. Furthermore, a model trained on EEG data generalizes more efficiently to new EEG data than one trained on ECoG data. These findings support the development of EEG-based prediction tools for stroke rehabilitation outcomes, given the non-invasive nature and easier accessibility of EEG compared to ECoG. Our research also demonstrated the presence of distinct neural populations associated with different motor functions in both EEG and ECoG signals, indicating their individual utility in predicting poststroke rehabilitation outcomes. Ultimately, our results highlight the importance of motor function prediction across both EEG and ECoG signals and encourage further investigation into the underlying neural mechanisms governing these associations. Our study's data and analysis are available online for community use and feedback. We define a specific type of action that a right-angled Artin group can take on a tree, which we call a tree-like action. We then investigate the conditions under which a tree-like action result in a group that acts on a tree. Furthermore, we establish an algorithm for determining whether a given finite graph allows a tree-like action, as well as identifying the associated tree if such an action exists. Additionally, we explore relationships between tree-like actions and minimal cut-edges, demonstrating that they are equivalent to the set of separating subgraphs, and providing a formula for calculating the number of separating subgraphs of a given finite graph. Finally, we discuss the properties of a group that arises from a tree-like action, specifically its being infinite, being non-trivial but finite, or being the fundamental group of a surface boundary group, depending on the structure of its defining graph. This research expands upon the concepts initially presented in the paper "The Surface Group Theorem" by Scott and Swarup, as well as the "Cut-Vertex Subgroup" portion of the Surface Group Theorem. Many real-world applications involve dynamic graphs that evolve over time, and accurately modeling these changes is crucial for tasks like node classification and link prediction. Despite the success of graph neural networks in static graphs, extending their applications to dynamic graphs remains challenging due to the lack of a unified framework that effectively captures temporal relationships. We propose DECENNT, a novel, time-aware graph neural network architecture that leverages attention and graph convolutional networks to capture both short-term and long-term dependencies in dynamic graphs. Unlike conventional methods that treat each graph snapshot independently, DECENNT utilizes an attention-based mechanism to weigh the importance of past snapshots, integrating this information into node representations. We further introduce a graph attention module to capture local, short-term dependencies among neighboring nodes and neighboring node representations. DECENNT is a unified framework that can handle dynamic graphs of varying structures and scales, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, achieving superior performance to state-of-the-art methods. The analysis of long-term movements of individual animals or groups of animals is a key area of study in biology, yet it is challenging to differentiate the patterns of biological entities from those of inanimate objects. Machine learning techniques, particularly deep learning methods, have shown significant progress in modeling complex temporal dependencies in movement data. However, the effectiveness of these models in accurately capturing the underlying dynamics of biological movements, particularly in comparison to traditional statistical models, has not been thoroughly examined. This study uses a combination of statistical and machine learning approaches to model the movement of birds in Europe and the Mediterranean region during migration seasons, using data from the International Waterbird and Wetland Centre. We evaluated the performance of different models by assessing their ability to predict bird populations at specific locations and times, and found that the machine learning models overfit the data, whereas the Gaussian process regression model demonstrated superior predictive accuracy with a more regularized distribution of predicted values. Our findings highlight the importance of model simplicity and regularity in accurately predicting the long-term movements of bird populations. Furthermore, we identified key migration pathways and identified areas with high conservation value, and made the data and analysis tools available through an interactive web application at www.birdmigration.eu. This study's methodology serves as a framework for integrating machine learning models with ecological knowledge to better understand and manage complex biological movements.systemassistant

Quantum many-body systems rely on rigorous guidelines to maintain their stability and accuracy. For lattice-based systems, a recent theory mandates that quench dynamics be free from thermalization, and we have discovered a method to identify this lack of thermalization through topological measurements. Specifically, we found that the absence of thermalization in these systems corresponds to a unique feature of their spatial structure, known as a topological "signature." Building upon this understanding, we developed an indicator to detect this characteristic, enabling us to visually represent the system's topological features. Furthermore, we discovered that this indicator can distinguish between different non-equilibrium phases of the system, revealing its topological "landscape." If the system is not isolated, we can also determine its evolution over time. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our indicator in various scenarios, including both one-dimensional and two-dimensional systems. Notably, our findings show that the system's topological features can persist even after the system has reached a steady state, and we propose a statistical method to distinguish Anderson insulators from other non-equilibrium phases based on topological characteristics. Additionally, our research revealed that the system's topological features can be controlled by modifying its initial state. Collectively, our results highlight the significance of detecting topological characteristics in non-equilibrium many-body systems and the potential applications in artificial neural networks. We also introduced an indicator to measure the complexity of these systems' time-evolution trajectories. Lastly, we believe that our findings have implications for understanding the topological characteristics of driven-dissipative systems. For example, these systems can exhibit spontaneous phase transitions and robust edge states, and our research suggests that the driven-dissipative systems' topological characteristics are determined by their cavity-based atomic structure rather than their driven dynamics. Consequently, our discovery opens up the possibility of engineering robust edge states in these systems. We also found that the time-evolution trajectories of these systems possess unique topological characteristics that reflect their underlying cavity-based atomic structure. Consequently, our research suggests that the complexity of these trajectories is directly related to the complexity of the system's topology. We believe that our findings have significant implications for artificial neural networks, particularly those based on non-equilibrium many-body systems, as they provide a mechanism for generating complex, topologically-structured trajectories that reflect the system's underlying topology. We propose that these trajectories could serve as inputs for neural networks, enabling them to learn complex patterns and relationships rooted in the underlying topology of the system. We also found that these networks can learn to recognize and reproduce these patterns

We've developed an efficient method for calculating a wide range of invariants associated with genus-one curves over finite fields, specifically for curves defined by cubic polynomials in one variable. This computation is rapid and employs relatively little memory. As a result, our approach enables the examination of relationships between these invariants and their geometric properties, uncovering intriguing patterns that were previously unknown. Our findings demonstrate that the values of certain invariants from a subset exhibit distinct distribution patterns when compared to random selections of similar numbers, indicating that the set has a specific structure. Conjectures arising from our data suggest that many genus-one curves over finite fields fulfill a particular divisibility condition, a hypothesis we tested on large, randomly generated sets of numbers. Our research tools also facilitate the discovery of specific prime factors among curve curves' $j$-invariants, as well as the determination of the minimal interval required to capture all $j$-invariant values within a given field size. Our field-size extension experiments reveal that our methods can lead to significant improvements in the efficiency of the Number Field Sieve algorithm. Our results also demonstrate that the distribution of $j$-invariant values among genus-one curves over finite fields matches the predicted uniform distribution when the field size is sufficiently large, a discovery that sheds light on the underlying structure of these curves. Our research tools and associated techniques have been applied to enhance the prime field extension of the Number Field Sieve algorithm, resulting in a speedup of our record-setting achievement for a 60-bit factorization, from 1 minute and 46 seconds to just 1 second. Our methods have been utilized in the factorization record for a 69-bit number, mentioned in the accompanying note.
