We investigate the impact of squark effects on the production of heavy Higgs bosons at a linear collider, considering the influence of complex parameters in the supersymmetry context. Our analysis focuses on the $gg \to C$ and $q \bar{q} \to C$ processes for the charged Higgs boson $C$, and extends to the $q \bar{q} \to A_0$ and $gg \to A_0$ processes for the neutral, CP-odd Higgs boson $A_0$. We examine the effects of complex stop and gluino mass parameters on the phase space and squark interactions with the heavy Higgs bosons. Our findings reveal that the influence of these complex parameters can be significant, potentially leading to the disappearance of the $C$ signal via the reduction of the $gg \to C$ cross-section, and may cause the $A_0$ signal to appear under a different invariant mass scale than expected. As a result, we stress the importance of considering the complex stop and gluino mass parameters in the simulation of heavy Higgs boson production at a linear collider, particularly at higher energy levels. For the most general case with complex parameters, we present the relevant effective couplings and identify the effective stop and gluino mass scales, which can be crucial for accurately interpreting future experimental data. Our research demonstrates that the $C$ and $A_0$ production cross-sections can be expressed in terms of the effective stop and gluino mass scales, and the corresponding thresholds, allowing for a more precise understanding of the underlying physics. Our study also reveals that the optimal choice of polarisation in the search for the heavy Higgs bosons depends on the complex stop and gluino mass parameters. In contextual linear bandits, determining an optimal linear representation can significantly reduce communication costs, as actions are chosen based on action representations rather than contextual values. We establish an upper bound on regret and communication in polynomial time, considering a context distribution with a finite number of representative contexts, which allows us to select an optimal linear representation with polynomial complexity. Specifically, we find that, with high probability, our algorithm achieves a regret of $O(B\sqrt{T})$ and a communication cost of $O(B^2T\log(DN)/\epsilon)$ within polynomial time, where the number of contexts, arms, and time steps are denoted by D, N, and T respectively, and the distribution of context vectors, action vectors, and linear representation coefficients satisfy certain conditions. Our results demonstrate that, in the linear contextual bandit problem, we can obtain an optimal linear representation that yields a polynomial time solution, thereby achieving the same performance as the linear contextual bandit algorithm using linear function estimation. Our research also yields a contextual linear bandit solution using linear function estimation, which includes an action-dependent context elimination policy and an augmented linear regression estimator. Our results generalize previous linear contextual bandit solutions and yield the first context-free linear contextual bandit solution with an action-dependent elimination policy. Our research provides a new perspective on the linear contextual bandit problem, highlighting the significance of context-free linear representations in reducing communication costs. Our approach also offers a novel context-free linear representation learning strategy, which can be applied to other contextual bandit problems. Our results demonstrate that, under certain distribution assumptions, we can select an optimal context-free linear representation with polynomial complexity, thereby achieving the same performance as the linear contextual bandit algorithm using linear function estimation. Our research introduces a new perspective on the linear contextual bandit problem, emphasizing the importance of context-free linear representations in minimizing communication costs. Our approach also presents a novel strategy for learning context-free linear representations, which can be applied to other contextual bandit problems. Our solution to the contextual linear bandit problem is notable for its use of an action-dependent context elimination policy, which we believe is a novel contribution. Our research on contextual linear bandits is relevant to applications in online advertising, where the context refers to user attributes and the action refers to ad placement. Our research demonstrates that, under certain distribution assumptions, we can select an optimal context-free linear representation with polynomial complexity, which we believe is a significant finding. which yields value function estimates that require fewer data than traditional methods. 
Our approach can be applied to various sample-efficient policy learning techniques, 
including linear and nonlinear importance sampling, generalized linear regression, 
and synthetic control methods. 
We demonstrate that under mild assumptions, the optimal value function estimate 
can be obtained using a smaller testing sample size, in particular one that is 
$\sqrt{d}$ times smaller than the number of features in high-dimensional settings. 
Our framework's applicability is further shown to encompass existing efficient 
policy learning algorithms as special cases.

estimate can be significantly reduced from $\sqrt{d}$ times the sample size

parameters.

Our methodology is tested using simulated and real-world data.

Our research examined the transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons, pions, kaons, and protons within various elliptic flow classes using data from the ALICE experiment at the LHC. Following the application of elliptic flow corrections, we found that the transverse momentum distributions of all particles or combinations of particles, regardless of their production geometry, consistently align with specific patterns. These patterns are characterized by differential curves based on particle mass and temperature, and exhibit similar behavior across different collision energies. The overlap region of our curves aligns with calculations from Ultra-Relativistic Quantum Chromodynamics, and the widening of our curves towards higher transverse momenta suggests the presence of additional particle production influenced by collisions between particles rather than initial geometry. The study of these distributions also enables the measurement of temperature, a key parameter in the equation of state of quark-gluon plasma, as well as the inelastic collision cross-section between particles rather than initial geometry. The latter value was found to be 7.63 plus or minus 0.48 millibarn per square GeV per unit rapidity for lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV. The measured temperature under various conditions allows for the estimation of the ratio of strange to light quark chemical potentials, which is consistent with predictions from various models that assume full chemical equilibrium. The duration of the quark-gluon plasma state can be estimated from the spread of our curves towards higher transverse momenta. The estimates obtained are 7.75 plus or minus 1.47 millibarns per square GeV per unit rapidity for lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV. The findings of our research support existing evidence for the existence of quark-gluon plasma and provide a detailed understanding of its properties. The discovery of a collision cross-section between particles rather than initial geometry also opens up avenues for further investigation into the characteristics of this state of matter. The methods employed in this research can be applied to future high-energy collisions and may help in distinguishing different theories of strong interaction. The temperature measurements obtained can be used in the development of future theories of strong interaction. The duration of the quark-gluon plasma state can be compared with predictions from different models of heavy ion collisions. The research was based on data from 0.5 billion lead-lead collisions at the LHC. The results were confirmed using an independent set of 1 billion collisions. The findings of this research were presented at a conference and made available in an online database

lower power level. We also show that, in our model, the optimal power control
settings yield an approximate formula for the throughput, which in turn yields

a linear time complexity and requires only a single pass through the list of
transmitters in the network. In contrast, alternative methods of power control
have a higher time complexity. Our research also includes a binary power control
scheme that prioritizes transmitters with lower signal strengths and shows that

We've developed a ``multiple-time-step integration scheme," a new method with variable step sizes for simulating complex interactions between particles and fluid flow. This algorithm allows us to use large step sizes to solve the fluid equations efficiently and a smaller step size to solve the particle equations, significantly speeding up our simulations. Compared to standard methods, our approach requires less computational time, especially when modeling large numbers of particles. As proof of concept, we applied our technique to simulate the settling of small particles at the bottom of a stagnant fluid, obtaining results that match real-world data. Our code is now available online for other researchers to use. In the future, we plan to adapt our multiple-time-step integration scheme for simulations of turbulent fluid flows. Our results also show that when particles are far apart, their individual settling rates are essentially the same, a previously unreported finding. To understand the robot's dynamics during multiple-bounce interactions with variable-stiffness terrain, we employed a reduced-order model that accounts for the deformation of the ground within each jump cycle. The growing complexity of modern data necessitates the development of more sophisticated analytical tools. For our purposes, we're focusing on a model that structures information networks using a hierarchical framework, allowing for the cohesiveness and categorization of topics. The Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), a Bayesian approach, provides a hierarchical organization of topics and allows researchers to explore high-level categories of the network. We've adapted the LDA algorithm to create the LHTM model, which uses a collapsed Gibbs sampler for parameter estimation. The efficacy of LHTM is demonstrated through a network of scientific abstracts, revealing the model's capacity to identify latent topics and distinguish them from high-level categories. Furthermore, the model's performance is compared to existing topic models using a range of evaluation metrics, including a newly introduced measure that assesses the coherence of topics. The results indicate that LHTM outperforms existing models in terms of topic coherence and produces interpretable output. The code for LHTM is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanfei/LHTM. The model's potential for analyzing complex networks and identifying meaningful categories is highlighted by the examples presented. The approach can be applied to various domains of interest, including but not limited to, biomedical research, finance, and social media analysis. The model's performance can be further improved by exploring techniques for initializing the random topics and employing multi-step iterations to enhance the accuracy of results. The research presented contributes to the development of a hierarchical topic model that can be applied to large-scale networks and open-ended text, and offers a novel assessment of topic coherence based on intrinsic properties. Quantum annealing enables the solution of complex optimization problems by gradually transitioning from an easily implementable initial Hamiltonian to a desired target Hamiltonian. However, the effectiveness of quantum annealing relies on its ability to navigate through the annealing schedule without becoming trapped in suboptimal solutions, a challenge that has been studied in terms of the 'annealing gap'. This gap refers to the difference between the time it takes to solve a problem via quantum annealing and the minimum required time. In this research, a quantum annealing algorithm is presented that leverages a distinguishability metric to guide the transition towards the target solution. The resulting quantum annealing sequence can be distinguished from an arbitrary initial state, allowing for the calculation of the annealing time required to solve a specific problem. In contrast to traditional quantum annealing, this protocol exhibits a gap that is directly related to its actual performance. As a result, optimizing the protocol is equivalent to minimizing the annealing gap, and in turn, maximizing the success probability of solving the problem of interest. In this study, the performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated using both random instances of a specific problem and a real-world application involving the solution of protein structures. The resulting annealing schedules demonstrate improved performance when compared to existing protocols. Additionally, the research reveals that the gap can be further reduced by adjusting the parameters of the protocol, paving the way for its adaptation to other complex optimization problems. The associated code is available online for community use and modification. The developed algorithm is specifically tailored for the design of quantum circuits using Qiskit, but its underlying principles can be applied to other quantum annealing platforms. The performance of the protocol has been tested using real quantum processors, demonstrating the practical utility of this approach. The resulting protocol has been made available on ZEN, a cloud-based quantum development and execution platform. The code and associated documentation can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/QuantumClassicalHybrid/QuantumAnnealingProtocolDesign. The design of the protocol has been further explained in the accompanying documentation available at: https://qisk.org/projects/quantum-annealing-protocol-design. The protocol has been made available on the following cloud-based platforms: IBM Quantum Experience and Qisk.org. Quantum metrology leverages the strength of entangled systems to achieve precise measurements of variables such as time-voltage damping. In this research, we examine compass states made up of N identical harmonic oscillators to determine their effectiveness in estimating a uniform damping rate. Mathematically, we calculate the Fisher information and resulting variance of the compass state's expectation value in relation to the damping parameter. Our findings indicate a significant decline in variance as the number of entangled oscillators increases, in line with established scaling norms. However, when the entanglement is disrupted by damping, we observe its negative impact on variance, especially during the early stages. Our data also reveal that variance can be accurately represented by a modified entanglement figure of merit, specifically the Schrödinger-Newton variance factor, even in the presence of uniform damping. This model can be applied to more complex scenarios with non-uniform damping. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that compass states exhibit a predictable decline in measurement precision in proportion to the level of damping, providing a crucial consideration for metrological applications. Additionally, we outline a feasible experimental realization using superconducting resonators and Josephson junctions for a system comprising N oscillators. This system has previously demonstrated the ability to generate compass states for up to N=4. Our research highlights the potential for expanding this to a larger N. Our findings are further validated by numerical simulations of both single and multi-qubit systems. In these simulations, we observe a direct correlation between the accuracy of damping parameter estimation and the level of entanglement maintained within the system. In the case of a single qubit, we explore various drive strengths and their effects on this relationship. In the multi-qubit scenario, we examine various qubit coupling strengths and their impact on the system's ability to maintain compass states and accurately estimate the damping parameter. In both cases, our results are compared against theoretical predictions. In the single-qubit scenario, we find that under weak drive conditions, the system behaves in accordance with expected Metrological performance metrics. Deep neural networks are susceptible to insidious "backdoor" attacks, where a seemingly accurate model actually surrenders to misleading inputs embedded with a hidden pattern. However, creating dynamic backdoor attacks is extremely difficult, especially when aiming to deceive multiple classification tasks simultaneously. Current methods typically introduce a one-dimensional label signal, which limits the effectiveness of attacks, especially when facing real-world data with complex and varied characteristics. We propose a novel dynamic backdoor attack framework called Time-Embedding Neural Network, which incorporates a separate neural network to generate a high-dimensional label embedding that is fed into the main classification model, allowing it to identify and respond to hidden time-varying patterns. This approach enables us to create dynamic backdoor attacks even on complex classification tasks and demonstrates improved resilience in the face of data perturbations. We further enhance the framework by developing a method to control the duration of the attack and present several data poisoning strategies to compromise deep neural networks. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various classification tasks and networks, as evidenced by our comprehensive experimental results. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhengyong-yu/TENN.

A team of researchers used precise astrometric measurements from the Gaia satellite's data to identify variations in the positions of solar-type stars near the plane of our solar system. A statistical analysis revealed a pattern of positional changes directly tied to the speed at which these stars orbit the Sun. As expected, the most significant shift was seen in the direction of their motion, yet unexpected was a detectable shift in the perpendicular direction, which grew more pronounced with increasing distance from the Sun. A computational model was developed to account for the effects of nearby stars and the movement of objects within the solar system, ultimately pointing to a source of the observed shift: the collective parallax of the numerous small bodies in the solar system. This finding was further validated by examining regions around the Earth and Mars. As the search for this phenomenon was limited to a specific region around the solar system's center, the researchers estimated that the total parallax of the solar system would be observable with even more precise astrometric measurements. As expected, the magnitude of this effect was greater for stars positioned closer to the plane of the solar system, and it provided a unique indicator of the solar system's overall structure. The study's results also hinted at a slight discrepancy between the predicted and observed variations in position, which the researchers attributed to the presence of a small, unseen mass within the solar system. The effect of this mass was more pronounced in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius, suggesting that any search for dark matter in the solar system should prioritize this region. The researchers concluded that precise astrometric measurements of the positions of nearby stars could serve as a valuable tool in understanding the solar system's structure and the nature of dark matter. The study's findings were derived from data covering approximately 1 billion solar-type stars and were validated using simulated satellite data. The effect in question was found to be observable in approximately 1 in 10,000 stars, and the associated error margin was estimated to be around 10%. The study's limitations included the inability to distinguish between the effects of individual small bodies and the collective parallax of the solar system. The researchers proposed that future missions with even greater precision could potentially reveal further details about the solar system's structure and the masses of individual small bodies. The study's results were also found to be consistent with existing knowledge of the solar system, although they offered a more comprehensive understanding of the solar system's overall structure. Deep neural network-based question answering systems have achieved remarkable performance, yet these models often lack human-like understanding of the knowledge they draw from. To bridge this gap, we've developed a framework that leverages a knowledge base and incorporates explicit representations of meaning through abstract semantic structures, specifically directed acyclic graphs. By integrating a directed acyclic graph into the neural network, we've created a model that excels in incorporating knowledge and exhibits improved performance in several evaluation metrics. Our approach allows for various knowledge representations, including both structured and embedded formats, and our data-driven method enables automatic graph-based knowledge incorporation without the need for explicit annotation. We've tested this approach on multiple datasets and observed significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhongyuan-liu/KG-QA.

Calculating vibrational spectra for the smallest oxygen-containing molecular cations, such as O2+ and O3+, has been a complex task due to the absence of reliable experimental data and theoretical methods with equal parity for these asymmetrical species. As a result, their assigned spectra are primarily based on assumptions of complete degeneracy or symmetry breaking, which lacks direct evidence. In this study, we used multi-configuration time-dependent Hartree (MCDT) methods to accurately determine the vibrational spectra of O2+ and O3+ by accounting for the mixing of electronic states. Our results show that the application of equal parity in theoretical methods is crucial for obtaining reliable spectra of these cations. Furthermore, we found that the bond length in O2+ is shorter than 100 pm, the bond length in O2 is 120 pm, and the bond length in O3+ varies between 100 to 120 pm. Our calculated vibrational levels for O2+ and O3+ show good agreement with previous studies using other methods. Additionally, we found that the harmonic approximation significantly overestimates the energy differences between the ground state and excited states of these cations. In the case of O3+, we found that the 1$\Pi$u state has a very low energy barrier to rotationless isomerization, which could be important for understanding the behavior of these ions in laboratory and astrophysical environments. Our study highlights the importance of considering multi-configurational electronic wave functions when analyzing the vibrational spectra of these cations. Our results are relevant to ongoing and planned experiments that aim to study these ions through infrared spectroscopy. Our MCDT method can be applied to a wide range of molecular ions with multiple electronic states and temporary or permanent bonds. Distributed machine learning models often struggle with significant communication costs due to large data sets being used to train them. This issue is particularly problematic in settings where training on local data is necessary, such as with user-specific data on mobile devices. To address this challenge, a decentralized learning method has been developed that uses a random walk algorithm on a graph, in effect creating a collaborative framework among participants, and it does so without requiring them to share their local data. This approach leverages the random walk's ability to generate signals based on node importance, and it does so in a way that allows for efficient and precise data sampling, even when the number of nodes is substantial. We developed a computational method to calculate relativistic, anisotropic stellar models composed of two fluids, using the Einstein equations in a 1.5 split formalism, where metric and fluid variables are solved separately. This approach allows us to transform existing single-fluid solutions into two-fluid solutions. We applied this method to well-known static, spherically symmetric solutions, including the relativistic isothermal solutions, the Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff solutions, the Neutron Star Models, and the Schwarzschild solutions, and demonstrated its effectiveness by examining the behavior of these solutions. We also investigated the location of neutron star solutions within the mass--radius diagram and found that the two-fluid solutions can exhibit a first-order phase transition similar to that observed in single-fluid models. Furthermore, we found that the two-fluid solutions yield larger mass--radius relationships than their single-fluid counterparts. We believe our method provides a useful tool for investigating two-fluid solutions and studying the behavior of compact stars composed of multiple fluids. We intend to extend this method to time-dependent and rotating star solutions in future research. We emphasize that our two-fluid solutions do not imply the existence of two-fluid solutions for individual compact stars, but rather represent a generalization of the Einstein equations for multiple fluid components within a single compact star. We intend to apply this method to studying the behavior of compact stars composed of multiple fluids, such as neutron stars with crusts and cores, and to investigating the behavior of relativistic, anisotropic stars composed of multiple fluids in rotational instability and shock waves. We also plan to investigate the behavior of compact stars composed of multiple fluids in binary star mergers and supernovae explosions. This study proposes an innovative method for adapting Generalized End-to-End Conditional Random Fields (GECs) without additional annotated data, leveraging the grammatical knowledge embedded in neural machine translation (MT) models. Unlike conventional multi-task transfer learning methods, our approach modifies the NMT model to predict part-of-speech tags and dependency labels for the target language, leveraging the existing NMT models as a source of guidance. We then integrate the NECReader GEC model's output with the predicted labels using a weighted average. Evaluations on four publicly available datasets reveal that our adaptation method outperforms standard multi-task transfer learning and yields comparable F-score results to supervised training. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates enhanced performance when compared to other unsupervised GEC adaptation methods, thereby validating the effectiveness of our method. Our code and models are openly accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yu/MTGEC.

We introduce a new method for allocating divisible goods among multiple agents with private valuations, building upon the round-robin allocation framework and incorporating the benefits of the cut-and-choose algorithm. In the round-robin method, each agent is assigned a continuous share of a good based on their relative ranking within their group, with groups determined by total value contributions. In contrast to the original round-robin approach, this variation allows for positive allocations for up to n^{\delta} agents out of a total of n, where $\delta$ can be any real number greater than 0, without relying on the assumption of agent-specific distinct values. In addition, we establish that this new method yields a more equitable distribution than the cut-and-choose algorithm in terms of the proportion of the most valuable group each agent receives, at the cost of possibly smaller allocations for some agents. To achieve this, we first show that this new method can be viewed as implementing the outcome of a specific second-price auction in which bids are determined by group rather than individually. This leads to a general characterization of the fair proportion each group should receive, and from this, the specific proportions for each agent within a group emerge. This approach also enables us to establish the optimality of the allocated shares in terms of maximizing the total value obtained, as well as the fairness guarantee mentioned above. This is accomplished without assuming that the goods are perfectly divisible, as is necessary in other related studies. This is particularly notable given the difficulty of inducing desired behavior through pricing mechanisms in settings where goods can be fragmented. This new method is then applied to a range of related problems, including the allocation of multiple divisible goods among multiple agents, and the procurement of a divisible good from multiple sellers. This is accompanied by an empirical study demonstrating the practical value of the round-robin mechanism in a real-world context. To better understand this phenomenon, we developed a statistical model that accounted for the time it takes for a star to lose its inner disk, the time it takes for a star to lose its outer disk, and the time it takes for a star to no longer be visible, a process known as veiling dissipation. By fitting this model to our data, we found that the time it takes for a star to lose its outer disk is highly variable, with some disks dissipating in less than 1.5 million years and others taking over 10 million years to dissipate. We also found that the time it takes for a star to lose its inner disk is significantly shorter, ranging from 1 to 4 million years. We believe that extreme variability in accretion rates could explain the wide range of times it takes for a star to lose its outer disk, with high accretion rates leading to disk dissipation in less than 1.5 million years and low accretion rates taking over 10 million years to dissipate. If this is the case, it challenges our current understanding of disk evolution, which suggests that the time it takes for a star to lose its outer disk is primarily determined by the time it takes for the star to lose its inner disk. We also found that the time it takes for a star to lose its outer disk is influenced by the mass of the star, with more massive stars taking longer to lose their outer disks. We believe that this could be due to more massive stars having stronger magnetic fields that slow down the dissipation of their outer disks. We also found that the time it takes for a star to lose its outer disk is influenced by the presence of a binary companion, with stars in binary systems taking longer to lose their outer disks. We believe that this could be due to the presence of a binary companion leading to a decrease in the mass loss from the outer disk. Offline learning for complex multi-agent systems with sequential decisions as their primary application, has encountered significant challenges. To address limitations in abductive reasoning, we present the Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework, which represents the underlying dynamics of a system through shared trajectories and individual agents' policies. The Shared Individual Trajectories Abduction (SITA) algorithm, a novel offline learning method, leverages the SIT framework to effectively utilize experience data. The algorithm generates a model that, when combined with an agent's policy, produces a trajectory similar to past observations, thereby enhancing the generalization capability of the model. Through rigorous evaluation, we find that SITA yields performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods in multiple scenarios and significantly outperforms them in highly dynamic environments. Additionally, SITA demonstrates the efficacy of its abduction-based evaluation to identify and rectify model biases. Our approach provides a versatile solution for offline learning across various domains, including complex multi-agent systems with sequential decision-making. V392 Persei, a binary system that underwent a nova eruption in 2010, has been monitored over the past decade. Observations from the Kiso 1.8m telescope reveal that V392 Persei has been exhibiting B-type symbiotic characteristics, with a combination of high temperatures emanating from the binary system's white dwarf and a surrounding accretion disk. As the system transitioned from a high to a low state, the temperature from the white dwarf decreased, while the temperature from the secondary star, likely a main-sequence or subgiant companion, increased. This shift in temperatures suggests that the white dwarf's surface was heated by a thermonuclear burst, likely a residual from the 2010 nova eruption. This phenomenon is comparable to that seen in RW Monocerotis, another binary system exhibiting symbiotic characteristics, and supports the hypothesis that novae can enter a state of increased mass transfer following a nova eruption. Furthermore, V392 Persei's behavior may be an indication that binary systems with a high mass transfer rate can exhibit characteristics similar to those of classical novae that have undergone eruptions. This discovery highlights the significance of long-term monitoring of binary systems that have undergone nova eruptions, as it provides valuable insights into the post-eruption evolution of these systems. This research also contributes to the understanding of binary systems that exhibit symbiotic characteristics, particularly those with a mass transfer rate that is high enough to prevent the formation of an accretion disk around the white dwarf. This phenomenon is thought to be a precursor to supernovae Type Ia explosions. This discovery was made possible by the unique combination of low interstellar extinction in V392 Persei's direction and the telescope's sensitivity to detect the faint radiation from the system's surrounding accretion disk. We investigate surface currents in two-dimensional semi-infinite systems driven by periodic driving forces and demonstrate that non-trivial surface currents show robustness across various fermionization processes. Our findings reveal that surface currents retain their symmetry-protected characteristics even after a system undergoes a change from fermionic to bosonic behavior. Furthermore, in a one-dimensional chain with a dimerized lattice structure, we observe that surface currents remain unaffected by the degree of dimerization. Our study also reveals the existence of surface current robustness in a system with spontaneous symmetry breaking. Our work is applicable to various discrete symmetries, including time-reversal, parity, and combined symmetries, and we demonstrate the surface current robustness in various models, including the driven Jaynes-Cummings system, driven spin chains, and driven phonon chains. Notably, our results are supported by numerical kernel polynomial method simulations. Our study sheds light on the surface current robustness in mesoscopic systems and provides a potential platform for investigating topological phenomena in small-scale, experimentally controllable setups.

To mitigate the adverse impact of the all-or-none order design in redispatch markets on the grid operator's procurement, we propose a modified rule where the acceptance of all-or-none orders depends on the current imbalance levels. In this framework, orders are accepted all-or-none if imbalances are high, but are settled partially when imbalances are low. We show that the proposed mechanism makes the all-or-none order design compatible with optimal grid procurement strategies, thereby preventing the grid operator from favoring the all-or-none design over partial settlement through strategic manipulation of imbalances. Furthermore, we find that the proposed mechanism results in the same social cost as the all-or-none design in scenarios with high imbalances and reduces costs in scenarios with low imbalances. In addition, we examine the effects of introducing the proposed mechanism in real-world use cases. In these studies, we observe that the all-or-none order design often leads to the grid operator engaging in costly redispatch trades with market participants who have already completed their own redispatch, and that the proposed mechanism can mitigate this issue by inducing the grid operator to settle partial orders with these participants. In contrast, without the proposed mechanism, the grid operator may prefer the all-or-none design over partial settlement, and that this preference can result in higher social costs following unexpected generation or demand outages. Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable performance, but their susceptibility to data corruption poses a significant problem in real-world applications. Although various methods have been developed to enhance robustness, they often rely on uniform data range constraints or artificial noise, which can limit their practical value. We introduce a novel non-uniform weight pruning technique called "Efficient Neural Architecture through Selective Training" that targets specific parameter ranges, resulting in a more compact and corruption-resistant model. By identifying and removing redundant weights, our approach minimizes silent data corruptions caused by normal training. We demonstrate that it is possible to create models with both improved accuracy and lower parameter counts when compared to state-of-the-art compression techniques. Furthermore, our method yields a neural network that is more resilient to data corruptions, achieving a $3.5\times$ decrease in corruption-induced errors when training with corrupted data. Our approach is particularly effective for large-scale neural networks, as evidenced by our LLM benchmark using JAX, which shows that our method can decrease parameter counts by 11% and $15\%$ while maintaining high accuracy on the ConLL-2003 and SQuAD 1.1 datasets, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyong-pan/EAST.

Transferring knowledge from high-resource languages can significantly enhance the accuracy of name tagging in low-resource languages. This research focuses on developing a method to leverage medium to high-level resources, specifically expanding the set of labeled words that can be trained on, by employing a word-piece subword model to handle out-of-vocabulary words. A novel training schedule is proposed to prevent over-segmentation, and the effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through name tagging using CRF in four low-resource languages, with results showing improved F-score scores by 3.5% on average in the most challenging setting, and improving the baseline by 5.5% F-score in the easiest setting. This approach is particularly beneficial for languages with complex writing systems like Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, and can be used with multiple tag sets. System implementation is available at https://github.com/zhuyichao/name-tag-transfer. This research is part of a larger project that aims to develop a name tagging system for 100 languages, with system outputs and evaluation data available at https://www.namejoiner.org/. We develop a symbolic decision procedure to determine if one regular expression is contained within another using regular expression antiderivatives. This method leverages Brzozowski's operator and our previously established connection to the antiderivatives of regular expressions, along with a modified version of the antiderivatives that enables us to check containment. By employing a parametrized version of Brzozowski's operator and our established regular expression antiderivatives, we can determine containment between two regular expressions by means of a symbolic test of equality. This is achieved through a transformation of the two regular expressions into the form of E(X) ≡ f(X) and E(X) ≡ g(X), followed by the computation of (f ∘ σ)(X) and (g ∘ σ)(X), and finally examining the antiderivatives of f ∘ σ and g ∘ σ for equality. This procedure is underpinned by a regular tree characterisation of the regular languages corresponding to (f ∘ σ)(X) and (g ∘ σ)(X), enabling us to examine the equality of these languages by examining the equality of their corresponding tree automata, and thereby determining the containment of one regular expression within another. This decision procedure serves as the basis for an algorithm to check containment between regular expressions using regular expression antiderivatives, and this algorithm has been implemented as part of the RegVerif verification tool. This tool leverages the decision procedure to check safety properties of programs that process regular data types, and has been successfully applied to the verification of several programs. To illustrate the limitations of this decision procedure, we also examine the containment of regular expression antiderivatives for the regular expression X*, and in doing so, we derive a regular tree whose corresponding language is equivalent to the language corresponding to O(X) = X/(1-X), and we show that this regular tree is infinite and has an infinite number of states in its underlying finite state automaton. Recently, VIO methods utilizing deep learning have demonstrated superior accuracy, largely surpassing the performance of conventional VIO algorithms. Despite the advancements, the underlying techniques and optimization methods employed in these high-performance VIO models remain unclear, hindering their widespread adoption. To address this challenge, this paper delves into the design of a state-of-the-art VIO model using a monocular camera and a wheel odometry stream, with a focus on deconstructing its underlying components and optimizing its implementation for embedded systems. By dissecting the model's structure and refining its architecture through a series of optimizations, this study demonstrates a 4.5 times improvement in VIO solution accuracy and a 7.5 times reduction in computational requirements on an automotive platform. Furthermore, a novel, efficient VIO model is introduced, leveraging a graph-based representation to achieve a 2.5 times boost in processing efficiency while maintaining high solution precision. The research and development presented in this paper are accompanied by publicly accessible code and data.

The Weyl semimetal has been extensively studied as a novel topological phase of matter with linear energy dispersion along three dimensions. Recent discoveries have revealed various higher-order Weyl semimetals in three-dimensional systems, characterized by non-linear energy dispersion at multiple points in the Brillouin zone. We propose a theoretical model of a three-dimensional material, based on a fcc crystal structure, and demonstrate that it exhibits square-root topology. This is achieved through a careful arrangement of Dirac nodal line rings in the Brillouin zone, ensuring that the Weyl points in the 3D momentum space are connected by tubular structures that intersect with the $\Gamma$ point at the center of the zone. This unique feature distinguishes our proposed material from other three-dimensional Weyl semimetals. Notably, square-root topology arises from a type of crystal symmetry that is commonly observed in materials, and it is expected to lead to novel electronic properties, including Fermi arc surfaces and square-root disclination rotons, and potentially, a photoinduced phase with a Weyl semimetal and Mott-insulator coexistence. Our theoretical model provides a starting point for experimental realization and investigation of square-root topology in three-dimensional materials. This includes predictions for the electronic structure, optical conductivity, and possible phase transitions in these materials. Our work highlights the significance of considering three-dimensional momentum space topology in the search for novel topological materials. Our proposed material can be realized using transition metal compounds with a fcc crystal structure, such as Sr$_3$Ir$_2$O$_7$ and Sr$_2$IrO$_4$. Our theoretical predictions are relevant to Sr$_3$Ir$_2$O$_7$ and Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, as well as other materials with a fcc crystal structure that exhibit square-root topology. This includes LaIrO$_3$ and LaOsO$_3$, which exhibit Weyl semimetal and square-root topology, respectively. Our work also highlights the potential for photoinduced phase transitions in materials with a Weyl semimetal and Mott-insulator coexistence, which can be realized in Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ under an optical pump-probe experiment. Our predictions for the electronic structure, optical conductivity, and possible phase transitions in these materials can be experimentally verified using a range of techniques, including angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), optical conductivity measurements, and X-ray diffraction

Theoretical convergence rates for the relative $H^1$ norm error are established under certain conditions, with specific cases revealing the feasibility of achieving the optimal rate $1/2$. The performance of the edge finite element methods is then demonstrated through a set of numerical experiments, including the reconstruction of missing function values in both one and two dimensions. The presented results highlight the effectiveness of the edge finite element approach and confirm the theoretical convergence rate of $\frac{1}{2}$ for the relative $H^1$ norm error when utilizing these methods. The corresponding MATLAB code is provided as part of the submitted material. The study also highlights the connection between the edge finite element method and the use of piecewise constant finite elements within a nonconforming framework. The utility of the edge finite element method is further illustrated through the solution of a nonlinear minimization problem, representing the completed data as the solution to a system of nonlinear equations. The implementation is accompanied by a visual representation of the computational time required to achieve a specific level of data resolution, demonstrating the edge method's ability to produce high-resolution data efficiently. The developed code is available for use or modification at https://github.com/andrewlucerno/edge_fem_tv. Deep neural networks require vast amounts of data to achieve high accuracy, which can be a significant challenge for certain applications. As a result, there's growing interest in using a saliency-based method to transfer knowledge from a highly accurate, complex teacher network to a less complex student network, which has fewer parameters. This technique aims to identify crucial features for a classification task that contribute to the network's classification performance. Initially, this method was applied in a single-task setting, but our research extends it to a multi-task setting by introducing a new algorithm that incorporates knowledge from multiple teachers. Our algorithm generates a shared set of important features that are subsequently used to train multiple student networks, each for a different task. Our results show that this approach yields better performance than the single-task method and facilitates the training process by introducing a form of regularization. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that this method excels in a multi-task setting when compared to traditional transfer learning techniques. Our research and findings are validated through extensive experiments conducted using six popular datasets. Our code is available online for public use.

We investigated the carrier concentration in silicon wafers that have undergone two different surface treatments: etching the silicon surface or etching the oxide buffer layer on top of the silicon. Our research compared and contrasted these two approaches using various techniques such as Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy, Scanning Acoustic Microscopy, and Monte Carlo simulations. We found that carrier concentration is significantly higher in the etched silicon method, specifically in areas with surface roughening, and that the oxide etching method primarily affects the near-surface carrier distribution rather than altering the bulk carrier concentration. Additionally, we found that the carrier concentration in the bulk region remains relatively stable in both surface treatment methods. We also observed that the carrier concentration in the oxide etched method exhibits a gradual increase towards the oxide-silicon interface, and that this distribution can be effectively managed by adjusting the etching time. We believe our findings have implications for the development of silicon-based nanogenerator technology.

The interior and exterior of a planet are dynamically interconnected through various processes including mass transfer, tidal heating, atmospheric escape, and planetary cooling. We propose a new framework that considers the reciprocal relationship between a planet's interior and exterior, which we call interior-exterior cycling. This framework's cyclic components can influence a planet's atmospheric evolution over time. For instance, a cooler planet loses more atmospheric gas, which in turn leads to increased tidal heating and potential atmospheric restoration. We also introduce a simple atmospheric model that accounts for gas transfer between a planet and its surrounding space environment. This model's parameters can be estimated from observations of a planet's mass, radius, and temperature. Using these estimates and numerical simulations, we explore the long-term consequences of interior-exterior cycling for a hypothetical terrestrial planet similar to Mars. Our findings suggest that interior-exterior cycling can counteract atmospheric gas loss and even drive atmospheric gas accumulation, leading to increased surface pressure and temperature. Consequently, this could enhance tidal heating, slow planetary cooling, and perpetuate a cycle of atmospheric gas retention. If validated by further study, this hypothesis offers a new explanation for the observed geological activity on Mars and provides a fresh perspective on the long-term evolution of planetary atmospheres. Additionally, interior-exterior cycling may also influence the atmospheres of gas giants and terrestrial planets within stellar clusters, and could have implications for the search for life on exoplanets. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of interior-exterior cycling is crucial for accurately predicting the long-term atmospheric evolution of planets and for identifying biosignatures in future spectroscopic observations of exoplanets. Based on this framework, we propose a set of testable predictions for atmospheric evolution that can be validated by future research in astrobiology, exoplanetary science, and planetary physics. Given the complex interactions between a planet's interior and exterior, we believe that a comprehensive understanding of interior-exterior cycling is essential for accurately predicting the long-term evolution of planetary atmospheres and for identifying the conditions necessary for life to thrive on other planets. Given the potential of future high-precision spectroscopic observations to detect biosignatures in exoplanetary atmospheres, it is crucial to consider the interior and exterior dynamics of planets in order to accurately predict their long-term evolution and prevent misinterpretation of life-related signals. The nonlinear Hawkes process is an extension of the nonlinear point process model, which incorporates interactions and feedback mechanisms in a flexible and flexible GRX-based framework. We provide a counting process theorem to treat nonlinear Hawkes processes and achieve Poisson processes through change of measure, known as beta-transforms. These beta-transforms are then utilized to derive a stochastic maximum likelihood estimator and an unbiased estimator for the glass network's score function. Our study is accompanied by numerical experiments that demonstrate the nonlinear Hawkes process's ability to capture complex interaction patterns and feedback mechanisms, even in scenarios with significant over-saturation. Furthermore, nonlinear Hawkes processes are applied to an empirical example involving a high-frequency dataset of a financial tick stream from the NASDAQ stock exchange. The resulting model is shown to accurately capture the complex feedback mechanisms and short-term memory observed in financial data. The code used for this research is publicly accessible on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/zhengyiwang/nonlinear_hawkes_process. The R package 'nHP' is also available on CRAN at the following link: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nHP/index.html. The nonlinear Hawkes process is a promising tool for modeling and forecasting point processes in various fields, including finance, economics, and social sciences. The code and R package provided offer a practical solution for researchers and practitioners looking to apply nonlinear Hawkes processes in their work. The research presented in this paper is relevant to the fields of applied mathematics, statistics, economics, finance, and computer science. The study's findings and methodology can be applied to various real-world problems and scenarios. The tau electric dipole moment's potential magnitude can be examined through a two-Higgs doublet extension of the Standard Model, specifically its type-II variant. This type of model includes five unique Higgs interactions affecting the tau lepton, four of which have previously been considered, and one newly identified, contributing to the tau electric dipole moment: the CP-violating dot-product term of two Higgs VEVs in the neutral sector. We calculate the tau electric dipole moment induced by this previously unexplored interaction and find it to be particularly significant when the lighter CP-even Higgs mass falls within a specific range, potentially leading to a substantial enhancement of the predicted tau electric dipole moment, especially when taking into account existing constraints on the lighter CP-even Higgs mass. As a result, the lighter CP-even Higgs mass limit from LEP and LHC data may need to be reevaluated, offering a new avenue for exploring this type of two-Higgs doublet scenario. Additionally, we find that the tau electric dipole moment's magnitude can be further increased by considering the lighter CP-even Higgs in the $125$ GeV range, a possibility that deserves experimental investigation. We provide a comprehensive error correction capability analysis for rank metric codes, effectively extending previous research on codes with rates greater and less than one-half. When attempting to correct up to t rank errors, our main finding shows that the rank metric code capability can be characterized as $\frac{K}{D_t(R)} - \frac{1}{2}$ for $R \geq \frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{K}{D_t(R)} - 1$ for $R < \frac{1}{2}$. Notably, our results reveal that for rates below one-half, there are rank metric codes that outperform Reed-Solomon codes under erasure and rank attacks. Additionally, our study includes a general construction method for codes with optimal distance properties and a specific example of a Gaussian code. Our research also highlights the limitations of codes with certain parameters and presents a formula for calculating the minimum cut rank in metric tree structures. Furthermore, we establish a connection between our capability formula and the list decoding of rank metric codes. Our findings on capability and code construction can be applied to various related problems, including the security of a cryptographic protocol and the solvability of systems of linear equations over finite fields. This work extends our previous research on codes with rates greater than one-half and provides a foundation for exploring similar questions in other metric-based code structures. The peculiar Type Ia supernova SN~2020jfo has been studied in depth, and new spectroscopic and photometric data have been incorporated into its analysis. By examining the absorption lines in the supernova's spectra, researchers found that the relative amounts of nickel and iron being produced are lower than usual, with a ratio to the solar abundance of about one-tenth. This unusual ratio is particularly striking given the short time frame in which the absorption lines associated with nickel and iron formed, and the fact that the iron absorption lines are weaker than expected in relation to nickel. A team of scientists also simulated the behavior of a massive, interacting binary system using a computer model, and found that it could produce a supernova with a similar chemical composition to SN~2020jfo, and one that matches the observed characteristics of this supernova. Notably, this model predicts that the supernova will be accompanied by a strong optical and near-infrared radiation, and a fast and massive outflow of gas, and it could help explain the observed features of several other supernovae, including SN~2018gv. Furthermore, this model suggests that SN~2020jfo may have occurred in a satellite galaxy that was interacting with the main galaxy it is associated with, and it could provide valuable insights into how galaxies interact and merge with each other.

This work develops a level set approach for an equation representing surface shrinker in the Euclidean space and uses it to create a new algorithm for computing the surface sender. Initially, a level set type method is applied to the equation defining surface shrinker, which results in modifying the method to accommodate the orthogonal condition in the Hamilton-Jacobi equation its level set form includes a sign-changing coefficient. To achieve this, the equation is reformulated as a system of two Hamilton-Jacobi equations. This level set method-based framework can be applied to solve the surface sender equation, which is equivalent to solving two coupled Hamilton-Jacobi equations with changing sign coefficients. This leads to developing an algorithm to find surface sender, which is more efficient than the current method of using the flow of diffeomorphisms. This algorithm's efficiency is demonstrated by computing the surface sender for a given surface shrinker in the Euclidean 2-space. This level set method-based framework can be applied to find surface sender in a given Riemannian manifold if an efficient algorithm for Hamilton-Jacobi equations with changing sign coefficients is developed in that specific setting. This approach allows us to bypass traditional N-body simulations and focus on developing highly effective density models. By applying this method to highly accurate simulations with $\sigma_8 = 0.8$, we obtained a density-only N-body model and trained a conditional extension based on neural halo occupation numbers (NENH). Our results show that this two-step approach yields highly accurate predictions for halo masses, with an overestimation of less than 1% when compared to direct simulations. Furthermore, we found that using this method results in a 2-fold improvement in halo mass prediction precision when halo mass is overestimated using simulations with $\sigma_8 = 1.0$. Our findings indicate that this two-step approach has significant potential for reducing the computational costs associated with cosmological simulations and halo occupation number modeling. We introduce a novel approach to analyzing the evolution of rotating stars, where the mass, specific angular momentum, and entropy of fluid elements are described through a multi-dimensional conserved quantity field. This method, which uses a combination of Eulerian and Lagrangian frameworks, allows us to bypass the difficulties associated with the anisotropic nature of the star's angular velocity distribution. By applying this framework, we derive a set of nonlinear partial differential equations that relate the angular velocity, entropy, and density of the star, and which we solve numerically to study its evolution during main sequence and giant phases. Our results demonstrate the anisotropic mass transport during the star's evolution, and we find that the mass transport patterns exhibit symmetry about the star's rotation axis, with mass transported to the equator during the main sequence phase and to the poles during the giant phase. Our approach also enables us to investigate the stability of the star to axisymmetric perturbations, and we find that the star's evolution is influenced by a heat-engine mechanism that drives mass transport from the poles to the equator, and which we attribute to the anisotropic thermal expansion associated with the star's evolution. Our findings are consistent with previous studies based on the anelastic approximation, and we demonstrate that this approximation is valid for a wide range of rotation rates. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of rotating stars, from low-mass to high-mass stars, and we expect it to be particularly useful for studying the evolution of rotating massive stars, whose cores undergo strong differential rotation during their evolution. Our results also provide a theoretical explanation for the observed mass transport patterns in rotating massive stars, which we attribute to the anisotropic mass transport associated with their angular momentum distribution. Our approach can be used to investigate the stability of rotating stars to non-axisymmetric perturbations, and we expect it to be particularly useful for studying rotating stars with strong differential rotation, whose stability is influenced by their angular velocity gradient. A potential solution to this issue is collective incremental learning, where new data is used to update previously acquired knowledge rather than starting from a blank slate. This approach is particularly beneficial when labeling individual items is time-consuming and costly. A key consideration in this method is the selection of data to label, which can be thought of as assigning priority to each piece of data based on its potential to improve the accuracy of the model following incremental learning. This process can be viewed as solving an optimization problem that takes into account both the effectiveness of a model in processing the data and the impact of labeling that data has on the model's performance after it has been updated. A collaborative incremental learning framework is proposed that accounts for the relationships between different data items, leading to an Ising model-based representation that facilitates the prioritization of data for labeling. This approach is demonstrated through experiments using both synthetic and real-world data, and the results show that it is possible to improve the performance of machine learning models by focusing on the most critical data. The observation of gravitational waves from neutron star mergers has given rise to a new field of multi-messenger astrophysics, allowing us to study these rare and distant events through both electromagnetic and gravitational radiation. In this review, we discuss the breakthroughs made possible by combining data from the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Detector (LIGO) and various electromagnetic telescopes, including those that detected radiation across the electromagnetic spectrum. We examine the insights gained from the two confirmed GW events, GW 170817 and GW 190425, and the prospects for continued discovery in this field. This review also delves into the potential for future detections, considering the increased sensitivity of upgraded gravitational wave detectors and the role of wide-field telescopes in observing faint electromagnetic signals from distant mergers. By integrating the power of both gravitational and electromagnetic observations, we can better understand the properties of merging neutron stars, their aftermath, and the surrounding environment. This research examines the urban encounter diversity in Milan during Italy's nationwide lockdown and subsequent recovery period following the 2020 pandemic. We analyze aggregated data on Milan residents' interactions within their community, incorporating various urban features and their impact on encounter diversity. Our findings reveal that the pandemic significantly reduced encounter diversity by limiting interactions between people of different ages and socioeconomic backgrounds. However, during the recovery phase, encounters became more homogeneous once again, primarily due to increased mobility and community isolation. Our study proposes a framework for assessing community resilience through the lens of encounter diversity and urban theory, highlighting the importance of inclusive community design to foster diversity and mitigate the negative effects of crises on urban communities. By exploring the interplay between urban structure, encounter diversity, and community resilience, we identify strategies for policymakers to promote community resilience through targeted interventions in areas such as mobility, community engagement, and inclusive urban planning. By applying our framework to Milan's data, we demonstrate that a more inclusive urban structure can enhance community resilience by reducing the homogenization of encounters and promoting diversity, ultimately contributing to a more robust and adaptable community in the face of crisis. We examine the interplay between geometric curvature, thermodynamic hysteresis, and the evolution of entropy in a broad class of first-order phase transition models, both dynamically and under periodic driving forces. Through simulations and theoretical analysis, our findings reveal that positive curvature accelerates the onset of phase transitions and boosts entropy growth in both dynamic and driven scenarios. Conversely, negative curvature hinders the transition and slows the rise in entropy. These effects become more pronounced as curvature intensity increases, and we identify distinct threshold values where the behavior shifts abruptly. The impact of hysteresis on entropy is more complex, but generally it broadens the range where the phase transition occurs, thus increasing the range over which entropy accelerates. Our work provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the interrelated effects of curvature, hysteresis, and entropy within non-equilibrium phase transition systems. Our research further reveals that curvature can induce multiple coexisting phases within finite domains, a phenomenon previously observed in specific contexts. Our results are applicable to various real-world phenomena, including biological, chemical, and material science applications. Our findings are based on numerical simulations of a two-dimensional discrete curvature-driven Edwards-Anderson model, but our theoretical analysis suggests that our conclusions are broadly generalizable to other model types. Specifically, we developed a convolutional neural network to address convolutional semantic labeling and a recurrent neural network to address sequential labeling. Our model incorporates an expectation-maximization algorithm to account for label noise, which we found to be effective in handling inconsistent annotations. Our results show that our framework outperforms the current state of the art on large-scale convolutional and sequential labeling tasks. We also observed that checking the consistency of annotations enhances labeling performance, particularly when the model is trained on clean data. Our framework also enables the creation of high-quality training data by filtering out inconsistent annotations, which we found to be effective in reducing label noise to 10%. Our investigation examines the sensitivity of a magnetometer using atomic interference, with a local magnetic field detected as a change in frequency. We found that, with two pulse interferometry, a minimum frequency change of two times the photon recoil factor, or 4.76 Hz, can be distinguished. This corresponds to a local magnetic field of 0.57 nT, achieved through our experimental setup. However, with three-pulse interferometry, the minimum frequency change that can be detected increases to 6.67 Hz, resulting in a detectable local magnetic field of 0.72 nT. Our research demonstrates that atomic interferometry can effectively measure a local magnetic field with a strength as low as 0.57 nT, which could be improved with better laser stability. Additionally, we observed that the detected phase shift in our two-pulse interferometry setup is directly proportional to the magnetic field strength, with a calculated proportionality constant of 0.98 radians per Tesla. Notably, our results show that even with a small atomic sample and a short interaction time, atomic interferometry can identify a local magnetic field as small as 10 picotesla, equivalent to about 3.10^-8 times the strength of the Earth's magnetic field. Our findings also highlight the importance of minimizing laser phase fluctuations to improve the accuracy of the measurement, and we suggest that with a more stable laser, a local magnetic field as small as 10^-9 times the strength of the Earth's magnetic field may be detectable using this method. Our research further indicates that atomic interferometry can measure small local magnetic fields through the detection of neutrally charged atoms, without the need for magnetic shielding, and with a sensitivity that approaches, but has not yet reached, the limit set by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Our experiments demonstrate that the minimum detectable magnetic field can be reduced by increasing the interaction time, and we propose that with an interaction time of one second, a local magnetic field as small as 10^-9 times the strength of the Earth's magnetic field can be identified. Our study demonstrates that atomic interferometry can be used to measure small local magnetic fields in atomic samples in a wide range of applications, and we suggest that with further improvements in laser stability, this method could be highly effective in searching for dark matter or other subtle phenomena. We introduce a Bayesian nonparametric hierarchical model, wherein a Dirichlet process mixture model's density components and admixture weights are given prior distributions, even when the model is potentially misspecified and the weights are identifiable. This model allows for inferences about the weights, overcoming an issue that prevents direct application of methods like posterior sampling and maximum marginal likelihood estimation. Theoretical and practical weight-identification guarantees are provided, showing that the model's admixture-weight posterior distribution converges to an asymptotically consistent and identifiable estimate as data samples increase. Moreover, we establish that the model's admixture-weight posterior distribution can be used to create point and interval estimates of the weights. These results are validated through simulated and real-world examples. Our approach is demonstrated using both synthetic and real data, and we show that our method compares favourably to alternative approaches. Our model and associated methods can be used in a wide range of applications, including, but not limited to, topic modelling, clustering, and image segmentation. Traditional GPU memory management systems rely on separate memory pools for object allocation, leading to significant fragmentation and poor performance. In contrast, host memory can be leveraged for object storage on the GPU, reducing memory waste and enhancing efficiency. However, implementing such a strategy on multiple GPUs within a single node poses a significant challenge due to synchronization requirements and limited access to memory locations. Our DynaSOAr system addresses these issues by introducing a novel, lock-free co-allocator that utilizes shared memory on multiple GPUs, minimizing memory fragmentation and boosting performance. By further optimizing memory usage through object recycling and compression, DynaSOAr achieves substantial improvements over current memory allocators in both CPU and GPU memory. Specifically, our experiments reveal DynaSOAr's co-allocator to deliver a 2.5x speedup and 3.5x reduction in memory fragmentation when utilizing a single GPU, and further gains of 1.5x in speedup and 2x in memory savings when employing four GPUs within a single node. Moreover, DynaSOAr's co-allocator's scalability enables seamless integration into existing applications with minimal modifications. Our findings demonstrate that DynaSOAr's innovative memory management approach can serve as a foundational solution for the development of future GPU memory management systems. System implementation codes and evaluation data are available at https://github.com/kuangguan/DynaSOAr. Furthermore, our research highlights key challenges associated with GPU memory management on multiple GPUs and provides actionable advice for future system optimization. Our team invites the broader community to collaborate and contribute to the advancement of DynaSOAr in an effort to drive future breakthroughs in this area. The concept of Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states is being utilized to study the interaction between a superconductor and localized magnetic moments. In this research, we examine the behavior of YSR states resulting from a single cobalt adatom or a pair of cobalt adatoms on an iridium (111) surface using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy. Due to the significant impact of spin-orbit coupling on iridium, the positions of YSR state peaks exhibit notable shifts in both scenarios, with the single adatom showing four distinct states instead of the typical three, and the adatom pair displaying four pairs of states that hybridize and form two branches with different behavior. Our findings are supported by calculations conducted using a tight-binding model and a single-impurity Anderson model, and provide a clear explanation for previous observations of YSR states on gold surfaces. Moreover, our research reveals that the spin-orbit coupling affects the distribution of charge within YSR states, leading to a redistribution of charge between states with opposite spins, and causing the disappearance of states located at the Fermi level in the presence of magnetic adatoms or dimers. This phenomenon is particularly evident for adatoms with high orbital momenta, and could be crucial for understanding various phenomena related to magnetic adatoms on superconducting surfaces. Our study also reveals that N atoms in the $t_2g$ site have a higher formation energy than those in the substitutional Ti sites, suggesting that in TiO2, N atoms tend to occupy both interstitial and substitutional locations equally, whereas C atoms primarily occupy the interstitial locations. Let's consider the problem of coloring the edges of a given graph $G$ with $c$ colors, such that the edges forming any given subgraph $F$ within $G$ contain at least a specific number $r$ of distinct colors. This problem is equivalent to determining the minimum number $c$ of colors required to achieve the desired level of color diversity within the subgraphs of $F$ from $G$. This value is denoted as the upper bound $\chi_F(G)$ of $G$. In this paper, we explore the specific cases of triangles and squares of graphs. For any graph $G$, we establish a lower bound of $3$ for $\Delta_1(G)$, which represents the smallest number of colors needed to ensure that each edge in $G$ has a different color than its adjacent edges. In addition, we examine the relationship between the number of colors used in an edge-coloring of a given graph and the maximum number of colors used within any subgraph of a specific type. Qubits are the fundamental units of measurement in quantum computing and are susceptible to errors due to interactions with their surroundings. The accuracy of mass-based calibration is directly affected by the noise it tolerates. Our research compares the mass-determination methods for qubits and qutrits in various error scenarios, revealing that qutrits exhibit significantly better noise tolerance under both amplitude damping and decoherence errors. Specifically, the standard deviation of the average mass increases with the number of qubits, whereas it remains stable for qutrits in both cases. Our findings highlight the potential advantages of qutrits in robust calibration and suggest that qutrits may be more suitable for applications in noisy conditions. Our study also reveals that the average mass becomes skewed in the presence of decoherence and that qutrits exhibit a higher noise tolerance when the damping coefficient approaches 1. Our work provides a theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of qutrits in calibration measurements and lays the groundwork for experimental verification. We provide an infinite number of examples of infinitely generated groups with a finite number of conjugacy classes, demonstrating that they have a polynomial diameter that increases at a rate of $n^{3}$ for n nilpotent subgroups, and show that these groups are computationally recognizable. Additionally, groups with a polynomial diameter related to the number of irreducible characters mod n were initially proposed as conjectural characteristics of braid groups, and our findings confirm this conjecture for specific braid groups. Furthermore, our analysis yields new information about the group Out(F_n), the group of outer automorphisms of free groups, and its connection to the groups presented in our examples. Our results also establish that for certain values of m and n, the group G_{m,n} generated by automorphisms of free groups has specific properties, and we demonstrate that these groups share similarities with groups from our examples. Our research on these groups G_{m,n} leads to a broader investigation of groups resulting from the extension of the group of outer automorphisms of free groups by the symmetric group S_n, and S_n's action on the set of homomorphisms from the free group F_n to the free group F_n. Our study of these groups reveals their connection to the groups presented in our examples and provides a description of their structure. Our research also uncovers a connection between the group G_{m,n} and the group of birational automorphisms of the affine plane of degree m, denoted as Birk_m, and establishes that these groups are distinct from the groups presented in our examples for values of m and n other than 2, 2 respectively. Our study of Birk_m reveals its structure, and our investigation of this group leads to the development of a new approach to understanding the group Birk_n for any n. Our research on Birk_n uncovers a connection to the group of automorphisms of the free group F_n that fix a specific subgroup of rank n-1, and our findings enable us to determine the number of conjugacy classes of the group Birk_n for any n. Our study of the group Birk_n also yields information about its conjugacy classes, and our investigation allows us to establish that the group Birk_n has a polynomial diameter that increases at a rate of n^2 for n nilpotent subgroups, and we show that this diameter is optimal.
