Building on the work of Moerdijk and Prestel, we show that there is a natural equivalence between the category of topological groupoid extensions and the category of gerbes over topological stacks. Furthermore, we establish a connection between Atiyah sequences and the underlying local transition functions of gerbes over topological stacks. This connection enables us to interpret 2-cocycles associated with the 2-categorical 2-cocycle sequence as specific types of gerbes over the 2-stacks defined by a given category of functors. As a result, we gain insight into the relationship between 2-cocycles and gerbes within the context of 2-stacks. Additionally, this understanding allows us to establish a connection between the gerbes over the 2-stacks defined by a category of functors and the 2-cocycles associated with the 2-categorical 2-cocycle sequence. This connection, in turn, facilitates the construction of gerbes over 2-stacks through the 2-cocycles of the 2-categorical 2-cocycle sequence. This construction is analogous to the construction of gerbes over topological stacks from the 2-cocycles of the 2-categorical 2-cocycle sequence. This analogy is reflective of the underlying relationship between the 2-categorical 2-cocycle sequence and the associated 2-stacks. This interpretation enables us to establish that the 2-cocycles associated with the 2-categorical 2-cocycle sequence are precisely the gerbes over the 2-stacks defined by a given category of functors. This finding is a key aspect of our research and is presented in Theorem 4.5.2. This theorem demonstrates that the 2-cocycles associated with the 2-categorical 2-cocycle sequence capture the essence of the gerbes over 2-stacks defined by a given category of functors. We discovered that applying repeated differentiation or integration to a zonal function results in another zonal function. Furthermore, we established an explicit formula for the repeated differentiation or integration of a zonal function. Our findings extend previous work by Gelfand and Naimark, Gelfand and Shapiro, and Helstroöm. Additionally, we provide a method for calculating the values of certain integrals involving zonal functions, which were previously unknown. This includes determining specific integrals of Bessel functions and generalized hypergeometric functions. Our approach to addressing these integrals is distinct from existing solutions. This research was motivated by the study of the heat equation on spheres and the resulting associated functional, which led to the discovery of connections between the solutions of this equation and zonal functions. Our results also uncovered relationships between certain Bessel functions and generalized hypergeometric functions, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding these functions within the context of the heat equation on spheres. This framework includes identifying specific functions that can be expressed as sums of zonal functions, as well as determining the limits of certain functions as their defining variable approaches specific values. This knowledge can be applied to the solutions of the heat equation on spheres, which in turn has implications for the study of the asymptotic behavior of certain random processes associated with these spheres. This research also introduces a new method for calculating the values of certain expectations associated with the heat equation on spheres, which was previously unknown. This expectation value can be expressed as a sum of values of certain functions at specific points, which can be determined using our developed formula for repeated differentiation of zonal functions. This enabled us to derive a formula for the expectation value of a specific random variable, which in turn allowed us to establish an inequality related to the maximum value of this random variable. This inequality provides a bound on the probability that this random variable exceeds a given value, which can be used to estimate the cost of certain financial options associated with the heat equation on spheres. which can be characterized by examining the distribution of surface area. Based on 
this concept, we introduce a new roughness factor that considers the standard 
deviation of the surface area distribution in addition to its mean value. This 
approach is particularly effective for modeling the shear stress experienced by the 
foam during flow. By incorporating the standard deviation of the surface area 
distribution, our model demonstrates improved accuracy in predicting the shear 
stress, particularly at high shear rates. Furthermore, we observe that the 
distribution of surface area evolves over time, even in the absence of external 
forces, and its changes can be described by a diffusion-like equation. This 
diffusion process affects the shear stress experienced by the foam and influences 
its structural evolution. Our findings are supported by experimental data and 
provide a theoretical basis for understanding the flow behavior of liquid foams. 
Our model has been tested using ultrasound velocity measurements and images of 
bubbles from X-ray tomography. Our study offers insights into the dynamics of 
liquid foams and highlights the importance of considering the distribution of

Deep convolutional neural networks have achieved superior performance in various image classification tasks, but their high complexity and limited interpretability have hindered their practical applications. Ensemble-based deep models have been found to balance precision and simplicity by enhancing the classification capabilities of individual networks. This paper introduces a novel ensemble framework called Ensemble Residual, which leverages a specially designed residual unit to create a diverse set of networks with enhanced features for classification. Unlike conventional ensemble methods that combine deep networks, Ensemble Residual employs a shallow network to achieve state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets by exploiting a valuable property of residual units. The results indicate that the ensemble network exhibits a linear relationship with the sum of individual networks, enabling the identification of the dominant networks and the removal of less contributory ones to achieve further performance improvement. This approach also facilitates the selection of optimal networks for a particular classification task, demonstrating the versatility and adaptability of Ensemble Residual. Our code is publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/zhengyong-yu/ER-Net}. This research has been accepted for publication at the IEEE/CVF CVPR 2024 conference.

This approach examines the impact of future context on the current attention weights and uses this information to direct the attention towards more significant elements of the target sentence. In our experiments using the WMT datasets for English-German and English-French translation, look-ahead attention demonstrated substantial gains in performance. A grid computing system can be effectively developed and utilized by applying a translational approach, which bridges the gap between technical advancements and practical uses through iterative feedback. This approach enables the evaluation and refinement of the system based on real-world experiences and observations. Consequently, the system's technical aspects evolve in tandem with the solutions it provides to societal problems. By taking this perspective, we can reframe the history of the grid computing project as an illustration of this translational process. It began with a focus on making the internet a global, distributed computing resource and has since transformed into the infrastructure for the Amazon Mechanical Turk workforce segmentation platform. This evolution serves as a prime example of how a grid computing system adapts to new requirements and purposes through a cycle of experimentation, innovation, and feedback. Ultimately, this experience highlights the potential benefits and limitations of applying a translational approach to complex technological systems. It also provides insights into the development of future grid computing platforms that leverage the participation of ordinary people, as seen in current crowdsourcing practices. Such platforms can be realized by reconfiguring existing system architectures to prioritize the engagement of large numbers of individuals with varying levels of technical expertise. This is particularly crucial for solving problems that require the collective input of many people, such as managing large datasets and resolving complex social dilemmas. By embracing this approach, we can harness the power of crowds to fuel the advancement of grid computing technologies and, in turn, make these technologies more accessible to the crowds that drive their development. This cycle of co-evolution will be critical for addressing the challenges posed by massive, open online courses and other large-scale educational initiatives that rely heavily on citizen participation in the development of their own learning environments. This phenomenon is already evident in the growth of Wikipedia and other collaborative knowledge-sharing platforms. As a result, future grid computing platforms must be designed with the ability to manage diverse, distributed knowledge bases and facilitate the participation of diverse crowds in their development and application. This will enable these systems to adapt to the changing needs of society and the evolving requirements of crowds, thereby ensuring their continued relevance and effectiveness in addressing complex problems and advancing knowledge and learning. Current limits on dark matter-nucleon scattering cross sections, derived from $J/\psi$ decay data, are found to be more stringent than existing limits, with cross section limits of $1.4 \times 10^{-2}$ and $3.1 \times 10^{-3}$ barns for dark matter masses 1.5 GeV and 3.5 GeV, respectively. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a single learned dynamics model can lead to a significant negative impact, causing the agent to become stuck in a suboptimal policy due to the model's limited applicability and resulting instability. This issue arises because the agent optimizes the dynamics model to match the transition probabilities generated by its own actions, causing it to prioritize the most frequent experiences over rare but crucial ones, leading to a biased model that is unstable in unfamiliar situations. To address this challenge, we introduce a new method called Priorized Dynamics Learning with Regularization (PDLR), which incorporates a regularization technique to prevent overfitting to the most common experiences and promotes the dynamics model to capture the underlying structure of the unobserved states and actions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in various complex scenarios, including a multi-stage decision-making process and a high-dimensional gridworld environment, and show that PDLR significantly outperforms multiple baselines in terms of cumulative rewards. We introduce a novel regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which we've termed RCWGAN, to efficiently produce synthetic posterior samples under partial information conditions. Our model, characterized by a straightforward optimization problem, involves two primary components: a standard WGAN with an optimized regularizer to ensure the diversity of generated samples. Theoretical performance guarantees for RCWGAN are established, demonstrating its superior sampling capabilities compared to standard GANs. Furthermore, we derive an explicit lower bound for the expected posterior density of generated samples, thereby providing a quantitative measure of sample authenticity. To validate the efficacy of our proposed method, we conduct comprehensive experiments in both low-dimensional and high-dimensional settings, demonstrating notable performance gains over existing GAN-based sampling techniques. Our code is available online at: \url{https://github.com/zhengyiliu/RCWGAN}.

Observations of the millisecond pulsar PSR B1133+16 have revealed 18 distinct scattering screens around the pulsar, at a distance of approximately 1.9 billion light-years from Earth. The data, spanning over 2 years with the radio telescope in Arecibo, measure the timescales of variations in the pulsar signal and the orientation of the polarization plane. The wide separation of the screens suggests that the scattering medium is intergalactic, and we estimate the density of the medium to be significantly lower than expected based on local observations. The absence of screen motion over time, as expected from Einstein's theory of general relativity, may indicate that the scattering medium is not associated with the Milky Way galaxy. The detailed analysis of the pulsar signal and the polarization plane allows for precise measurements of the pulsar's characteristics, including its rotation axis orientation and the properties of its neutron star wind. The study also sheds light on the distribution of free electrons in the vicinity of the pulsar. The research highlights the potential of observing scattering effects around pulsars and suggests that future telescopes with higher sensitivity and better frequency coverage may reveal more detailed information about the environment of these distant objects. The data and analysis tools used in this study are available online. The observations of PSR B1133+16 also demonstrate the value of long-term, multi-frequency observations of pulsars and provide a foundation for further investigation into the properties of this particular pulsar and the scattering environment of the galaxy. The study's findings are consistent with previous observations of this pulsar, made over a decade ago with the Arecibo telescope. We introduce a concept called THH shadows, which extends topological Hochschild homology to bicategorical settings and reveals its connection to the topological cyclic homology of bicategorical algebras. This leads to a natural interpretation of the negative cyclic cone of bicategorical functors, and its resulting THH can be used to derive fundamental properties of bicategorical algebras under assumptions similar to those found in the classical framework. This framework allows us to generalize results about THH and the connection between THH and TCT in the bicategorical context. Additionally, we demonstrate how to apply these findings to specific examples of bicategories, including the one related to topological K-theory of spaces with local systems. This yields an alternative formulation of the negative THH of the bicategorical algebra associated with a space and its local system, and shows that this is equivalent to the THH of the algebra associated with the space alone. This has implications for the relationship between THH and TCT in this setting. This research is inspired by the work of Thomas Kragh and John R. Klein on the topic of THH of bicategorical algebras. This study introduces the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), a model that performs graph representation learning within the framework of Lorentzian manifolds and hyperbolic geometry. LGCN is demonstrated to be a more efficient model than current hyperbolic GCNs in terms of node feature representation, and its performance can be comparable to that of spherical GCNs. Furthermore, a novel Lorentzian graph convolutional layer is proposed, and the model's effectiveness is shown through applications in node classification and molecular property prediction. Evaluations using existing hyperbolic GCNs as baselines reveal that Lorentzian GCNs achieve improved results in both tasks. Additionally, the model's parameters can be analytically regularized, enabling the direct optimization of the model's complexity through gradient descent. This approach facilitates the exploration of the model's complexity space without incurring additional training costs. Relevant code can be found at https://github.com/zhengyong-yu/LGCN.

This research focuses on solving an inverse problem identifying a boundary control function that achieves a specific distribution of heat within a given time frame in an enclosed space. The problem is formulated as minimizing the difference between an unknown temperature function and a desired target in a given space, over a specific time period. The chapter's results are demonstrated to hold under the assumption of smooth boundary controls. The chapter's methodology can be applied to various types of enclosed spaces, including three-dimensional domains. In a linearized gravity theory, we investigate how adding a mass term to gravitational perturbations affects the included degrees of freedom. To achieve this, we adopt a Hamiltonian formulation within a Hamiltonian constraint algebra approach. Initially, a Hamiltonian formulation of a linearized gravity theory is established using a Hamiltonian constraint algebra that includes a Hamiltonian for the gravitational part and a Hamiltonian for matter. We then develop a Hamiltonian formulation for a linearized gravity theory with a mass term for gravitational perturbations in both $3+1$ and $d+1$ dimensions. Furthermore, we examine the Hamiltonian formulation in both $3+1$ and $d+1$ dimensions in the presence of a mass term for gravitational perturbations and find that the Hamiltonian for the gravitational part is replaced by two separate Hamiltonians for tensor and scalar parts of gravitational perturbations in both $3+1$ and $d+1$ dimensions. Additionally, we observe that the mass term leads to an unwanted degree of freedom in linearized gravity theory, resulting from the generation of a scalar part of gravitational perturbations from the original tensor part. This finding is consistent with previous results obtained through other approaches. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Hamiltonian constraint algebra remains first-class even after including a mass term for gravitational perturbations in both $3+1$ and $d+1$ dimensions. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for linearized gravity theory in the presence of a mass term for gravitational perturbations within the Hamiltonian constraint algebra approach. This work lays the groundwork for further investigation into linearized gravity theory in the presence of a mass term for gravitational perturbations within the Hamiltonian constraint algebra approach. This research can be applied to various contexts, including Brans-Dicke theory and massive gravities. This work is relevant to the study of massive gravities and Brans-Dicke theory within the Hamiltonian constraint algebra approach. This paper was originally published in the journal Physical Review D, and it has been established that the Hamiltonian constraint algebra approach can be applied to both $3+1$ and $d+1$ dimensions. This work demonstrates that the Hamiltonian constraint algebra approach can be utilized in both $3+1$ and $d+1$ dimensions, and it provides the underlying framework for examining the Hamiltonian constraint algebra in both $3+1$ and $d+1$ dimensions. We examine the relationship between Hamiltonian dynamics and quantum equilibrium states within the Gelfand-Naimark-Segal (GNS) framework. Following the GNS construction, we identify four fundamental equilibrium state quantum probabilities through the covariance equation, and then establish that all equilibrium states can be obtained by applying Hamiltonian dynamics to these basic states. This analysis is performed within the context of quantum lattice systems, specifically for both finite- and infinite-dimensional lattices. Additionally, we provide a detailed exploration of the properties of these basic equilibrium state quantum probabilities, including their characterization through the covariance equation and their relation to the canonical anti-automorphism of the quantum algebra. Furthermore, we discuss the concept of quantum symmetries and their connection to the Hamiltonian dynamics of quantum systems. A key finding is that the covariance equation itself is sufficient to guarantee the existence of quantum symmetries, without the need for the assumption of faithful representation of the quantum algebra. This research builds upon the earlier work of Raggio and Seeger, as well as the findings of Brannen and Seeger, and provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the interplay between Hamiltonian dynamics, quantum symmetries, and equilibrium states within the GNS framework. This work also introduces a novel definition of quantum equilibrium state covariance, which is shown to be equivalent to the covariance of the corresponding GNS representation. This research has implications for the study of quantum thermodynamics and its connection to the underlying classical thermodynamics. This study also reveals that the mean sector of the GNS representation contains all the information necessary to determine the classical thermodynamics associated with a given quantum system. This research further highlights the significance of the mean sector in the GNS representation, which is shown to be invariant under Hamiltonian dynamics. This invariance property of the mean sector is demonstrated to be equivalent to the covariance of the GNS representation, which in turn is shown to be a necessary condition for the validity of quantum Jarzynski equality. A quantum system with a negative temperature can be visualized using a two-level system analogy, where a spinning top serves as a metaphor for this concept. We examine how this theoretical model behaves under various conditions and constraints, specifically in a classical and quantized magnetic field setting. Numerical simulations demonstrate the onset of a negative temperature in the two-level system, along with the effects of its duration and intensity. Furthermore, we explore the application of this model to describe phonon decay and provide numerical evidence for the existence of negative temperature in phonon populations. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between this model and previous studies of a spinning top, as well as its connection to recent experimental findings involving a negative temperature in phonon populations resulting from a spinning top precession.

We've developed a beyond-Hubble approach to address the cosmological consistency of dark parity symmetry within a type of leptonic Seesaw models, incorporating a minimal dark sector. This framework involves a two-step process where we first examine the impact of the dark sector on the stability of the vacuum and the consistency of dark parity symmetry, and then explore the effects on the neutrino sector. We've discovered that the incorporation of a minimal dark sector alters the vanishing of the neutrino masses to an extremely small value, approximately 10^-60 GeV, and results in a very short lifetime for one of the dark scalar fields. This leads to either the scalar field's decay causing the dark sector to dominate the universe before the end of inflation or the scalar field's rapid decay making its lifetime too brief to influence neutrino mass generation. We've also identified that the dark sector's influence gives rise to a type of lepton number symmetry that restricts the neutrino mass matrix to a specific form, leading to a nearly massless neutrino and a nearly dark parity symmetric dark sector. This framework predicts the existence of a dark scalar with a mass in the range of 10^-3 to 10^-2 TeV, and we propose that this scalar could be detectable through high-energy lepton colliders or future dark matter experiments. This approach also offers a new perspective on the cosmological consistency of dark parity symmetry, revealing that the failure of this symmetry at the vacuum level is insufficient to guarantee its cosmological validity. This research further highlights the significance of considering the impact of the universe's large-scale structure on particle physics theories and highlights the potential for future high-energy particle colliders to uncover evidence of a dark scalar that could shed light on the cosmological consistency of dark parity symmetry. The interplay between spin-orbit coupling, crystal field splitting, and electron correlations in transition metal oxides is crucial for determining material properties. Theoretical modeling of these systems often relies on a single-band Hubbard model, where essential physics is captured by a single energy level at the Fermi level, but loses information about the strength of effective spin-orbit coupling. We have developed a Hubbard model with spin-orbit coupling, applicable to $d^1$ systems, which allows us to express its parameters in terms of material-specific quantities, including crystal field splitting and spin-orbit coupling. As a result, we can study the behavior of materials like TiO and VO by adjusting the Hubbard model's parameters to match each material's unique characteristics. Using this approach, we investigated the topological nature of zero-energy Kondo resonance states in these systems. Interestingly, we found that the $s$-wave symmetry of these states, observed in experiments, results from a combination of spin-orbit coupling, crystal field splitting, and electron correlations, rather than symmetry of the underlying crystal structure. Our findings also revealed that the topological nature of these states depends on the effective spin-orbit coupling strength, and we identified regions in the parameter space where materials can exhibit non-trivial topology and zero-energy Fano resonance states. Our work highlights the significance of considering spin-orbit coupling and crystal field effects in transition metal oxides and provides a theoretical basis for searching for materials with zero-energy Fano resonance states. We propose a method to enhance generative adversarial networks (GANs) for medical image representations by incorporating safety and fairness constraints into their training. Our approach, known as Adversarial Fair Representations for medical Imaging through Latent Code manipulation (AFRICI), introduces an additional adversarial encoder that generates a virtual patient by perturbing the latent code of an actual patient, with the aim of representing both actual and virtual patients as medically authentic and typical individuals. This encourages the model to produce representations that are both free from bias and robust to code manipulation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AFRICI in improving the fairness of abdominal image representations by conducting a human-based study in which subjects classify medical images based on their contents, and show that AFRICI significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art approach in terms of both accuracy and the time it takes to classify images accurately. Furthermore, AFRICI yields a model that generalizes well to new datasets, as validated through an image classification task using both ChestX-ray14 and LIDC-IDRI datasets. Our code is publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/zhengyiwang/AFRICI}. 

The code can be found at: https://github.com/zhengyiwang/AFRICI. 

Highlight 1:  AFRICI is the first GAN-based approach that integrates fairness constraints into the training process to improve the medical image representations. 

Highlight 2:  AFRICI's fairness constraint is designed to prevent biased representations by ensuring that a model-generated, perturbed version of an image is represented in the same way as the original image. 

Highlight 3:  AFRICI's safety constraint prevents a model from representing an image as both authentic and abnormal at the same time. 

Highlight 4:  AFRICI outperforms the current state-of-the-art approach in terms of classification accuracy and reduces the time it takes to classify medical images accurately in a human-based study.

ViDaExpert is a user-friendly tool designed to facilitate the visualization and
examination of high-dimensional data. It offers a range of graphical displays that
can be combined to effectively present multidimensional information. A key feature
of ViDaExpert is its ability to create a hierarchical structure of the data, as
indicated by a decision tree, and a neighboring region around a point of interest.
These capabilities make ViDaExpert particularly suitable for exploring and
visualizing data associated with complex decision-making processes. The system's
hierarchical visualization capabilities can be employed in various contexts, such
as in the examination of a decision tree, around a leaf node, and in the display
of nearest neighbors within a specified distance. ViDaExpert is also an interactive
system that allows users to click on specific data points to view their neighboring
information. The system's features can be applied to different types of data,
including both continuous and categorical information. The system's source code
is available for public use. The paper that follows provides an overview of the
ViDaExpert system and its underlying concepts, in addition to presenting the
methodology and results of a user study that examined users' perceptions of the
system's effectiveness in visualizing complex data. The study involved 30 participants
who were presented with various types of data sets, each containing different
levels of complexity, and were asked to evaluate the system's ability to make
these data sets understandable. The study revealed that the majority of participants
found the system to be highly effective in presenting complex data, and that
they were able to make the data sets presented to them understandable in a significantly
shorter period of time compared to other visualization methods. The study
also gathered participants' feedback on the system, which included suggestions
for improving the system's layout and the way it displays data. The paper
that follows also includes a discussion of the system's limitations, in addition
to presenting the results of the user study. The study was conducted in collaboration
with the Italian National Research Council. The system's source code is available
at the address http://vaidaexpert.sourceforge.net/. The paper that follows
is an expanded version of the paper that was presented at the IASTED Conference
on Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, which was held in Gaborone, Botswana
in July 2007. The system's initial version was presented at the IASTED Conference
on Knowledge and Knowledge Based Systems, which was held in Woslaw, Poland
